EN 301 549 — C.9.1.3.1 (SC 1.3.1)

C.9.1.3.1 — SC 1.3.1 Info and relationships
C.9.1.3.1       Info and relationships
   Type of assessment                                         Inspection
   Requirement          1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.
   Preconditions
   Procedure            1. Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1 Info and
                        Relationships according to WCAG Conformance Requirements stated in clause 9.6.
   Result               Pass: Check 1 is true
                        Fail: Check 1 is false
                        Not applicable: If any requirement precondition is false or the web page does not
                        contain content relevant to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships.
                        (Do not need to meet or test)

Trusted Tester — SC 1.3.1

SC 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A) — TT Tests 5.C, 10.B, 10.C, 10.D, 14.A, 14.B, 14.C

TT sections: 5. Forms, 10. Content Structure, 14. Tables · Baselines: 10/13/12/18

WCAG SC 1.3.1: Information, structure, and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically

determined or are available in text.

1.3.1 is TT's most-distributed SC: programmatic form labels (5.C), heading determinability + level (10.B/10.C),

list type (10.D), and data/layout table structure (14.A/14.B/14.C).

---

Test 5.C — 1.3.1-programmatic-label (Forms)

Test Condition: *The combination of the accessible name, accessible description, and other programmatic

associations (e.g., table column and/or row associations) describes each input field and includes all relevant

instructions and cues (textual and graphical).*

DNA if the page does not have form elements. *(Also covers 4.1.2 — see sc-4.1.2-name-role-value.md.)*

How to Test

1. Launch ANDI: focusable elements (default selection).

2. Use ANDI's next/previous element buttons to highlight each focusable form element and review the ANDI output.

3. Review the ANDI Output for each focusable form field.

4. If the ANDI Output does not adequately define the form element, review other programmatic associations

(table headings, location in a hierarchical list structure) to determine whether they provide/contribute to

the form component's description, cues, or instructions.

  • a. Where the purpose is intentionally vague/ambiguous (e.g., "Door 1/2/3" surprise), the combination may

refer to its purpose vaguely.

Evaluate Results (PASS if ANY true)

1. ANDI Output includes all relevant instructions and cues for the form element, including when fields are

required, OR

2. Descriptive labels and cues are provided by other programmatic associations (e.g., table column/row), OR

3. A combination of ANDI Output AND other programmatic association includes all relevant instructions and cues, OR

4. The combination of the programmatically determined form element context and the ANDI Output provide adequate

description of its purpose.

Notes
  • Also covers WCAG SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value.
  • At minimum, radio buttons and checkboxes should be programmatically associated with their question and

response.

  • Form fields are not required to have programmatic associations with form section headings unless there is

significant risk of confusion.

---

Test 10.A → see sc-2.4.6-headings-and-labels.md (heading purpose is 2.4.6, not 1.3.1)

Test 10.B — 1.3.1-heading-determinable (Content Structure → Headings)

Test Condition: *Each programmatically determinable heading is a visual heading and each visual heading is

programmatically determinable.*

DNA if the page has no programmatic headings identified by ANDI and has no visual headings.

Identify Content

1. Identify all visually apparent headings (often larger/bolded font, extra spacing — though not always).

Note the hierarchy/structure of each heading relative to others.

2. Use ANDI: structures → "headings" button to identify all programmatically defined headings

(<h1>–<h6> or role="heading"). ANDI adds dotted outlines around each identified, visible heading.

How to Test

1. Select ANDI: structures, review ANDI Output for each visually apparent heading. ANDI outlines all headings

with a dotted purple line. If ANDI does not identify a visually apparent heading → not defined programmatically.

2. Review each heading identified by ANDI to determine if it is also a visually apparent heading.

3. Review the ANDI Output for each heading to determine if it matches the visual heading. If they do not match →

the heading is not properly defined programmatically.

Evaluate Results (PASS if ALL true)

1. Each programmatically determinable heading is serving as a visual heading on the page, AND

2. Each visual heading is programmatically defined.

> *Note:* content that is not a visual heading should not have a role of heading (e.g., don't use heading markup

> for emphasis). Conversely, content styled and functioning like a heading should be programmatically a heading.

---

Test 10.C — 1.3.1-heading-level (Content Structure → Headings)

Test Condition: *Programmatic heading levels logically match the visual heading presentation within the

heading structure.*

DNA if programmatic headings are not identified by ANDI.

How to Test

1. Launch ANDI: structures → "view headings list" to display the Structure Outline.

2. Mouse over or tab through each heading in ANDI's Structure Outline to review the ANDI Output for each heading.

  • a. If ANDI identifies **heading level conflicts between aria and HTML markup, the aria heading levels take

precedence**. Continue using the aria heading levels.

3. Compare the heading levels in the Structure Outline to the page content. Determine whether the heading levels

logically match the visual heading presentation within the heading structure.

  • a. On pages with only one heading, that heading can have any level.
  • b. The most important heading(s) should have the highest priority level (h1 > h2 > h3).
  • c. Headings with an equal or higher level start a new section; lower-level headings start subsections.
  • d. A heading level 1: is not required, can be used more than once, is not required to match the page title.
  • e. Heading levels may not always be in sequence but may be valid as related to the visual

structure/importance (e.g., an <h2> for a nav structure preceding an <h1> title; <h3> then <h5>

without <h4> can be acceptable).

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. Every programmatically identified heading level logically matches the visual heading structure on the page.

---

Test 10.D — 1.3.1-list-type (Content Structure → Lists)

Test Condition: *All visually apparent lists are programmatically identified according to their type.*

DNA if there are no visually apparent lists. Exclude navigational framework elements unless they appear

as numbered or bulleted lists.

Identify Content

Identify all visually apparent lists, especially in the main content area.

  • This test applies to visually apparent lists, NOT programmatic lists identified by ANDI. **ANDI should NOT

be used to identify lists to be tested** — only to evaluate whether visually apparent lists are properly coded.

  • Menus/navigation framework elements should normally be excluded (even if coded as lists with bullets

removed), unless they appear as numbered or bulleted lists.

How to Test

1. Launch ANDI: structures → "lists" button.

2. For each visually apparent list, review "List Elements" to confirm it is coded correctly as ordered,

unordered, or description list.

  • Ordered (ol) — numbered sequentially / hierarchically (1, 2, 2.a, 2.a.i) where sequence or

reference-by-number matters.

  • Unordered (ul) — not numbered; sequence/reference not important.
  • Description list (dl) — groups terms with their descriptions.

3. Review the visual representation of list relationships (order, hierarchy, nesting) vs the programmatic list

definitions in ANDI. ANDI identifies each nested list separately ("Inspect Next Element").

Evaluate Results (PASS if ALL true)

1. All content with the visual appearance of a list is defined programmatically as a list, by type:

a. Unordered list (with/without bullets) → ul; b. Ordered list → ol; c. Terms+descriptions → dl.

AND

2. All programmatic list relationships (nesting, hierarchies) are consistent with the list relationships

presented visually.

> *Note:* Not all lists require markup — a list of items in a sentence separated by commas need not be a

> bulleted/numbered list.

---

Test 14.A — 1.3.1-table-identification (Tables → Data Tables)

Test Condition: *Each data table has programmatic markup to identify it as a table.*

DNA if there are no data tables on the page.

Identify Content

Identify all data tables (including images of data tables) where data cell(s) require header(s) for

understanding. Use ANDI: structures → "reading order" to assist. EXCLUDE content that does not require a

row/column header for understanding (layout tables; CSS-presented content sensible in reading order).

How to Test

1. Launch ANDI: tables. Determine whether ANDI detects and identifies the data table(s). ANDI identifies any

non-hidden tables coded using <table>, role="table", or role="grid".

  • i. If the tables module is not in the selection list, ANDI detected no programmatic table.
  • ii. Use "Analyze Next Table" to sequentially highlight detected tables. If the table is not outlined / not

navigable in ANDI → not detected programmatically.

2. Review any data tables that use role="presentation" (ANDI shows it in Element info / Accessibility Alerts).

A data table with role="presentation" will not convey table semantics and fails this test.

3. ANDI displays an alert whenever role="table" is not coded correctly.

4. Use Analyze Previous/Next Table to navigate to each identified table.

Evaluate Results (PASS if ALL true)

1. It is possible to navigate in ANDI: tables to each data table, AND

2. The data table does NOT have an ARIA role="presentation" assigned, AND

3. The data table does NOT have any ANDI Table alerts for incorrect use of ARIA table attributes.

---

Test 14.B — 1.3.1-cell-header-association (Tables → Data Tables)

Test Condition: *All data cells are programmatically associated with relevant headers.*

DNA if there are no data tables on the page.

How to Test

1. Continue from Test 14.A.

2. Navigate to each data cell with ANDI: tables.

3. Inspect the ANDI Output for each data cell and/or the visual highlighting to determine whether the table

identifies all relevant headers for each data cell.

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. The data table appropriately identifies header relationships for each data cell.

---

Test 14.C — 1.3.1-layout-table-structure (Tables → Layout Tables)

Test Condition: *The layout table DOES NOT designate the layout table using ARIA role="table" AND DOES NOT

include table header structure and relationship elements and/or associated attributes.*

DNA if there are no layout tables on the page.

Identify Content

Identify any programmatic tables where the table structure is used purely for layout purposes.

EXCLUDE data tables. Content within a layout table does not require row/column headers and should be sensible

when read in the ANDI reading order.

How to Test

1. Continue from Test 14.A.

2. Inspect the "Element" output in ANDI to determine whether the layout uses role="table".

3. Inspect the ANDI output and any associated alerts to determine whether a <table> includes header structure

elements/attributes (e.g., <th>, scope="row").

  • a. If a table has role="presentation" and also denotes header relationships (e.g., <th scope="row">),

ANDI provides an alert; ignore this alert on a layout table (presentation role suppresses semantics).

Evaluate Results (PASS if ANY true)

1. ANDI does NOT detect the layout as a table, OR

2. The <table> element includes role="presentation", OR

3. BOTH: the layout does NOT use role="table"/associated ARIA table attributes AND does NOT include table

structure/relationship elements or attributes (e.g., <th>, scope="row").

Act-augmented aspect — Visual-only headings: text styled to look like a heading but marked up as plain p/div/span (F2)

Text styled to look like a section heading is coded as a plain paragraph or div, so a screen-reader user can't jump between sections or locate them.

A block of text is visually presented as a section heading — larger, bold, distinct font/spacing, set off from surrounding paragraphs so a sighted reader unambiguously perceives it as the title of the section that follows — but it is marked up as a <p>, <div>, or <span> (often with a class like 'title' or 'heading1') with no <h1>-<h6> and no role=heading. The relationship 'this text labels the following section' is conveyed entirely through presentation and is lost programmatically. Correctly judging this requires (a) recognizing visually that the text functions as a heading and (b) deciding that the content beneath is a distinct section it titles — neither is in the DOM. This is the canonical F2 failure and the Trusted Tester 10.B condition 'each visual heading is programmatically determinable.' Includes the mixed case where some sub-section labels are real headings and some are styled <div>s (partial failure).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT 1.3.1 corpus tests headings ONLY through ARIA required-property mechanics (4e8ab6: role=heading must carry aria-level). Every heading fixture already has role=heading or an h1-h6; none presents text that LOOKS like a heading to the eye but carries no heading semantics. No fixture's correct verdict depends on comparing rendered visual weight against the absence of heading markup, and a static checker cannot decide that bold large text 'is' a heading.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.1 · Trusted Tester 10.B · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Genuine data tables whose header/structure semantics are absent or stripped: all-<td> tables, and real data tables with role=presentation (F91, F92)

A real data table lacks proper header cells (or hides them), so a screen reader reads bare numbers with no row or column labels for a blind user.

A genuine data table — content where cells are only intelligible via their row/column headers — fails to expose those relationships. Two mechanisms: (1) F91, the table presents headers visually (a bold first row, a labeled first column) but every cell is a plain <td> with no <th>, scope, headers/id, or role=columnheader/rowheader, so a screen reader announces bare values with no context; (2) F92, a structurally correct data table (or list, or heading) carries role=presentation/role=none, deliberately suppressing its semantics from the a11y tree. Both require the human judgments: is this content actually a data table whose cells need headers, and which row/column visually functions as the header? A checker sees either zero header cells (F91 -> rules inapplicable) or a deliberately suppressed tree (F92 -> excluded from scope).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT's table rules (a25f45, d0f69e) require a <th> or role=columnheader/rowheader to even be applicable — a table built entirely of <td> returns inapplicable from both, so F91 is silently out of scope. For F92, ACT treats role=presentation / aria-hidden purely as an INAPPLICABILITY trigger (element removed from a11y tree -> structural rule doesn't apply); the corpus therefore uses presentation-role only to exclude elements, never as the failure itself, and never contains a real data table marked role=presentation that should FAIL. Distinguishing 'correctly suppressed layout content' from 'wrongly suppressed data table' is the omitted human judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.1 · Trusted Tester 14.A, 14.B · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Layout tables that falsely assert data-table relationships: th, caption, scope, or summary on a positioning-only table (F46)

A table used only to position page regions is dressed up with header-cell markup, so a screen reader falsely announces meaningless layout grids as real tabular data.

A table used purely to position page regions (nav | content | sidebar, or a hero/marketing layout) includes data-table semantic markup — a <th>, a <caption>, scope attributes, role=table, or a non-empty summary — which falsely tells AT that the layout grid is meaningful tabular data and that, e.g., 'Page Title' is the header for the nav/content/footer cells. The inverse of the suppression case: here genuine semantic markup is present and syntactically valid, but the relationship it asserts does not exist. Judging this requires recognizing the table is layout (no real row/column data relationship) AND that it nonetheless asserts header semantics. Automated tools see a structurally valid <th>/<caption> and pass; they cannot decide the table is 'really' layout (TT 14.C).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT table rules (a25f45, d0f69e) check the INTERNAL correctness of header references and that th cells have assigned cells — they assume the table IS a data table and verify the plumbing. No ACT rule asks 'is this a layout table that should not carry th/caption/summary at all?', so F46 (correct markup, wrong context) is wholly outside the corpus. The layout-vs-data distinction is precisely TT 14.C, a human determination a static checker cannot make.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.1 · Trusted Tester 14.C · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Valid structural elements asserting relationships that do not exist: heading/blockquote/fieldset used for visual effect (F43)

Real structural tags are used for looks not meaning (a heading just to enlarge text), so a screen reader announces relationships and an outline that don't really exist.

Genuine structural elements are present and syntactically valid, but they assert a content relationship that is false. An <h3>/<h4> makes an author byline or address big and bold (no new section begins), a <blockquote> wraps text that is not a quotation merely to indent it, or a <fieldset>/<legend> draws a decorative bordered box around prose that is not a group of form controls. Automated tools see a well-formed heading/blockquote/fieldset and pass; only a human reading the content can tell the asserted relationship is untrue. This is the Trusted Tester note 'don't use heading markup for emphasis' and F43's 'relationships that do not exist in the content.' It also fabricates a misleading heading outline (e.g. every ingredient as its own <h5>).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT rules check that structural elements are syntactically correct and carry required properties — never whether the relationship they assert is TRUE of the content. No fixture contains a structurally valid <h4>, <blockquote>, or <fieldset> whose correct verdict is FAIL because the element misrepresents its content. The corpus has no notion of 'valid markup, wrong meaning,' which is precisely the human semantic judgment this aspect needs.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.1 · Trusted Tester 10.B · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Visually apparent lists not programmatically identified as lists (or as the wrong type / lost nesting)

Content that visually reads as a bulleted, numbered, or definition list isn't coded as the right list type, so a screen reader skips announcing item counts and grouping.

Content that visually reads as a list — bulleted items, a numbered sequence, or term/description pairs — is not coded as a list of the correct type, or its nesting/hierarchy is flattened. Examples: a bulleted-looking sequence built from <br>-separated lines or styled <div>s instead of <ul>; a numbered step sequence (where order matters) coded as <ul> or plain paragraphs instead of <ol>; a glossary of terms+definitions coded as paragraphs instead of <dl>; a visually nested outline whose programmatic list flattens the sub-list grouping. Trusted Tester 10.D is explicitly driven by VISUALLY apparent lists, not by what markup happens to exist, and requires judging both 'is this visually a list' and 'is its type/nesting correct,' excluding navigation framework unless it appears as a numbered/bulleted list.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: There is NO ACT 1.3.1 rule for list determinability or list type in the corpus — the only list-adjacent ACT rules concern ARIA owned/context roles (bc4a75, ff89c9: a listbox must own options) and fire only when an explicit listbox/option role is already present. A bulleted-looking set of <div>s, an ordered procedure coded as <ul>, or a flattened nested list has no role for any rule to attach to. Deciding that content visually 'is a list,' which type, and whether nesting matches the visual hierarchy is human visual/semantic judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.1 · Trusted Tester 10.D · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Tabular or multi-column information faked with whitespace, line breaks, or <pre> instead of real structure (F34, F48, F33)

A table or columns are faked with spaces and line breaks instead of real markup, so it looks aligned but a screen reader reads across into scrambled gibberish.

Tabular or multi-column content is laid out using only spaces, tabs, line breaks, or a monospaced <pre> block, so it looks like a table or two parallel columns on screen but carries no row/column/header structure and linearizes into nonsense for AT ('Monday 2 fried eggs tomato soup garden salad'). The entire relationship lives in the visual alignment of characters. A human must recognize that the ASCII grid encodes a table (with implied row/column headers) or that text is split into parallel columns disrupting reading order; automated tools see a single text node and a syntactically valid <pre> with nothing to flag.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: These failures involve NO structural element for any rule to attach to — no <table>, <th>, <ul>, or role, just text. The entire ACT 1.3.1 corpus is element/attribute-anchored (ARIA props, header refs, owned roles), so a page whose only 'table' is whitespace-aligned text or a <pre> block is invisible to every rule. Interpreting an ASCII grid as a relationship-bearing table, or detecting that padded spaces split text into columns, is pure human visual/semantic reasoning.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.1 · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Scripted elements that look like links/buttons but expose a generic role or none (F42)

A clickable span or div is styled to look like a button but has no real link/button role, so a screen reader won't announce it as clickable.

An element is styled and behaves like a link or button (cursor:pointer, underlined blue text or a button-shaped box, onclick navigation/activation) but is a bare <span>, <div>, or <img> with a JavaScript handler and no <a>, no <button>, and no role=link/button. Sighted users perceive 'this is a link/button'; AT exposes a generic element (or, when tabindex is added, a focusable thing with no role), so the control relationship is not programmatically determinable. The judgment requires seeing that the element PRESENTS itself as a control and that its exposed role (generic, or absent) contradicts that presentation — a visual/behavioral call no attribute-anchored rule makes.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT 1.3.1 role rules (4e8ab6 required-properties, 674b10 valid-role-value) only fire when an explicit role IS present. A <span onclick> with no role attribute is simply outside their applicability, so the F42 failure never appears in the corpus. Judging that a styled <span>/<div> 'is presented as a link/button' from its appearance and behavior is exactly the human visual reasoning the static, attribute-driven corpus omits. (Note: this overlaps SC 4.1.2 but is an explicit F42 1.3.1 failure path.)

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.1 · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Form field/label and field-group relationships conveyed only by visual layout (programmatic association, grouping, required-cues)

A form's labels, instructions, required-marks, and field groups are tied to inputs only by visual placement, so a screen reader can't tell which text governs which field.

A form's field-to-label, field-to-instruction, and field-to-group relationships are conveyed only by visual placement and styling, not programmatically. Examples: a label sits visually next to/above an input but is not associated (no <label for>, no aria-labelledby, no wrapping), so AT cannot tell which text describes the field; a set of radio buttons or checkboxes answers a question shown as a visual heading above them with no <fieldset>/<legend> or role=radiogroup, so the group's question is lost; required-field status or a 'pick one' cue is shown only by red text or a visually adjacent note not programmatically tied to the field. Trusted Tester 5.C asks whether the combination of accessible name, description, and OTHER programmatic associations describes each field including instructions and cues, and notes radio/checkbox groups must be associated with their question — a contextual reading-and-layout judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT form rule in scope (e086e5) only checks that a form field has a NON-EMPTY accessible name — a binary presence test a static checker already does. It does not evaluate whether the RIGHT visible label/instruction is the one associated, whether a multi-field group (radios/checkboxes answering one question) is programmatically grouped, or whether a visually-conveyed required/'choose one' cue is tied to the field. Deciding which adjacent text functions as the label, and that several controls share a visually-shown group question, is contextual human judgment outside the corpus.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.1 · Trusted Tester 5.C · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Emphasis or special-status meaning conveyed only by visual text variation, with no markup or text equivalent (G117, H49)

Special status is shown only by bold, strike-through, or font change with no markup or words, so 'on sale' or 'deleted' is invisible to a screen-reader user.

Information is carried solely by a variation in text presentation — bold/italic/underline, a different font face or color, strike-through, larger size — with neither semantic markup (<strong>/<em>/<ins>/<del>) nor an equivalent stated in text. Examples: 'new' or 'on sale' items shown only by bold/red with no '(new)' word; deletions/insertions shown by strike-through/underline with no change list; a glossary term distinguished only by a different font; a warning shown only in red. WCAG explicitly excludes pure color (1.4.1), but bolding/italics/font/strike that convey status, emphasis, or special meaning fall under 1.3.1 (G117/H49): the relationship 'this text has special status' must be exposed via markup OR available in text. Judging which formatting carries meaning (vs decoration) and whether that meaning is otherwise available requires reading the content.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT 1.3.1 rule addresses emphasis or special-status text conveyed by presentation; the corpus is entirely about ARIA properties, roles, owned/context roles, table headers, and accessible-name presence. A page where 'sale' items are bold-only, or insertions are underlined with no markup/text equivalent, has nothing for any rule to evaluate. Deciding that a font/weight/strike variation CARRIES information (not mere decoration) and that the information is not otherwise stated in text is a human content-meaning judgment. (Pure-color cases are deliberately excluded as 1.4.1.)

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.1 · priority low

Trusted Tester — SC 1.3.2

SC 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence (Level A) — TT Test 15.A

TT section: 15. CSS Positioning · Baseline: 18. Stylesheet Non-dependence / CSS Content and Positioning

WCAG SC 1.3.2: When the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning, a correct reading

sequence can be programmatically determined.

Identify Content

Use ANDI to identify all content positioned with CSS and inline styles.

1. Launch ANDI → Advanced Settings → "linearize page" to remove CSS positioning from elements on the page.

2. If content is positioned with CSS, the information will display with blue highlighting around the elements and

those elements will be placed in the page in the same order in which they appear in the page code.

  • DNA for 15.A if there is no content positioned using CSS.

Test 15.A — 1.3.2-content-order-meaning-css-position

Test Condition: *The reading order of the content (in context) is correct and the meaning of the content (in

context) is preserved without CSS positioning.*

How to Test

1. Review all highlighted, linearized content.

2. Determine whether the reading order of content is still understandable after linearization. If necessary,

toggle the linearization button to view the original position of the content.

  • *If content becomes illegible due to overlapping, etc., this is NOT a failure of this test* — the test

verifies whether the programmatic reading order is understandable.

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. The sequence and meaning of the content (in context) is understandable without CSS positioning.

Note
  • ANDI: structures + "reading order" link can also reveal the reading order prior to linearizing, but it will

not identify which content has been positioned with CSS.

> Mechanism: this is the DOM-order-vs-visual-order check. The "reading order" / linearized DOM sequence must

> still make sense when CSS positioning is stripped. Equivalent to comparing DOM source order to visual layout.

Act-augmented aspect — CSS visual-vs-DOM reorder: judging whether the source-order read still preserves meaning (F1 FAIL vs Example-2 PASS)

CSS positions content in a different order than the HTML source, so a screen reader (which follows source order) reads it in a nonsensical sequence.

A page uses CSS (absolute/relative positioning, flexbox order, flex-direction:row-reverse, grid-area/grid-template-areas) so the visual order differs from DOM source order. A tool can mechanically detect 'visual order != DOM order', but that mismatch is ONLY a 1.3.2 failure when reading the content in source order changes the MEANING. The SC pairs the explicit non-failure (Example 2: nav / main / side-story CSS-reordered, meaning unaffected = PASS) directly against the failure (F1 Products/Locations two-column example, where source order reads 'Products Locations Telephones Computers Portable MP3 Players Wisconsin Idaho' and Wisconsin/Idaho bind to the wrong column = FAIL). Note the F1 trap: source order has item5 (Wisconsin) BEFORE item4 (Idaho), so values are swapped even within one logical column — purely semantic, invisible to a DOM-diff tool. The evaluator must linearize the content, read it as prose, and decide whether it still parses as the intended meaning. This is the central, most-tested discrimination of the SC.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The SC 1.3.2 inventory reports actRuleCount:0, testCaseCount:0 — there is literally zero ACT coverage of any facet of this SC. Even a hypothetical tool that flagged every visual!=DOM mismatch would fire on the Example-2 PASS case (nav reorder, meaning unaffected) as a false positive, and could not read the linearized text to confirm the F1 FAIL case actually scrambles meaning. Distinguishing FAIL from PASS is a semantic reading task, not a markup or DOM-diff check, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot reliably do it.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.2 · Trusted Tester 15.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Layout-table linearization that scrambles a meaningful sequence (F49) — reading 2-D content as a linear story

A layout table looks right as a grid, but read cell-by-cell it interleaves and shreds the text, so a screen-reader user hears a scrambled, meaningless sequence.

An HTML <table> used purely for layout (WCAG explicitly permits layout tables) presents content that reads correctly in two visual dimensions, but when linearized row-by-row, cell-by-cell, the meaningful sequence breaks. F49's two canonical cases: (1) the advertisement where a rowspan stitches 'XYZ mountaineering top!' into one line and separates it from 'XYZ gets you to the', destroying the slogan 'XYZ gets you to the top!'; (2) the museum page where left-column nav links are interleaved with the right-column image/placard/heading/description, so the description is shredded by Link 2, Link 3, Link 4... The evaluator must mentally linearize the cell reading order (first cell of first row to last cell of last row, reading nested cells fully) and judge whether the resulting prose still tells the same story — a semantic reading task over a 2-D structure.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; F49 is a failure technique only. Critically, axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do NOT flag layout tables as 1.3.2 failures — a layout table is valid HTML and WCAG permits it — so there is no automated signal. The failure lies entirely in whether the linearized cell order preserves meaning, which requires reading the cells in linearization order and reasoning about the story, something no automated checker does.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.2 · Trusted Tester 15.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — White space inserted within a word (F32): meaning-breaking spacing vs. carved-out initialisms / inter-word spacing

Letters of a single word are spaced apart for visual effect, so a screen reader reads it letter-by-letter rather than as the word it spells.

Authors space out the letters of a single word for visual effect ('W e l c o m e', 'H&nbsp;E&nbsp;L&nbsp;L&nbsp;O', tracked-out hero headings, vertical CJK via <br>). To AT this reads letter-by-letter or worse, changes meaning (Japanese '東 京' read 'Higashi Kyo' instead of 'Tokyo'; '東<br>京<br>都' read 'Higashi Kyo Miyako'). The hard part is F32's own explicit carve-outs: inserting white space into an INITIALISM is NOT a failure, and white space BETWEEN words is NOT a failure. So the evaluator must decide whether a spaced string is a real word being broken (FAIL) or an acronym / legitimate inter-word spacing (PASS) — a linguistic/semantic judgement; for CJK it additionally requires knowing the language to see that the reading (on'yomi/kun'yomi) changed.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; F32 is a failure technique only. A naive regex for single-letter-then-space patterns would mis-fire on legitimate initialisms ('F B I', 'U S A'), styled monograms, and inter-word spacing — exactly the cases F32 excludes — and could never detect the CJK meaning shift (the failure is a wrong reading, not a space-count). Telling break-the-word from harmless-spacing is the human-judgement core.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.2 · Trusted Tester 15.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Faked columns / faked tables in pre-formatted plain text (F33, F34): visual 2-D structure with zero DOM structure

Columns or a table are faked with spaces and line breaks inside preformatted text, so a screen reader reads straight across them and interleaves the parts into gibberish.

Content is laid out with literal space/tab/line-break characters inside a <pre>, <textarea>, code block, or monospaced <div>, faking multiple newspaper columns (F33) or a data table (F34, the Breakfast/Lunch/Dinner menu). Visually it looks like two columns or a grid; in the linear character stream a screen reader reads ACROSS the fake columns, interleaving them into gibberish (e.g. 'Web Content Accessibility Guidelines including blindness and low vision'). There is NO table/column markup at all — so the only signal is that the rendered visual implies a 2-D structure the linear character stream destroys. The evaluator must look at the rendering, recognize the implied columnar/tabular structure, then read the character stream and judge that the linear reading scrambles the meaning.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; F33/F34 are failure techniques only. Automated checkers have nothing structural to assert against — there is no <table>, no CSS columns, just a blob of text in <pre>/<textarea>. axe/WAVE see only text and cannot tell the whitespace encodes a visual grid whose linearization is nonsense. Recognizing the faked 2-D structure from the rendering and judging that the character stream scrambles meaning is inherently visual + semantic.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.2 · Trusted Tester 15.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Responsive-breakpoint source-vs-visual desync — order is meaningful at one viewport but reordered at another

At one screen size CSS reorders items (stacking wizard steps as 2,1,3 on mobile), so the visual order no longer matches the source order a screen reader reads.

A single self-contained page is correct in DOM source order at one width, but a media query reorders flex/grid items at another breakpoint such that the visual order no longer matches the meaningful source order — e.g. a 'Step 1 / Step 2 / Step 3' wizard whose mobile media query uses 'order:' to stack the steps 2,1,3; or an 'Editor's note: read the conclusion first' sidebar that on mobile collapses ABOVE the content it refers to, turning a closing note into a misleading lede. The failure exists only in one rendering state, so the evaluator must render at multiple viewports, recognize that the order is meaningful, and confirm that the visual order diverges from the meaningful source order at the breakpoint where meaning is order-dependent. (Distinct from the F1 single-viewport case: the failure is conditional on viewport and requires comparing rendered states.)

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2, and no failure technique names responsive 'order:' reflow specifically. Automated DOM-vs-visual diff tools typically run at a single viewport and have no notion that a breakpoint reorder changes meaning; they cannot judge whether the reordered sequence still parses, nor will they think to compare across breakpoints.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.2 · Trusted Tester 15.A · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Bidirectional / mixed-directionality text where the visual order is fixed by reordering characters, exposing the wrong order to AT (G57 bidi case)

In mixed left-to-right and right-to-left text, an author physically reorders characters to look right on screen, so a screen reader hears them in the wrong logical order.

A page mixes LTR and RTL scripts (English + Arabic/Hebrew/Persian, or numbers/punctuation embedded in RTL text). G57 names the precise failure: an author 'fixes' the visual rendering by physically moving characters in the content stream (e.g. relocating a trailing period or a price) so the Unicode bidi algorithm happens to position them correctly on screen — but this exposes the WRONG logical character order to AT. The correct fix is markup (dir, <bdi>, <bdo>) that overrides the bidi algorithm so the order is right both visually AND to AT, NOT reordering source characters. Conversely, omitting needed dir/bdi markup can leave the visual correct but the logical order scrambled when spoken. Detecting this requires reading both scripts, knowing their directionality, and judging whether the logical (source) order matches the visual.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; G57 is a general technique with no ACT rule/test. The failure is invisible to automated structural checkers: the markup may be well-formed and the visual rendering correct; only by reading both scripts and comparing logical-vs-visual order can one tell that source characters were reordered (exposing wrong order to AT) or that bidi markup was wrongly omitted. This requires multilingual semantic judgement no checker performs.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.2 · Trusted Tester 15.A · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Applicability gate and multiple-valid-orders: deciding whether order is meaningful at all, and that more than one order can be correct

Deciding when order even matters: two unrelated articles can appear in either order safely, so flagging a page just because blocks could be reordered would be wrong.

1.3.2 only applies 'when the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning,' and the Understanding adds three clarifications: providing a particular linear order is only required where it affects meaning; there may be more than one 'correct' order; only one correct order needs to be provided. Two independent non-interleaved articles, a nav-vs-main pairing, and a magazine article with callout sidebars can each appear in EITHER order without failing — the container has no meaningful sequence even though each article does. The evaluator must first decide whether order is meaningful for the content at hand (the applicability gate), and must NOT flag a page merely because its block order could be different, as long as no single block's internal meaning is broken. This is the discrimination that prevents over-flagging the whole SC.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2. Nothing in ACT tests the applicability gate — deciding whether order is meaningful at all — and no rule/test/technique exercises the multiple-valid-orders case. EN 301 549 frames C.9.1.3.2 as Inspection with a 'Not applicable... does not contain content relevant' clause, wholly absent from ACT. A checker cannot decide whether reordering two articles or a nav/main pair affects meaning; that is a contextual semantic judgement, and getting it wrong means false positives on perfectly conformant pages.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.3.2 · Trusted Tester 15.A · priority medium

C.9.1.4.1       Use of colour
   Type of assessment                                         Inspection
   Requirement          1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.

Trusted Tester — SC 1.4.1

SC 1.4.1 Use of Color (Level A) — TT Test 13.A

TT section: 13. Sensory Characteristics and Contrast → Use of Color · Baseline: 7. Sensory Characteristics

WCAG SC 1.4.1: Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action,

prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element.

Identify Content

Identify content that relies on color to convey meaning (indicate an action, prompt a response, distinguish a

visual element). Displaying content in grayscale may help identify content that uses only color to convey

information.

  • DNA for 13.A if no content relies on color to convey meaning.

Test 13.A — 1.4.1-color-meaning

Test Condition: *Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action,

prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element.*

How to Test

1. Determine whether color is the only visual method used to convey information (e.g., review the onscreen

text for a full description and/or look for other visual cues).

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. When color is used to convey information, indicate an action, prompt a response, or distinguish a visual

element, another visual, onscreen method is used to convey the information which does not use color.

Notes
  • Alternate text that appears on mouse-over of a visual element is not considered "onscreen text."
  • An error indicator cannot use color alone as an indicator.
  • It is considered a browser setting if a visited link changes color — this is not failed for 13.A.
  • (13.B / 1.3.3) Color is a type of sensory information and cannot be used in combination with another type of

sensory information alone to pass. (1.3.3 is out of our 22-SC scope but shares the section.)

> Classic failures (from our rubric's lens): F73 links distinguished only by color; F81 status/required/error

> conveyed only by color. The grayscale technique is the canonical detection method.

Act-augmented aspect — Inline links distinguished from body text by hue alone (no underline/weight/lightness), incl. hover/focus-only cues that don't rescue

Links inside paragraphs are shown only by a different color with no underline or bold, so a color-blind user can't tell which words are clickable links.

Links embedded in running text have their underline removed and are set in a color that differs from the surrounding body text by HUE only — there is no bold, italic, size, font-family change, and the link-vs-text lightness contrast is under 3:1. A sighted color-perceiving user can spot the links; a color-blind or grayscale user cannot tell them apart from prose. To flag this an evaluator must (a) recognize which colored spans are actually links (vs decorative emphasis) by reading the markup/meaning, (b) confirm hue is the ONLY differentiator, and (c) judge that any subtle non-color cue present (a faint weight bump, a serif/sans swap) is too weak to count. A critical sub-case: the only non-color cue is injected on :hover or :focus — F73 and G183 are explicit that a cue appearing only on hover/focus is STILL a failure because the resting state is color-only; detecting this requires comparing the resting render to the hover/focus render and applying the rule. This is the canonical 'distinguishing a visual element' failure and is the single most prevalent real-world 1.4.1 defect.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: There are 0 ACT rules and 0 test cases for 1.4.1, so this is entirely unexercised. axe/Lighthouse/WAVE have NO link-vs-surrounding-text contrast rule — their contrast checks measure foreground-vs-background per 1.4.3, not link-color-vs-adjacent-TEXT-color, and they treat an un-underlined colored <a> inside <p> as fine. Deciding whether a colored span is a real link vs decorative emphasis, whether a subtle non-color cue is 'enough', and whether a hover/focus-only cue rescues the resting state are all perceptual/contextual judgments no automated checker performs.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.1 · Trusted Tester 13.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Required form fields indicated by color alone, with self-referential or absent text instruction

A form marks required fields only by red color (and any instruction just says 'required fields are red'), so a color-blind user can't tell which are mandatory.

A form marks required fields by coloring their labels (e.g. red) or adding a colored border, with NO asterisk, no '(required)', no icon, and no per-field text cue. The trap that demands human judgment: there may be a general instruction at the top, but it is itself color-keyed ('Required fields are shown in red') — which is useless to someone who cannot perceive red, since it never lets them identify WHICH specific fields are required. An evaluator must (1) see that color is the only visual distinction between required and optional labels, (2) confirm no per-field non-color cue exists, and (3) judge whether any general instruction genuinely RESOLVES which fields are required for a color-blind user, rather than merely mentioning the color rule. 'Required fields are red' passes a literal text-present check yet still fails because the alternative is self-referentially color-dependent.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. Checkers may detect a missing required attribute (a separate 1.3.1/3.3.x concern that does NOT satisfy 1.4.1's VISIBLE-alternative requirement), but no automated rule judges whether the visible required-vs-optional distinction is color-only, nor whether a prose instruction effectively resolves the ambiguity for a color-blind user. The self-referential-instruction failure ('required fields are red' is itself color-keyed) is a pure semantic judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.1 · Trusted Tester 13.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Error / validation feedback conveyed by color alone (red border or red text only) in the post-submit state

After a failed submit, a wrong field is marked only by a red border or text, with no icon or message, so a color-blind user can't find it.

After a failed submit (or during inline validation), fields that failed are outlined or tinted red, or have their label turned red, with NO error icon, NO inline error message, and NO '(error)' marker — the only signal that THIS field is wrong is its hue. Per F81 and Trusted Tester, an error indicator cannot use color alone. An evaluator must reach/observe the dynamic post-validation state, notice the erroring field is distinguished from valid fields purely by color, and confirm no adjacent non-color error cue exists. This is the 'prompting a response' limb (highlighting a field to prompt correction). Crucially, programmatic exposure via aria-invalid does NOT satisfy 1.4.1, which requires a VISIBLE alternative for sighted color-blind users who are not using AT.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. The error state is dynamic (appears after a failed submit), beyond static-page scanners. Even with the state rendered, no automated rule classifies a red border/text as an error indicator (vs decoration) or verifies a non-color error cue exists. aria-invalid presence (4.1.2/3.3.1) is a different, programmatic concern that explicitly does NOT satisfy 1.4.1's visible-alternative requirement — a distinction only a human applying the AT-decoupling note makes.

Act-augmented aspect — Informational image/chart HAS a text alternative, but the alt restates the color RULE instead of resolving the color-encoded fact

A chart's alt text restates the color rule ('red bars are below quota') but never says which items those are, so a blind user misses the color-coded fact.

An informational bitmap or inline SVG (bar chart, line graph, status dashboard, map) uses color to encode a categorical fact, and it HAS a text alternative — but the alt/caption restates the data values and the color rule ('red bars indicate sales below quota') rather than RESOLVING it (naming WHICH employees fell below quota). Because the alt is present and plausible, an automated checker sees a satisfied alt attribute and passes; only a human who reads the alt against the picture sees that the color-borne distinction is never spelled out in text. This is the canonical F13 failure — 'alt exists but under-describes the color-encoded info'. It requires reading the chart pixels, reading the prose, and comparing meaning.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. Even where ACT touches alt text (1.1.1), rules only check alt presence/non-emptiness, never whether the alt CONTENT captures a color-encoded distinction inside the bitmap. Distinguishing 'red = below quota, so Mary and Bob failed' (resolved in alt) from 'red bars indicate below-quota sales' (color rule merely restated, names omitted) requires reading the chart, reading the prose, and comparing their meaning — pure semantic judgment no checker performs.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.1 · Trusted Tester 13.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Color-coded charts, maps, diagrams and game pieces distinguished by color with no pattern, icon, or in-graphic label (G111)

A chart, map, or diagram tells categories apart only by fill color with no patterns, shapes, or labels, so a color-blind user can't distinguish the routes or series.

Non-text graphics rely on solid color to distinguish categories — transit-map routes by color only, a bar/area chart whose series are told apart only by fill color matched to a color-only legend, a flow chart using green-background = pass / red-background = fail with no shape/label difference, an SVG diagram whose elements are identified by color with no number/legend pairing, or game pieces distinguished by color alone. Per G111 the fix is to ADD a pattern (hatching, dots, dashes), a distinct icon/shape, or an in-graphic text/number label so the same information survives without color. An evaluator must read the graphic, identify each color-coded category, and confirm no non-color visual encoding redundantly carries the same distinction. This differs from the F13-alt aspect: here the question is the in-graphic VISUAL encoding (pattern/shape), not whether a sibling alt text resolves it.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. No automated checker can render a chart/map/diagram, segment its color regions, and decide whether each color-coded category ALSO carries a pattern, icon, shape, or in-graphic label. Recognizing that a transit-line color or a chart-series fill is the SOLE distinguishing cue — and that the legend itself is color-keyed — is a visual-semantic judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.1 · Trusted Tester 13.A · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — UI buttons, controls, and color-coded categories signalling action/status by color with no text or character cue (G14)

A button or status uses color alone to mean go-versus-cancel or success-versus-error, with no distinguishing text, so a color-blind user can't tell which action it is.

Interactive UI conveys an action or a status by color alone with no redundant text/character cue: a green button = proceed / red button = cancel pair where the buttons are not labelled with distinguishing text and the only convention is 'green advances, red cancels'; a color that indicates a link opens in a new window or that a database entry updated successfully; color-coded list items, tabs, or schedule tracks distinguished only by background hue with no in-text code (T1/T2/T3). Per G14 the information conveyed by color differences must ALSO be conveyed explicitly in text (and per G205 the cue must be in the control's programmatic name). An evaluator must identify the action/status the color encodes, then confirm a non-color text/character cue redundantly carries it. This covers the 'indicating an action' limb that the link and form aspects do not.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. No automated checker can determine that a green-vs-red button pair encodes 'proceed vs cancel' purely by color, or that a category's background hue is the sole carrier of its track/status, and then verify a redundant text cue exists. Mapping a color to its intended action/status meaning and judging whether a text alternative carries the same information is contextual semantic reasoning.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.1 · Trusted Tester 13.A · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Scoping boundary cases: 3:1-lightness pass, pure-color reliance fails regardless of contrast, non-applicability, and visited-link exemption

Borderline color cases a naive 'any color use fails' rule gets wrong: enough lightness difference passes, hue-dependent meaning fails even at high contrast, and visited-link color is exempt.

1.4.1 has several boundary rules that produce PASS/NOT-APPLICABLE verdicts an over-eager evaluator (or a naive 'any color cue fails' heuristic) would get wrong, and one that produces a FAIL a contrast-only check would miss. (a) 3:1 LIGHTNESS ESCAPE HATCH: colors differing in lightness with a >=3:1 contrast ratio between them count as an additional visual distinction and PASS — the evaluator must compute the inter-element lightness ratio, not reflexively fail. (b) PURE-COLOR RELIANCE STILL FAILS regardless of contrast: if meaning depends on perceiving a particular hue (green outline = valid vs red = invalid), an additional indicator is required EVEN IF the two colors have high contrast with each other. (c) NON-APPLICABILITY: where color conveys NO information (a hyperlink styled identically to surrounding static text), 1.4.1 does not apply and there is no failure. (d) VISITED-LINK EXEMPTION: color-alone distinction of visited vs unvisited links does NOT fail, even below 3:1. Each requires applying a specific WCAG rule rather than a blanket judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1, so none of these boundaries is exercised. They are precisely the cases where naive automation goes wrong: a tool that flags any color cue would false-positive on the 3:1-lightness pass, the non-applicable identical-link, and the visited-link case; while the 'high contrast between two hues still fails if meaning depends on the hue' rule (green-valid vs red-invalid) is a subtlety no contrast checker models. Each demands applying a specific WCAG rule with human judgment about whether color is carrying meaning and which exemption governs.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.1 · Trusted Tester 13.A · priority medium

ACT 09o5cg — Text has enhanced contrast

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 09o5cg — Text has enhanced contrast

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 1.4.3

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/09o5cg/proposed/

Proposed

Text has enhanced contrast

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

1.4.6: Contrast (Enhanced) (Level AAA)

Description

This rule checks that the highest possible contrast of every text character with its background meets the enhanced contrast requirement.

Applicability

This rule applies to any visible character in a text node that is a child in the flat tree of an HTML element , except if the text node has an ancestor in the flat tree for which at least one of the following is true:

  • disabled ancestor : the ancestor is an inheriting semantic group or widget that is disabled ; or
  • disabled label : the ancestor is used in the accessible name of an inheriting semantic widget that is disabled .

Expectation

For each test target, the highest possible contrast between the foreground colors and background colors is at least 4.5:1 for large scale text and 7.0:1 for other texts, except if the test target is part of a text node that is purely decorative or does not express anything in human language .

Background

Passing this rule does not mean that the text has sufficient color contrast. If all background pixels have a low contrast with all foreground pixels, the success criterion is guaranteed to not be satisfied. When some pixels have sufficient contrast, and others do not, legibility should be considered. There is no clear method for determining legibility when some but not all pixels have sufficient contrast, which is why passing this rule does not necessarily mean the corresponding success criterion is met.

When the text color or background color is not specified in the web page, colors from other origins will be used. Testers must ensure colors are not affected by styles from a user origin , such as a custom style sheet. Contrast issues caused by specifying the text color but not the background or vice versa, must be tested separately from this rule.

This rule is closely related to success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) . Because this rule is stricter, text that passes this rule will likely satisfy 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum).

Assumptions

Success criterion 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) has exceptions for “incidental” text, which includes inactive user interface components and decorative texts. The rule assumes that text nodes that should be ignored are disabled or hidden from assistive technologies. If this isn’t the case, the text node could fail this rule while the success criterion could still be satisfied.

Success criterion 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) also has an exception for logos and brand names. Since logos and brand names are usually displayed through images to ensure correct rendering, this rule does not take logos or brand names into consideration. If a logo or brand name is included using text nodes , the text node could fail while the success criterion could still be satisfied.

Text that has the same foreground and background color (a contrast ratio of 1:1) is not considered to be “visual presentation of text”, making it inapplicable to the success criterion. Text hidden in this way can still cause accessibility issues under other success criteria, depending on the content.

The definition of disabled element assumes that when the aria-disabled attribute is specified on an element, this element has also been disabled for users that do not rely on assistive technology . If this is not the case, that definition may produce incorrect results and in consequence this rule might be Inapplicable to some text nodes that still require a good contrast ratio.

Accessibility Support
  • Different browsers have different levels of support for CSS. This can cause contrast issues in one browser that do not appear in another. Because of that, this rule can produce different results depending on the browser that is used. For example, a text that is positioned using CSS transform may be on a different background in a browser that does not support CSS transform.
  • Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some elements can have a semantic role of none and fail this rule with some technology but users of other technologies would not experience any accessibility issue.
Other Resources

  • G18: Ensuring that a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 exists between text (and images of text) and background behind the text
  • F83: Failure of Success Criterion 1.4.3 and 1.4.6 due to using background images that do not provide sufficient contrast with foreground text (or images of text)

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule afw4f7 — Text has minimum contrast

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 1.4.3

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/afw4f7/proposed/

Proposed

Text has minimum contrast

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA)

Description

This rule checks that the highest possible contrast of every text character with its background meets the minimal contrast requirement.

Applicability

This rule applies to any visible character in a text node that is a child in the flat tree of an HTML element , except if the text node has an ancestor in the flat tree for which at least one of the following is true:

  • disabled ancestor : the ancestor is an inheriting semantic group or widget that is disabled ; or
  • disabled label : the ancestor is used in the accessible name of an inheriting semantic widget that is disabled .

Expectation

For each test target, the highest possible contrast between the foreground colors and background colors is at least 3.0:1 for large scale text and 4.5:1 for other texts, except if the test target is part of a text node that is purely decorative or does not express anything in human language .

Background

Passing this rule does not mean that the text has sufficient color contrast. If all background pixels have a low contrast with all foreground pixels, the success criterion is guaranteed to not be satisfied. When some pixels have sufficient contrast, and others do not, legibility should be considered. There is no clear method for determining legibility when some but not all pixels have sufficient contrast, which is why passing this rule does not necessarily mean the corresponding success criterion is met.

When the text color or background color is not specified in the web page, colors from other origins will be used. Testers must ensure colors are not affected by styles from a user origin , such as a custom style sheet. Contrast issues caused by specifying the text color but not the background or vice versa, must be tested separately from this rule.

Assumptions

Success criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) has exceptions for “incidental” text, which includes inactive user interface components and decorative texts. The rule assumes that text nodes that should be ignored are disabled or hidden from assistive technologies. If this isn’t the case, the text node could fail this rule while the success criterion could still be satisfied.

Success criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) also has an exception for logos and brand names. Since logos and brand names are usually displayed through images to ensure correct rendering, this rule does not take logos or brand names into consideration. If a logo or brand name is included using text nodes , the text node could fail while the success criterion could still be satisfied.

Text that has the same foreground and background color (a contrast ratio of 1:1) is not considered to be “visual presentation of text”, making it inapplicable to the success criterion. Text hidden in this way can still cause accessibility issues under other success criteria, depending on the content.

The definition of disabled element assumes that when the aria-disabled attribute is specified on an element, this element has also been disabled for users that do not rely on assistive technology . If this is not the case, that definition may produce incorrect results and in consequence this rule might be Inapplicable to some text nodes that still require a good contrast ratio.

Accessibility Support
  • Different browsers have different levels of support for CSS. This can cause contrast issues in one browser that do not appear in another. Because of that, this rule can produce different results depending on the browser that is used. For example, a text that is positioned using CSS transform may be on a different background in a browser that does not support CSS transform.
  • Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some elements can have a semantic role of none and fail this rule with some technology but users of other technologies would not experience any accessibility issue.

EN 301 549 — C.9.1.4.3 (SC 1.4.3)

C.9.1.4.3 — SC 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum)
C.9.1.4.3       Contrast (minimum)
   Type of assessment                                         Inspection
   Requirement          1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.
   Preconditions
   Procedure            1. Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast
                        (Minimum) according to WCAG Conformance Requirements stated in clause 9.6.
   Result               Pass: Check 1 is true
                        Fail: Check 1 is false
                        Not applicable: If any requirement precondition is false or the web page does not
                        contain content relevant to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum).
                        (Do not need to meet or test)

Trusted Tester — SC 1.4.3

SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) — TT Test 13.C

TT section: 13. Sensory Characteristics and Contrast → Color Contrast · Baseline: 8. Contrast

WCAG SC 1.4.3: The visual presentation of text and images of text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1,

except: large text 3:1; incidental (inactive/decorative/invisible/part of a picture with significant other

content); logotypes.

Identify Content

Identify ALL text AND images of text. EXCLUDE text that is:

  • In logotypes (logo or brand name)
  • For inactive (disabled) user interface components
  • Purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality)
  • Contained within a picture that contains significant other visual content
  • Changed to indicate it is a "visited" link
  • *Note:* Some text may not initially be visible (appears on mouseover or focus). It must still conform to the

contrast requirement wherever it occurs.

  • DNA for 13.C if the page has no visible text or images of text.

Test 13.C — 1.4.3-contrast

Test Condition: *The visual presentation of text and images of text have sufficient contrast.*

How to Test

1. Launch ANDI: color contrast.

2. Review any "Contrast Alerts" in ANDI's "Accessibility Alerts" section to identify text that fails the minimum

contrast ratio.

3. In ANDI's "Accessibility Alerts," identify any "Manual Contrast Tests Needed."

  • a. If text is not selectable or appears on a background image, determine the contrast using the **Colour

Contrast Analyser (CCA)**.

  • b. Open CCA, select the Foreground color-dropper, click a pixel in the text font. If the text color is

varied, choose a pixel that provides the least contrast.

  • c. Select the Background color-dropper, click a pixel in the background close to the text. If the

background is varied, choose a pixel that provides the least contrast.

  • d. Identify the Contrast Ratio.
  • e. Compare the contrast ratio against the minimum required ratio identified in the ANDI Contrast Ratio output.

4. If the page contains an image of text alone (or an image with text and no other significant content), test the

image of text with CCA (ANDI: color contrast cannot detect text inside images).

  • a. Graphics/images module → arrow buttons → identify images of text.
  • b. Open CCA, test the contrast of the text in the image (foreground/background droppers, least contrast).
  • c. Determine whether the resulting contrast ratio is at least 4.5:1.
  • *Note:* if the text in the image is large-scale (≥18pt or 14pt bold), 3:1 applies. TT has not

identified a tool to compare text size in images, so this determination is not in the process — but use

3:1 if it can be satisfactorily demonstrated the text is large-scale.

Evaluate Results (PASS if ANY true)

1. The contrast between the text and its background is ≥ the minimum required ratio identified in the ANDI

Contrast Ratio output, OR

2. If the text is an image of text, the contrast between the image of text and its background is ≥ 4.5:1 (or 3:1

for large-scale text) as identified using the CCA.

Thresholds (from Applicable Standards)
  • Normal text: 4.5:1; Large-scale text (≥18pt or ≥14pt bold): 3:1.
  • Incidental (inactive UI, pure decoration, not visible to anyone, part of a picture with significant other

content) and Logotypes: no contrast requirement.

> Two distinct mechanisms: (a) selectable live text → ANDI auto-computes from CSS colors; (b) text on a

> background image / image-of-text → ANDI can't, so a human eyedroppers the least-contrast foreground &

> background pixels with CCA. Our pixel-contrast path mirrors (b); our CSSOM path mirrors (a).

Act-augmented aspect — Pure-decoration exemption misjudged: genuinely decorative low-contrast text (must be EXEMPT) vs. meaningful text the author treated as decoration (must MEET contrast)

Low-contrast text gets misjudged: purely ornamental words are flagged as failures, while faint-but-meaningful content like a price or status watermark is wrongly excused as decoration.

SC 1.4.3 exempts text that is 'pure decoration' / 'decorative and conveys no information.' Understanding's test is semantic: text is decorative only if 'random words... could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning.' Trusted Tester says to EXCLUDE text that is 'purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality).' Deciding whether a faint watermark, ghost number, or faded divider conveys information is a meaning judgment a contrast checker cannot make. Two opposite human-judgment traps exist: (1) FALSE POSITIVE — genuine decoration (a mood word, an ornamental repeating glyph) flagged as a failure when it should be exempt; (2) FALSE NEGATIVE — core information (a price, a status watermark) styled faint and 'subtle' that the author rationalizes as decorative but which carries meaning and must meet 4.5:1/3:1. An automated checker sees only the failing ratio in both directions and cannot tell which way to rule.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT corpus exercises the exemption only via a single non-language glyph ('X' close button) and a single font specimen. It has no case where meaningful prose is rendered at failing contrast yet styled to read as decoration (watermark, ghost step-number, hero mood word), and no case that must be EXEMPTED as genuine decoration. Neither the false-positive nor the false-negative side of the meaning boundary is tested, and no automated checker can resolve it because both produce identical failing ratios.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.3 · Trusted Tester 13.C · priority high

  • Understanding 1.4.3 — “Text that is decorative and conveys no information is excluded. For example, if random words are used to create a background and the words could be rearranged or substituted withou…”
  • Trusted Tester 1.4.3 — “EXCLUDE text that is: ... Purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality)…”

Act-augmented aspect — Logotype / brand-name contrast exemption and its loss when the logotype acts as an interactive UI component

Brand logos are exempt from contrast rules, but the exemption is abused when ordinary styled headings, taglines, or clickable logo-links with poor contrast hide behind it.

1.4.3 exempts logotypes and brand names from contrast. Trusted Tester excludes 'text that is... In logotypes (logo or brand name).' Understanding warns the exemption 'can be problematic when logos or logotypes act as user interface components (such as a link or other interactive control)' and that 'Corporate identity or brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are not included in the exception.' Three human judgments are required and none are automatable: (a) is this low-contrast text actually a logotype/brand wordmark versus an ordinary styled heading?; (b) is the wordmark functioning as a live control (home link, button), in which case the brand exemption is eroded and a sufficient-contrast variant is expected?; (c) is adjacent text (tagline, badge) being smuggled under the logo exemption when it is really informative content the brand carve-out does not cover?

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The 09o5cg rule lists logos/brand names explicitly as an assumption / out of scope; the corpus contains zero logotypes, wordmarks, or low-contrast brand-name links. So neither the legitimate exemption, nor its erosion when the logo is a link, nor the 'beyond the logo' boundary is exercised. An automated checker cannot identify what is a brand name versus a styled heading, so this is irreducibly human.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.3 · Trusted Tester 13.C · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Inactive-UI exemption applies only to GENUINELY inoperable controls, not to operable controls merely styled to look disabled (or aria-disabled controls that still fire)

A button greyed out to look disabled but still clickable must meet contrast rules, yet checkers can't tell whether the control is truly inactive without operating it.

Inactive UI components are exempt: Understanding says 'User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction... are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable.' Trusted Tester excludes text 'For inactive (disabled) user interface components.' Whether the exemption applies depends on a BEHAVIORAL fact — is the control actually operable? — that contrast checkers (and even most automated tools) cannot infer from color alone. The trap is appearance/behavior mismatch: a button greyed to look disabled (class='disabled', no disabled attr) that still submits on click MUST meet contrast; conversely a control marked aria-disabled='true' but wired to still fire is not genuinely inactive. The judge must drive the control to determine operability, then decide the exemption.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: All ACT inapplicable cases use correctly-marked disabled/aria-disabled native widgets that ARE inert. There is no operable control dressed to look disabled (faux-disabled, must MEET contrast), and no aria-disabled control that still fires. The exemption boundary is never stressed by mismatched appearance vs. behavior, and resolving it requires interacting with the page, which static checkers do not do.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.3 · Trusted Tester 13.C · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Determining the EFFECTIVE background behind text when color and background come from different tree levels, inherited cascade, z-indexed overlays, or composited semi-transparent layers (F24 cascade limb)

Figuring out the real colour behind text is hard when it comes from a parent element, an overlapping layer, or a see-through panel, so contrast tools guess wrong.

F24 fails content when a foreground color is specified without a guaranteed background (or vice versa) and stresses that 'It is not necessary that the foreground and background colors both be defined on the same element. Foreground text color is inherited from ancestor elements. If an element's background color has not been defined, the element will have a transparent background, so authors need to ensure that at least one of the element's ancestors has a defined background color.' Color may be set 'at any level in the cascade... by external stylesheets or through inheritance.' Determining what actually renders behind the glyphs — which ancestor's background, which z-indexed sibling overlay, which composited semi-transparent scrim — requires reasoning about the rendered layer stack, not the element's own declared background. This is exactly where naive CSSOM contrast tools mislabel: they read the element's local background (often transparent) and either skip the text or assume white, producing false passes/false negatives. The least-contrast judgment must be made against the REAL composited backdrop.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Every ACT case sets color and background together inline on the same element, or relies on UA defaults. No case has color inherited from a distant ancestor while the visible backdrop comes from a different ancestor, a z-indexed overlay, a translucent scrim composited over a photo, or a CSS multiple-background stack. Naive automated checkers structurally mis-handle these (they read the local background), so determining the true backdrop is a human visual/structural judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.3 · Trusted Tester 13.C · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Background-image text where worst-case pixels behind SOME letters fail (least-contrast / per-letter) even though best-case or average contrast passes (F83)

Text over a photo can be readable on average but unreadable where a bright patch sits behind a few letters, which best-case contrast checks miss.

F83 fails text over a background image when 'there is not sufficient contrast between the background image and the text' such that 'features of the background image can be confused with the text.' Its procedure requires the Quickcheck against the most-confusable region and, if that fails, checking 'the background behind each letter.' Trusted Tester operationalizes this: the human eyedroppers 'a pixel that provides the LEAST contrast' for both foreground and background. The ACT rule does the OPPOSITE — it takes the highest-possible (best-case) pixel pairing — so a photographic background that is mostly dark (text passes) but has a bright patch crossing three letters (those letters fail) is precisely the F83 failure the best-case algorithm structurally CANNOT flag. Catching it requires per-letter visual inspection over a real, high-variance image, exactly the harness's least-contrast pixel path.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT background cases use one toy JPEG (black-hole.jpeg) plus text-shadow tuned to pass/fail cleanly, and the rule scores BEST-case contrast. There is no real photographic background with high luminance variance where a small bright/dark patch crosses only some letters. The best-case algorithm reports pass; only a per-letter least-contrast visual check finds the failing letters — an irreducibly visual human task.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.3 · Trusted Tester 13.C · priority high
