Act-augmented aspect — Applying the correct AA thresholds (4.5:1 normal / 3:1 large) and the human large-text-size determination, where ACT only scored the stricter AAA limits

Using the wrong contrast threshold: normal text needs 4.5:1 and large text only 3:1, but deciding whether a given font counts as 'large' takes human judgement.

SC 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large-scale text (>=18pt or >=14pt bold). The ACT 09o5cg rule is calibrated to the AAA 1.4.6 thresholds (7:1 / 4.5:1), so cases it FAILS (e.g. 5.7:1, 6.4:1) actually PASS 1.4.3. Correctly judging 1.4.3 requires (a) applying the right AA threshold, and (b) deciding whether text qualifies as 'large-scale,' which Understanding notes is not a clean pixel cutoff: '18 point and bold can both have different meanings in different fonts but, except for very thin or unusual fonts, they should be sufficient,' anti-aliasing of 'particularly thin or unusual fonts' can render text 'with a much fainter color than the actual text color,' and font size must be 'obtained from the user agent or calculated on font metrics.' The threshold band between 3:1 and 4.5:1 is where the size classification flips the verdict — a human judgment about whether the rendered font is genuinely large-scale (and not a thin/unusual face that should not get the relaxed ratio).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT only tests exactly 18pt and 14pt-bold at the AAA boundaries; it never tests the 1.4.3 band where a ratio is between 3:1 and 4.5:1 (passes if large, fails if normal), nor thin/unusual/condensed fonts where the relaxed large-text ratio is arguably unsafe, nor rem/em/zoom/responsive sizing that changes rendered size. Resolving the size classification near the boundary is a human judgment Understanding explicitly says depends on font metrics and weight, not a fixed pixel rule.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.3 · Trusted Tester 13.C · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Contrast of text only present in non-initial states: placeholder, hover, keyboard focus, active, selected, and error states (and visited-link exclusion)

Text that only appears on hover, focus, typing, or errors (like placeholder or error messages) must also be readable, but tools only check the initial page.

Understanding explicitly extends 1.4.3 to 'text in the page, including placeholder text and text that is shown when a pointer is hovering over an object or when an object has keyboard focus. If any of these are used in a page, the text needs to provide sufficient contrast.' F24's best-practice note lists 'text, link text, visited link text, link text with hover and keyboard focus.' Trusted Tester warns 'Some text may not initially be visible (appears on mouseover or focus). It must still conform to the contrast requirement wherever it occurs,' while excluding text 'Changed to indicate it is a visited link.' Evaluating these requires DRIVING the page into each state (hover, focus, type into a field, trigger an error) and judging whether the state is genuinely reachable — a behavioral exploration the static, initial-render ACT corpus never performs.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Every ACT case is scored at static initial render with no interaction; there are no :hover/:focus/:active/::placeholder/aria-selected variants, no error-state styling, and no driven states. The state-coverage breadth Understanding and F24 explicitly demand is entirely absent, and discovering these states requires interacting with the page rather than reading static markup.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.3 · Trusted Tester 13.C · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — The 'text in a picture that contains significant other visual content' exemption vs. an image of text done purely to get a particular look (which is NOT exempt)

Text inside a real photo (like a street sign) is exempt, but text drawn as an image just for a fancy look is not.

1.4.3 exempts text 'that are part of a picture that contains significant other visual content.' Understanding explains the boundary: 'This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look. Incidental text, such as in photographs that happen to include a street sign, are not included.' Trusted Tester excludes text 'Contained within a picture that contains significant other visual content' but requires testing 'an image of text alone (or an image with text and no other significant content)' against 4.5:1/3:1 using the eyedropper. Deciding whether a given image is a 'picture with significant other content' (exempt) versus an 'image of text' styled for look (in scope) is a holistic visual judgment about the image's purpose and composition — not something an automated checker (which cannot read text inside images at all) can do.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT never tests images-of-text at all (it only computes contrast for live text nodes), and certainly not the exemption boundary between an incidental-text photograph (exempt) and an image-of-text crafted for a particular look (in scope at 4.5:1/3:1). Automated checkers cannot read text inside raster images, so both the exemption and the in-scope image-of-text contrast check are human-only.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.3 · Trusted Tester 13.C · priority medium

EN 301 549 — C.9.1.4.5 (SC 1.4.5)

C.9.1.4.5 — SC 1.4.5 Images of text
C.9.1.4.5       Images of text
   Type of assessment                                         Inspection
   Requirement          1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.
   Preconditions
   Procedure            1. Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.5 Images of
                        Text according to WCAG Conformance Requirements stated in clause 9.6.
   Result               Pass: Check 1 is true
                        Fail: Check 1 is false
                        Not applicable: If any requirement precondition is false or the web page does not
                        contain content relevant to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.5 Images of Text. (Do not
                        need to meet or test)

Trusted Tester — SC 1.4.5

SC 1.4.5 Images of Text (Level AA) — TT Test 7.E

TT section: 7. Images → Images of Text · Baseline: 6. Images

WCAG SC 1.4.5: If the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation, text is used to convey

information rather than images of text, except for [customizable / essential].

Identify Content

Identify all images of text.

  • EXCLUDE text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content such as CAPTCHA,

graphs, screenshots, and diagrams, which visually convey important information more than just text.

  • DNA for 7.E if there are no images of text on the page.

Test 7.E — 1.4.5-image-of-text

Test Condition: *The image of text cannot be replaced by text or is customizable.*

How to Test

1. Determine if text can be used instead of the image of text to present the same effect and information.

  • a. Logotypes (text that is part of a logo or brand name) cannot be replaced by text.
  • b. Type samples, branding, images of specific fonts that are not widely supported are additional examples of

images of text that cannot be replaced by text.

2. Determine if the image of text can be visually customized: adjust the font, size, color, and background

with controls provided by the web page.

  • a. Customizing font size for an image of text also implies the ability to adjust the size without

pixelation (typically evident when simply using the browser resize functionality to resize images).

Evaluate Results (PASS if ANY true)

1. The image of text cannot be replaced with text, OR

2. The image of text can be visually customized.

> Detection step is OCR-like: the tester must first recognize that an image *contains text* (vs being a

> photo/diagram), then judge whether that text is essential (logotype) or could have been live text.

Act-augmented aspect — False logotype / branding exemption — informational text dressed up as a brand mark

Real logos may be pictures of text, but authors abuse this by saving taglines, slogans, or headings as images so low-vision users can't resize or recolour them.

TT step 1a and the Understanding 'A logo containing text' example exempt logotypes ('text that is part of a logo or brand name') from 1.4.5 because 'the visual presentation of the text is essential to the identity of the logo.' The genuinely hard, human-only judgment is distinguishing a real wordmark/brand identity from ordinary informational text (a tagline, marketing slogan, navigation label, deadline notice, or paragraph of prose) that an author has merely set in a nice typeface, exported as an image, and parked in a header or wrapped in class='logo' to dodge the SC. A one-word company wordmark is exempt; 'Free shipping on orders over $50', 'Apply for your permit before March 31', or a styled <h1> baked into a banner is NOT a logotype even when it sits in a branding zone. A checker cannot OCR the text and reason about whether it functions as a brand identity vs. conveys substantive information; only a human can.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT corpus holds exactly one logo case (W3C logo as role=img CSS background = PASS) and one plain-text-image FAIL (textimage.jpg) at opposite extremes. There is no borderline where an image's text is ambiguous between 'brand identity' and 'ordinary informational text styled nicely' — the exact distinction TT step 1a turns on. The corpus never puts non-logo content into a branding context.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.5 · Trusted Tester 7.E · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Customizability exception — image of text adjustable (or fake-adjustable) via on-page controls (C30)

A picture of text is allowed if on-page controls truly let users adjust its size, font, and colour, but those controls are sometimes fake, broken, or change nothing.

The SC text itself passes images of text 'where a particular presentation of text is essential or can be visually customized,' and TT Test 7.E condition 2 passes an image of text if it 'can be visually customized: adjust the font, size, color, and background with controls provided by the web page.' Technique C30 (CSS image-replacement with a switch control) and the Understanding 'Dynamically Generated Images' / 'Customizable font settings' examples are the canonical PASS-by-customization route. Evaluating this requires a human to find the controls, operate them, and judge whether activating them actually swaps the image for live text or genuinely re-renders the image to the user's font/size/color — and crucially to catch the FAILURE where controls are present but FAKE (decorative, broken, or only change unrelated styling). A static checker sees pixels and DOM, not whether a button truly re-renders an image of text; this is human-operable judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Every ACT case is a static flat raster/SVG image with no UI controls at all; the customizability limb of the SC is entirely unexercised in either direction. The corpus has no C30 switch and no dynamically-generated image, so neither a genuine PASS-by-customization nor a fake-controls FAIL is represented.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.5 · Trusted Tester 7.E · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — 'Significant other visual content' exclusion — graphs, screenshots, diagrams, infographics vs. text-only images

Charts, screenshots, and diagrams that contain words are exempt, so judging whether an image is mostly-graphic (allowed) or just styled text (not allowed) needs a human.

The images-of-text definition note excludes 'text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content,' citing 'graphs, screenshots, and diagrams which visually convey important information through more than just text' (TT adds CAPTCHA). The detection step is explicitly OCR-like: the tester must FIRST decide whether an image that contains text is fundamentally a graph/screenshot/diagram/infographic (out of scope, INAPPLICABLE) or is an image-of-text dressed up (in scope, potentially FAIL). This is the most subjective limb of the SC: a human must weigh whether the non-text graphics are 'significant' enough to exclude the image, or whether it is predominantly text laid out decoratively. No automated checker can make this gestalt judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT's INAPPLICABLE/PASS pictures contain no text at all (fireworks, Times Square, books — clear non-applicability) and its FAIL images are essentially pure text on a plain field (clear applicability). The genuinely hard middle — an image that is largely text but also carries chart geometry, UI chrome, or diagram structure — is absent. No case forces the 'does the non-text visual content make this NOT an image of text?' judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.5 · Trusted Tester 7.E · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — 'In addition to' MET condition — image of text accompanied by the same content as visible live text

A picture of text is fine when the exact same words also appear as real visible text nearby, but checkers can't confirm the live text truly matches.

The Understanding note: the SC 'is intended to address situations where images of text are used rather than text. Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.' The 'event poster + CMS text' example is the canonical PASS: the poster image would fail alone, but because the SAME text is ALSO posted as live, visible text next to it, 1.4.5 is satisfied. The hard human judgment is verifying EQUIVALENCE (same information, not a partial summary) AND VISIBILITY (genuinely presented to the user — not an alt attribute, not display:none, not sr-only, not stale content). A checker cannot judge semantic equivalence between an image's pixels and nearby live text, nor that both are 'presented.'

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT's decorative-image-plus-text pair (welcome.png with adjacent text) still FAILS, so the corpus never demonstrates the SC being MET because equivalent live text is present in addition to the image. There is no positive 'in addition to' PASS, and no case probing whether the accompanying text is genuinely equivalent and presented vs. only partial/hidden.

Act-augmented aspect — Essential-presentation exceptions beyond logos — type samples, font-family specimens, historical documents, symbolic glyphs

Some pictures of text are allowed because their exact look matters (a font sample, a scanned historical letter), and judging whether the look is essential needs a human.

Intent para 2 and the Understanding enumerate PASS-by-essential-presentation cases distinct from logotypes: a 'Representation of a font family' (substituting another font 'would defeat the purpose of the representation'), 'A representation of a letter' (an original historical document whose original format is essential to information about its time period), 'Symbolic text characters' (B/I/ABC editor buttons whose glyphs 'do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language'), and type samples. Judging these requires understanding WHY the presentation is essential — re-typesetting as live text would destroy the very thing communicated — and rejecting ABUSE where ordinary informational text is wrongly justified as 'a type sample' or 'historical look.' A checker cannot reason about whether a particular visual presentation is essential to meaning.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The corpus has the comic-cover type-sample (Ivanhoe) and maps the A/A resize buttons to symbolic characters, but never tests the historical/original-format-essential rationale, the symbolic-vs-human-language editor-glyph distinction in either direction, nor the abuse case where ordinary informational text is wrongly justified under the type-sample/font-representation exception. 'Essential' is asserted by the corpus rather than stress-tested.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.5 · Trusted Tester 7.E · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Core image-of-text-vs-live-text detection across delivery mechanisms and decoy live text

Words baked into images (CSS backgrounds, SVG, sprites) instead of real text can't be resized or recoloured, and tools often can't even detect that the image contains text.

The SC's foundational requirement — 'If the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation, text is used to convey information rather than images of text' — depends on a human first recognizing that an image actually contains rendered text (OCR-like detection) and then confirming the same visual effect was achievable in HTML/CSS so the content should have been live text. The hard cases require semantic judgment: text baked into a CSS background-image or pseudo-element (no <img>, no alt, invisible to most checkers), text rendered via SVG <text> inside an image vs. live selectable SVG <text>, web-font glyph text that looks like an image but is real text, and decoys where author-supplied alt or a hidden sr-only string makes a tool believe live text exists when the displayed content is still a bitmap. No automated tool reliably OCRs arbitrary images and judges achievability; this is core human semantic/visual work.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT exercises multiple embedding technologies but only at clear extremes (pure-text image FAIL vs. text-free photo PASS, plus one live-SVG-text INAPPLICABLE). It never tests the achievability gating clause (whether the desired visual effect was actually attainable in HTML/CSS), nor the deceptive middle where text is hidden in CSS backgrounds/pseudo-elements or where decoy live text/alt masks a bitmap. The threshold distinguishing achievable-so-must-be-live from genuinely-not-achievable is unexercised.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.5 · Trusted Tester 7.E · priority medium

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule b4f0c3 — Meta viewport allows for zoom

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 1.4.10

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/b4f0c3/proposed/

Proposed

Meta viewport allows for zoom

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

1.4.4: Resize text (Level AA)

Description

This rule checks that the meta element retains the user agent ability to zoom.

Applicability

This rule applies to each content attribute for which all of the following are true:

  • the attribute is defined on a meta element with a name attribute value of viewport ; and
  • the attribute value has at least one of the maximum-scale or user-scalable keys.

For the purpose of this rule, the attribute value of the content attribute is a list of key/value pairs.

Expectation 1

For each test target’s attribute value , at least one of the following is true:

  • user-scalable is not defined; or
  • user-scalable is yes , device-width or device-height ; or
  • user-scalable is a number which is not between -1 and 1 (excluded).

Note: This is equivalent to applying the translations into a @viewport descriptors and not obtaining a value of fixed for the user-zoom descriptor from the translation for user-scalable .

Expectation 2

For each test target’s attribute value , at least one of the following is true:

  • maximum-scale is not defined; or
  • maximum-scale is device-width or device-height ; or
  • maximum-scale is a negative number; or
  • maximum-scale is a number which is 2 or more.

Note: This is equivalent to applying the translations into a @viewport descriptors and not obtaining a value smaller than 2 for the max-zoom descriptor from the translation for maximum-scale .

Background

Assumptions

Pages for which any of the following is true may satisfy Success Criteria 1.4.4 Resize text and 1.4.10 Reflow , even if the rule results in a failed outcome.

  • The page has no visible content ; or
  • There is another mechanism available to resize the text content; or
  • The content does not need to reflow in order to fit in an area of 320 by 256 CSS pixels .
Accessibility Support

Desktop browsers ignore the viewport meta element, and most modern mobile browsers either ignore it by default or have an accessibility option which will allow zooming. This rule is not relevant for desktop browsers, nor for most modern mobile browsers. Only users with older mobile browsers can experience issues tested by this rule.

The exact way the content attribute should be parsed (notably, for error handling) is not fully specified. CSS specification includes a non-normative parsing algorithm . Different user agents may behave differently in some cases.

Other Resources
  • Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.4: Resize text
  • Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.10: Reflow
  • HTML Specification - The meta element
  • The initial-scale, minimum-scale, and maximum-scale properties
  • The user-scalable property

Accessibility Requirements Mapping

1.4.4 Resize text (Level AA)

  • Learn more about 1.4.4 Resize text
  • Required for conformance to WCAG 2.0 and later on level AA and higher.
  • Outcome mapping:
  • Any failed outcomes: success criterion is not satisfied
  • All passed outcomes: success criterion needs further testing
  • An inapplicable outcome: success criterion needs further testing
Secondary Requirements

This rule is related to the following accessibility requirements, but was

not designed to test this requirements directly. These

secondary requirements

can either be stricter than the rule requires, or may be satisfied in ways

not tested by the rule:

  • 1.4.10 Reflow (Level AA) : This success criterion is related to this rule. This is because a page that cannot be zoomed up to 200% often does not reflow sufficiently either. Most failed examples satisfy this success criterion.

Input Aspects

The following aspects are required in using this rule.

  • DOM Tree

Act-augmented aspect — Non-excepted content forces a horizontal scrollbar at 320 CSS px (fixed-width container, non-wrapping layout, layout-table-as-prose)

On a narrow phone-width screen, fixed-width or non-wrapping content spills sideways forcing horizontal scrolling, and a human must judge whether that overflow is a real failure.

The defining 1.4.10 failure: when the page is rendered at a width equivalent to 320 CSS px (the 1280px-at-400% equivalent), some section of NON-excepted content forces two-dimensional scrolling. Triggers include a fixed-width container (e.g. width:680px), a body/wrapper min-width, a flex/grid row that refuses to wrap, absolutely-positioned off-canvas content, or a layout table (a <table> used only to position prose side-by-side) that wrongly relies on the data-table exception. The viewport meta is permissive so b4f0c3 passes, yet the rendered page fails Reflow. The judgment that survives automation: a tool can see scrollWidth > clientWidth, but it CANNOT decide whether that overflow is a legitimate exception (real data table, map, video, fixed-dimension media) or a genuine failure, nor whether a wide <table> holds real tabular data versus prose that should reflow. A human must classify the overflowing element and confirm reflow is actually broken for content that should reflow.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The lone ACT rule b4f0c3 is a pure DOM-string check of the viewport meta content attribute; it never renders the page, never sets a 320px viewport, and never measures overflow. Its own mapping makes 1.4.4 primary and notes 'most failed examples [actually] satisfy' 1.4.10. The synthetic corpus pages are a title plus a single short Lorem-ipsum paragraph with no content wide enough to overflow. While raw page-overflow is partly machine-detectable, the disposition (legitimate exception vs failure, data table vs layout table) is an irreducible human classification.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.10 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — F102 — content/functionality present at desktop width disappears at 320px and is not reachable by any equivalent mechanism

Shrinking the page to phone width hides content (a sidebar, nav links, a search box) with no equivalent way to reach it, so functionality is simply lost.

The dedicated failure technique F102: a section visible at 1280px is hidden at 320px (via display:none in a max-width media query, a collapsed sidebar, a responsive nav that drops links, a search field that vanishes, labels replaced by placeholders) WITHOUT providing the same or equivalent content through a disclosure widget, hamburger menu, dialog, icon, or link to another view. The page reflows (no horizontal scroll) and the viewport meta is fine, so it looks compliant to a tool, but information or functionality has been lost. Judging it requires comparing the desktop and narrow renderings, diffing what content is reachable, and a semantic decision about whether a replacement mechanism genuinely surfaces the same information (does that hamburger button actually expose the dropped nav links, or is it dead? is placeholder text an acceptable label substitute? does the disclosure actually contain the hidden section?).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: F102 has no ACT rule and zero test cases; the corpus only has b4f0c3 (viewport string). Detecting it requires rendering at two widths, diffing reachable content, and a human judgment about whether a replacement mechanism (hamburger, disclosure, link) genuinely surfaces the same information. A tool cannot decide whether a hamburger icon actually leads to the dropped links or whether placeholder text is an acceptable label substitute.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.10 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Long unbroken strings (URLs, tokens, hashes, paths, emails, compound words) overflow at 320px without wrapping or a reveal alternative

A single long unbroken string like a URL, hash, or API key won't wrap, so it forces sideways scrolling even though the rest of the page reflows fine.

Technique C33 addresses long sets of characters with no spaces — a displayed full URL, an API/auth key, a long hash, a deep file path, a blockchain address, a German compound word — that the browser cannot wrap (no break opportunities and no overflow-wrap:break-word / word-break applied, or white-space:nowrap forced). At 320px the one string punches out a horizontal scrollbar even though every paragraph around it reflows perfectly. The viewport meta is fine and the page is 99% fluid, so a viewport-string check sees nothing. The judgment: render at 320px to find the single overflowing element, and decide the correct disposition — whether the string may break mid-word, versus the truncate-with-reveal pattern the Understanding doc describes (truncation is only acceptable if a link or mechanism reveals the full value).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT rule renders content or measures string overflow; corpus pages contain only short Lorem-ipsum with normal spaces, never a long unbreakable token. A static checker can heuristically spot a literal very-long string in markup but cannot determine whether it actually overflows at 320px (depends on font, container width, CSS) nor whether the surrounding design already wraps it nor whether a truncation has a valid reveal — this needs visual measurement plus judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.10 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Two-dimensional-layout exception over-claimed or mis-scoped: non-excepted surroundings of a table/map/grid fail to reflow

Because one table or map legitimately needs sideways scrolling, the developer lets the whole page scroll sideways, so headings and search boxes that should reflow don't.

1.4.10 exempts sections that genuinely require two-dimensional layout (data tables, maps, diagrams, grids, code where indentation is meaningful, presentations). The judgment-heavy failure mode is mis-scoping: a developer lets the WHOLE page scroll in two dimensions 'because there's a table', so the heading, intro paragraph, search field, and pagination that surround the table — none of which need 2D layout — also extend off-screen and require horizontal scrolling. The Understanding doc shows exactly this pass/fail pair. Conversely, flagging content that legitimately IS a data table/map/video would be a false positive. Deciding whether a given block legitimately 'requires two-dimensional layout for understanding or functionality', AND scoping the exception to only the excepted section, are irreducibly human contextual calls: is this <table> real tabular data or layout? is this wide block a map (exempt) or a poorly sized banner? must this heading/search/pagination reflow even though the adjacent table need not?

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT corpus has no rendered pages and no tables/maps/grids, so the exception is never exercised in either direction. The exception turns on the MEANING of the content and on scoping it to only the excepted section — both human judgments. Automated tools cannot distinguish a genuine data table from a layout table, nor decide that a surrounding heading/search/pagination is non-excepted and must reflow.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.10 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Sticky / fixed-position content (headers, footers, cookie bars, chat widgets, ads) consumes or obscures the 320x256 viewport so reflowed content cannot be read

On a tiny zoomed viewport, sticky headers, footers, cookie bars, or chat widgets eat most of the screen or cover content, leaving almost nothing readable.

Headers, footers, toolbars, cookie banners, chat widgets, and fixed ads that are reasonable at desktop become viewport-eating obstructions when zoomed to a 320px-wide / 256px-tall viewport. A sticky 130px-tall header over a 256px-tall viewport leaves almost nothing to read; a fixed-bottom cookie bar plus fixed-top nav can sandwich content into a sliver; a fixed-corner ad can cover the focused link, providing no way to dismiss it without keyboard-navigating to its close button. The Understanding doc's Focus-Not-Obscured overlap section and technique C34 both call for un-fixing these at small sizes. The page reflows horizontally (no h-scroll) and the viewport meta is permissive, so tools see nothing — but the rendered experience is broken. Judging it requires rendering at the narrow viewport (especially the 256px height) and a visual proportion assessment of how much readable space the sticky elements leave and whether they obscure content or keyboard focus.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Corpus pages have no sticky/fixed elements and are never rendered at 256px height. C34 is advisory with no ACT rule. The harm — a sticky element leaving too little room, or covering content/focus — is a visual proportion judgment at a specific small viewport; there is no static signal, and position:sticky/fixed are perfectly valid and ubiquitous, so their mere presence cannot be flagged. Only a human looking at the rendered narrow viewport can judge whether too little remains.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.10 · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Horizontally-scrolling carousel where an individual panel does not fit within 320 CSS px (G225)

A sideways-scrolling carousel is allowed, but one over-stuffed panel doesn't fit the narrow width, forcing extra horizontal scrolling inside that single panel.

Horizontally-scrolling carousels are explicitly allowed: the strip scrolls horizontally to move between panels, but EACH individual panel must fit within 320 CSS px so the user need only scroll vertically to read one panel's content. The Understanding doc gives a pass (each home-listing panel fits 320px) and a fail (the second panel's content does not fit 320px). The failure is subtle: the carousel mechanism is fine and most panels fit, but one over-stuffed panel (longer text, an extra-wide image, a wider card) forces horizontal scrolling WITHIN that panel. Catching it requires rendering at 320px, advancing through each panel, and judging per-panel whether its content overflows — AND judging that the horizontal strip-scroll itself is the intended carousel navigation and NOT the violation. A tool cannot tell which overflow is 'the carousel working' versus 'a panel too wide'.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No carousels exist in the corpus and nothing is rendered. G225 has no ACT rule. The distinction between acceptable strip-level horizontal scrolling (navigation between panels) and unacceptable within-panel horizontal scrolling requires interpreting the widget's purpose and inspecting each panel individually at 320px — beyond static markup analysis.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.10 · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Preformatted text / nested-list / code indentation: distinguishing meaningful (excepted) layout from gratuitous non-wrapping that should reflow

Code and nested lists may keep meaningful indentation that needs sideways scrolling, but ordinary prose forced not to wrap overflows when it should simply reflow.

Lists and code blocks often rely on indentation to convey hierarchy or meaning (nested <ul> levels, Python block structure, ascii art). Where indentation is genuinely meaningful, the section may legitimately need two-dimensional scrolling and is excepted (G224 / the Understanding 'Preformatted text conveys meaning' example). The judgment-heavy failure: a developer wraps ordinary prose in <pre> or applies white-space:nowrap to text whose layout carries NO meaning, so it refuses to wrap and overflows 320px when it should simply reflow — OR conversely, genuinely meaningful indented code that is force-flattened, losing meaning. Deciding whether the layout's meaning would be lost by wrapping (exempt) versus whether the non-wrapping is gratuitous (must reflow) is a semantic content call no tool can make. G224 also notes the conforming middle path: keep meaningful indentation but reduce it at zoomed levels and allow each nested level to be horizontally scrolled into view while its items read vertically.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The corpus has only plain Lorem-ipsum prose, no <pre>, code, or nested lists, and nothing is rendered. G224 has no ACT rule. Whether indentation/non-wrapping is meaningful (exempt) or gratuitous (must wrap) depends on reading and understanding the content's semantics — a tool sees white-space:pre and cannot decide if flattening would destroy meaning.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.10 · priority medium

State or Status Changes (cat_7)

Act-augmented aspect — Border/boundary contrast bites ONLY when it is the sole cue that a control exists

A faint border only needs strong contrast when it is the single hint a control exists, so the same grey border can fail on a borderless input yet pass elsewhere.

The SC's UI-component requirement only applies to the visual information NECESSARY to identify that a control is present. The Understanding text is explicit: a border indicating the hit area is required to contrast 3:1 only 'when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control'; if the control has visible text or a sufficiently contrasting icon, a low-contrast surrounding border is NOT subject to the requirement. So the identical low-contrast 2px grey border can be a PASS on a labelled, clearly-styled button and a FAIL on a borderless 'ghost' input whose ONLY cue is that same border. The verdict flips on a semantic reading of the whole component (is there any OTHER visual way a sighted low-vision user would know the control is there?), not on the border's contrast number alone. A purely automated checker either measures every border in isolation (false-positives on the labelled button) or does not measure non-text borders at all (misses the ghost input) -- neither evaluates 'is the boundary the only way to identify the control'.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Zero ACT test cases exist (testCaseCount:0). The discrimination resists encoding because the outcome turns on whether label text / contrasting icon / positional context already identify the control -- a human reading of the whole component, not a property of the border. Automated tools either over-flag every faint border or never measure non-text borders; neither performs the 'is the boundary the only cue' judgement.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.11 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — State-indicator (checked/selected/expanded) contrast against the CORRECT adjacent surface within the component

The mark showing a control's state (a checkbox's tick, a toggle's thumb) must contrast 3:1 against the correct neighbouring surface, which is easy to pick wrong.

Beyond identifying that a control exists, the SC requires the non-text information that conveys STATE -- the check in a checkbox, the dot in a radio, the thumb of a toggle/slider, the chevron showing an accordion is open -- to have 3:1 against ITS adjacent color, which may be another part of the component rather than the page. Two semantic judgements are needed that automation cannot make: (a) identifying which mark conveys state versus which is decorative, and (b) choosing the correct comparison surface (the check is measured against the box fill, not the page; the toggle thumb against the track, not the page). A flat-fill design where the indicator does NOT contrast with the component but the whole filled component contrasts with the page is explicitly allowed -- so the same physical pair of colors passes or fails depending on which surface is the relevant 'adjacent' one. Picking the wrong surface gives the wrong verdict.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT cases exist for checked/selected/expanded indicators. The hard part is not arithmetic but segmenting a custom control into 'state mark' + its correct adjacent surface, and recognizing the flat-fill exception (compare filled component to page) versus the mark-on-fill pattern (compare mark to fill). Automated tools cannot reliably segment a styled/SVG control into these regions, so they can neither locate the right two colors nor decide which design pattern applies.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.11 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Selecting WHICH parts of a complex graphic are 'required for understanding' and whether equivalent text exempts them

Parts of a chart or diagram needed to understand it must contrast 3:1, but deciding which parts matter, and whether nearby text labels excuse them, needs a human.

G207/G209 require 3:1 contrast only for graphical objects 'required for understanding.' The whole judgement is meaning-level: in a multi-part graphic (chart line, pie slice, infographic circle + its icon, map region, the magnet's U-shape and tips) the evaluator must decide WHICH parts a viewer must perceive to grasp the meaning, then test only those -- and crucially the graphic is EXEMPT if equivalent text (visible labels AND values, or a data table via a Long Description) conveys the same information. So a pie chart with adjoining 1.5:1 slices is a FAIL when the slices are the only data, NOT APPLICABLE when the same chart carries visible numeric labels and values, and a PASS only after a 3:1 border is added between slices (G209). The 'is it required / is the same info available another way' decision is exactly the determination only a human reading the graphic can make.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No chart/diagram/infographic ACT cases exist. Automated tools cannot parse a raster or SVG chart into 'graphical objects', cannot judge which are required for understanding, and cannot determine whether adjacent visible labels+values render the graphic non-essential. The same pixel pattern flips between Fail, NA, and Pass depending on accompanying text -- a semantic determination.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.11 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — F78: an author focus indicator that technically exists but is rendered non-visible by surrounding styling

A focus outline technically exists but is hidden by look-alike borders, so a keyboard user genuinely can't tell which control is currently focused.

F78 names failure modes beyond the trivial outline:none: (a) a non-focus outline/border that looks identical to the browser focus ring, so the user cannot tell which element is focused; and (b) a thick element border the same color as the focus indicator drawn just outside it, so the focus ring is swallowed by the border. In both cases an outline IS present on focus -- a CSS scraper or rule that merely detects a focus style reports a pass -- but a sighted keyboard user cannot perceive WHICH control has focus or that focus moved at all. Deciding this requires comparing the focused appearance against the persistent decorative styling and judging whether the change is humanly discernible.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The 1.4.11 ACT corpus has zero cases (testCaseCount:0); F78 exists only as a technique document with no synthetic page. Its own test procedure ('Set the focus to all focusable elements ... Check that the focus indicator is visible') is a manual keyboard-and-eyeball check no ACT rule encodes. Automated tools detect outline:none but cannot judge 'looks the same as the focus indicator' or 'occluded by a same-color border' -- both require visually comparing the focused state against the resting state and a same-element border.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.11 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Choosing the correct comparison surface: subsumed borders/shadows and controls between two backgrounds

Deciding which neighbouring colour to compare against is tricky: decorative borders and shadows should be ignored, and measuring the wrong pair gives the wrong pass/fail result.

The 'Adjacent colors' guidance requires the evaluator to pick the meaningful comparison and ignore decorative elements. A border between two contrasting backgrounds, or a 3D drop-shadow, is 'subsumed into the color closest in brightness' and is NOT measured; instead you measure inside vs outside background. A background-color-only input (no border) is measured against the page (#043464 example). Getting the verdict right means deciding which color is the meaningful adjacent one and which decorative element to ignore -- e.g. an input on a dark panel whose silver border is irrelevant because the white interior already contrasts with the dark panel. A naive tool that measures the silver border against the dark panel (and flags it) gets the WRONG answer; the correct test ignores the border entirely and compares interior-to-panel.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT cases exercise input-border-vs-internal-vs-external-background or background-color-only inputs. The subsumption rule ('considered to be subsumed into the color closest in brightness') is an interpretive step -- deciding a border doesn't interfere with identifying the component -- that contrast checkers don't perform; they measure each declared border/background pair literally and over- or under-report.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.11 · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Focus-indicator geometry: which adjacency the indicator must contrast with (inner / on-the-border / partly-outside)

Where a focus indicator sits (inside, outside, or on the control's edge) decides which surface it must contrast against, so geometry, not one number, determines pass or fail.

Where a focus indicator sits determines which adjacency it must contrast with, and the SC carves out specific patterns that automation cannot disambiguate. An indicator entirely OUTSIDE need only contrast with the page the component sits on. An indicator entirely INSIDE must contrast with the adjacent color(s) within the component. An indicator that IS the component's border must contrast with BOTH adjacencies. A partly-inside/partly-outside indicator passes if EITHER part contrasts. So an inner green border that contrasts with the black outer border but NOT with the blue component background FAILS, while an inner WHITE border that contrasts with both PASSES -- the geometry, not just a single contrast number, decides it. Determining where the indicator sits relative to the visible boundary, and therefore which surface(s) it must beat, is a visual/structural judgement.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT cases build from these figures. The verdict depends on segmenting the indicator's position relative to the component's visible boundary (inside / on the border / straddling) and then choosing the correct one-or-two adjacencies -- a structural/visual determination automated contrast checkers cannot perform; they have no notion of 'inner vs outer indicator' or 'either part may contrast'.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.11 · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Negative/NA boundaries: inactive controls, hover-only treatments, essential graphics & author-choice logos, and symbolic text characters

Several borderline cases (disabled controls, hover-only highlights, brand logos, symbolic glyphs like 'X' for close) need a human to decide whether the 3:1 contrast rule even applies.

The SC defines several carve-outs whose correct answer is 'Not Applicable / Pass' and which a naive contrast scan will wrongly FAIL, plus one inclusion (symbolic text) it will wrongly ignore. (1) Inactive/disabled controls are exempt -- a faint disabled button is NOT a failure. (2) Author-supplied HOVER treatments are supplemental and need not contrast 3:1 because the pointer position is the indicator. (3) The Essential exception exempts logos/flags/sensory photos/heatmaps/medical schematics -- BUT a logo presented low-contrast by AUTHOR CHOICE (not brand-mandated, e.g. dark-grey logos on a black page revealed only on hover) is NOT exempt and DOES fail. (4) Conversely, symbolic text characters used for appearance not language (an 'X' for close, '>' as an arrow) ARE non-text content and DO need 3:1. Every one of these requires deciding category/intent (is it disabled? is this hover or a persistent state? is the low contrast brand-mandated or an author choice? is this glyph linguistic or symbolic?), which is a semantic judgement, not a measurement.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT cases verify these negative/NA boundaries or the symbolic-text inclusion. Automated checkers measure contrast on every element and will FAIL disabled controls, supplemental hover treatments, and brand logos that are genuinely exempt, while having no way to recognize the author-choice-logo reversal or to treat an 'X'/'>' glyph as a graphical object. Each verdict hinges on category/intent recognition (disabled? hover vs state? brand-mandated vs author choice? symbol vs language) -- pure semantic judgement.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.11 · priority medium

Error Identification, Labels, and Instructions (cat_9)

Act-augmented aspect — F95 — author hover content is not itself hoverable (pop-up vanishes on the cursor path from trigger to content)

A tooltip or pop-up that appears on hover vanishes the moment you move the mouse toward it, so you can never reach it to read it.

The single normative failure technique for 1.4.13 (F95) describes author-built additional content that appears on pointer hover but DISAPPEARS the moment the user moves the pointer off the trigger toward the content to read it — because visibility is bound only to mouseover/mouseout on the trigger, there is a physical gap between trigger and pop-up, or there is no shared hover region. Judging this is a SPATIAL + BEHAVIORAL call: a reviewer mentally traces the cursor path and asks whether the pop-up is reachable without the mouseout firing. A static checker sees a span[role=tooltip] that toggles display:none on mouseout and cannot tell whether the content overlaps/adjoins the trigger or is separated by a dead-zone; the Understanding states the passing arrangement 'generally implies that the additional content overlaps or is positioned adjacent to the target.' This is the geometric/event-handler reasoning a human does by simulating pointer travel under magnification.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: testCaseCountsByExpected = {} — 0 ACT rules and 0 test cases for 1.4.13, so the only normative failure technique (F95) has no failing fixture and no passing counter-fixture. Nothing in the corpus exercises pointer travel from trigger to pop-up.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.13 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Applicability gate — author-controlled tooltip vs. user-agent title= tooltip (and modal-dialog carve-out)

Telling apart a browser's built-in title= tooltip (which this rule ignores) from a custom one the developer built to look identical, since only the custom one has to follow the rules.

The SC explicitly does NOT apply when the additional content's appearance is 'completely controlled by the user agent' — canonically the browser rendering of the title attribute — and modal dialogs are also out of scope. F95 bakes the UA carve-out into its test (condition #2: 'controlled by the user agent, not the author'). The judgment-heavy case is attributing WHO controls the appearance: distinguishing (a) a plain title= tooltip (out of scope, passes by exclusion) from (b) an AUTHOR-built div styled/scripted to LOOK native (in scope, must meet all three conditions) and (c) the inverse where the author suppresses the native tooltip (title='') and reimplements it in JS. A static tool sees both a title= and a div and cannot reason that the visible bubble is the author's div, not the UA's tooltip — yet getting this attribution wrong flips PASS↔FAIL for the entire criterion. The modal-dialog exclusion likewise needs an N/A judgment (a dialog takes focus, so it is not hover/focus-transient content).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The exclusion carve-outs are listed as corpus gaps (no case distinguishes a native title tooltip from an author-built tooltip; no N/A case for modals). With 0 fixtures there is no example anchoring the in-scope/out-of-scope boundary, so the whole gating predicate is unmodeled.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.13 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Dismissible Method 2 — no/broken keyboard dismiss (cannot clear content without moving hover or focus)

A hovered or focused pop-up covers other content but offers no key (like Escape) to clear it, forcing low-vision users to move the mouse and lose what they were reading.

SCR39 requires hover content 'can be closed without moving the pointer away from the trigger' and focus content 'closed without moving the focus away from the trigger' — by Esc, another documented shortcut, or activating the trigger. The judgment-heavy failures: (a) NO dismiss mechanism at all, so the user must physically move the pointer/focus to clear it, defeating the low-vision pan workaround; (b) an Esc handler scoped wrong (e.g., bound to the trigger which has lost focus, so Esc is inert while the bubble shows); (c) a 'close' that only works by moving focus INTO the pop-up, which can re-obscure. A static tool can detect that a keydown listener exists but cannot judge whether pressing Esc actually clears THIS content while hover/focus is retained on the trigger — that requires interpreting handler scope against the user's physical situation. The Understanding's whole motivation is the magnified user who cannot afford to move the pointer to dismiss obscuring text.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The Dismissible-mechanism limb is listed as absent — no case tests presence/absence of an Esc/keyboard dismissal without moving hover/focus. With no fixtures there is no failing 'no-Esc' or 'wrongly-scoped-Esc' example.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.13 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Dismissible Method 1 — pop-up obscures meaningful content (beyond the white-space / decorative exception)

A pop-up with no dismiss key sits on top of real content or controls rather than empty space, hiding information the user still needs.

When no dismiss mechanism is provided, the SC can still be met if the content is positioned 'so that it does not obscure any other content including the trigger, with the exception of white space and purely decorative content.' This is a VISUAL + SEMANTIC judgment: does the pop-up cover meaningful content/controls, or only white space or a 'background graphic which provides no information'? A checker can compute that two boxes overlap, but cannot judge whether the covered region is purely decorative versus information-bearing. It also cannot apply the Understanding's nuance that for a LARGE trigger, positioning content away to avoid overlap may itself harm discoverability, so only Method 2 is appropriate — meaning 'obscures the trigger/content' is not always disqualifying. Distinguishing acceptable overlap of decorative whitespace from unacceptable obscuring of content is squarely human and visual.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The positioning/obscuring limb is listed as absent — no case tests obscuring vs. non-obscuring placement, and there is no low-vision/magnification fixture exercising content that obscures the trigger or adjacent meaningful content.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.13 · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Persistent — auto-dismiss on timeout / closing for a disallowed reason vs. legitimate info-invalidation

A hover or focus pop-up closes itself on a timer or a stray mouse move while the user is still reading it, instead of staying until they leave or dismiss it.

SCR39 requires the content 'stays visible and does not automatically close after a time,' and the Understanding says it should remain until exactly one of: the user removes hover/focus, the user dismisses it, OR the conveyed information becomes invalid (e.g., a 'busy' message). The judgment-heavy failures: (a) a tooltip on a setTimeout that auto-hides after N seconds while the user is still hovering/focused (a magnifier user needs that time to change magnification and pan); (b) content that closes for the WRONG reason (scroll, slight pointer jitter within the trigger); versus the legitimate exception — (c) content that disappears because its info BECAME INVALID (a 'saving…' that becomes 'saved'), which must NOT be flagged. Telling a disallowed timeout from a legitimate information-invalidation requires understanding the MEANING of the content over time — a human reasoning, not a timer-presence check. A static checker that merely sees setTimeout cannot tell which case it is.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The Persistent limb is listed as absent — none of the three persistence-end conditions, nor the auto-dismiss-on-timeout failure ('does not automatically close after a time'), is tested; there is no outcome variety to anchor the valid-info-invalidation exception.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.13 · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Perceive-on-focus — hover-triggered content with NO keyboard-focus path to reveal it

Useful content shows only when you hover with a mouse and never appears on keyboard focus, so keyboard-only users can never see information that mouse users get.

The Additional Notes require that 'content which can be triggered via pointer hover should also be able to be triggered by keyboard focus' (cross-referencing 2.1.1), because the SC's core intent is that users can PERCEIVE the additional content; if the only reveal is mouse hover, keyboard and many AT users can never perceive it. The judgment is semantic and two-part: the reviewer must (a) recognize that the hover content carries information not otherwise available (not redundant decoration) AND (b) determine the trigger is non-focusable or has no focus handler. A static tool can note that a tooltip is bound to mouseover-but-not-focus, but cannot judge whether the trigger SHOULD be focusable (is it interactive? is the content meaningful?) — recognizing 'this hidden content matters and is unreachable by keyboard' is a contextual call. This is the focus-modality half of SCR39, which carries a DIFFERENT checklist than hover (persistent + dismissible only; no hoverable requirement).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The keyboard-focus-triggered variant is listed as wholly absent, and there is no input-modality split in the corpus (hover vs. focus require different SCR39 checklists). With 0 fixtures, the focus path of the trigger is entirely unmodeled.

Associates with: guideline SC 1.4.13 · priority medium

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 0ssw9k — Scrollable content can be reached with sequential focus navigation

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 2.1.1

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/0ssw9k/proposed/

Proposed

Scrollable content can be reached with sequential focus navigation

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

2.1.1: Keyboard (Level A) ,

2.1.3: Keyboard (No Exception) (Level AAA)

Description

This rule checks that scrollable elements or their descendants can be reached with sequential focus navigation so that they can be scrolled by keyboard

Applicability

This rule applies to any HTML element that has visible children in the flat tree , and for which at least one of the following is true:

  • the element has a horizontal scroll distance greater than the computed left or right padding of the element; or
  • the element has a vertical scroll distance greater than the computed top or bottom padding of the element.

Expectation

For each target element, at least one of the following is true:

  • the element is included in sequential focus navigation ; or
  • the element has a descendant in the flat tree that is included in sequential focus navigation ; or
  • the element is inert .

Background

To ensure there is some element from which arrow keys can be used to control the scroll position, focus must be on or in a scrollable region. If scripts are used to prevent the keyboard events from reaching the scrollable region, this could still cause a keyboard accessibility issue. This must be tested separately.

This rule only applies to elements who scroll content in the same document. Elements such as iframes that embed other documents may also be scrollable, but for them it is the embedded document that scrolls, not the content in the same document. Such scenarios are tested separately with rules such as Iframe with negative tabindex has no interactive elements .

Assumptions

This rule assumes that all scrollable elements with visible content need to be keyboard accessible. Scrollable elements that do not need to be keyboard accessible, perhaps because their content is purely decorative , the scroll area is whitespace, or because scroll can be controlled in some other keyboard accessible way such as through a button or custom scrollbar, may fail this rule but still satisfy success criterion 2.1.1 Keyboard .

Accessibility Support

Some browsers will automatically make any scrollable element focusable to ensure keyboard accessibility. However, the browser does not include these elements in sequential focus navigation when it has a negative number as a tabindex attribute value .

Some browsers restrict scrolling to the content box of elements; while others allow to scroll the full border box , hence including the element’s padding. This results in some elements being scrollable with a browser but not with another.

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule akn7bn — Iframe with interactive elements is not excluded from tab-order

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 2.1.1

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/akn7bn/proposed/

Proposed

Iframe with interactive elements is not excluded from tab-order

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

2.1.1: Keyboard (Level A) ,

2.1.3: Keyboard (No Exception) (Level AAA)

Description

This rule checks that iframe elements which contain keyboard focusable elements are not excluded from sequential focus navigation.

Applicability

This rule applies to any iframe element that is not inert and that contains at least one element for which all the following are true:

  • the element is visible ; and
  • the element is part of the sequential focus navigation order of the iframe ’s document .

An element is contained in a nested browsing context if its owner document is the container document of the nested browsing context .

Expectation

The test target does not have a negative number as a tabindex attribute value .

Background

Setting the tabindex attribute of an iframe element to a negative value effectively excludes its content from the tab-order of the page. A button may be in the tab-order of an iframe , but if the iframe itself is taken from the tab-order, the button is effectively keyboard inaccessible.

Each document, including documents inside an iframe , has its own sequential focus navigation order . These focus orders are combined to get the page’s global tab-order (called the flattened tabindex-ordered focus navigation scope ). For an iframe with a negative tabindex, its sequential focus navigation order is not included in the page’s global tab-order (as a consequence for the rules to build the tabindex-ordered focus navigation scope ).

Assumptions

This rule assumes that interactive content inside iframe elements is used to provide functionality. If the interactive content does not provide functionality, for example a button that does nothing when clicked, success criterion 2.1.1 may be satisfied, even if the rule is failed.

Accessibility Support

There are no accessibility support issues known.

  • WCAG Technique G202: Ensuring keyboard control for all functionality

Focus Traps and Visibility (cat_5)

Trusted Tester — SC 2.1.1

SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A) — TT Tests 4.A, 4.B

TT section: 4. Keyboard Access and Focus · Baseline: 1. Keyboard Access

WCAG SC 2.1.1: All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface without requiring

specific timings for individual keystrokes, except where the underlying function requires input that depends on

the path of the user's movement and not just the endpoints.

Identify Content (applicability)

1. Use the mouse/pointer to determine available functions provided by interactive elements (drop-down menus,

form fields, revealing/hiding content, tooltips, AND all interactive interface components).

2. Use the mouse to identify instances where interactive elements provide information essential to

understanding or operating page content.

  • Note (path-dependent exception): 2.1.1 does not apply to functions requiring input that depends on the

*path* of movement, not just endpoints (e.g., free-hand drawing). Don't omit functions that meet Identify

Content; a 508 exception may apply but is out of test scope.

  • DNA for 4.A and 4.B if the page has no user-activated functionality.

---

Test 4.A — 2.1.1-keyboard-access

Test Condition: *All functionality can be accessed and executed using only the keyboard.*

How to Test

1. Identify functionality and essential information provided by interactive elements.

  • a. Ways to identify functionality: mouse, touch screen, voice commands, documentation (e.g., shortcut keys).
  • b. ANDI "title attributes" feature (focusable elements) helps identify essential info in title attributes.

2. Use the keyboard to operate identified functionality and/or access the essential information: tab to the

element and execute (e.g., press Enter with focus on the element).

  • a. For interactive elements with title attributes, place keyboard focus; if the tooltip does not appear

within two seconds, keyboard focus will not reveal the title information.

  • b. If an element has no keyboard access, determine whether another keyboard-accessible method on the

page provides the same functionality (e.g., one of two print methods is keyboard accessible).

  • c. If an element does not provide access to essential information via keyboard, determine whether the

information is available elsewhere on the page (e.g., as text).

Evaluate Results (PASS if BOTH true)

1. All functionality can be accessed and executed using the keyboard, AND

2. All essential information can be accessed via keyboard OR is available elsewhere on the page.

Notes
  • Changes to functionality that occur automatically or as a result of interaction should be included.
  • Information is "essential" when necessary to execute an action or understand information and relationships.
  • Title/tooltip information that is not essential does not require keyboard access.
  • Not all browsers visually display the title as a tooltip on keyboard focus.

---

Test 4.B — 2.1.1-no-keystroke-timing

Test Condition: *Individual keystrokes do not require specific timings for activation of functionality.*

How to Test

1. Continue from Test 4.A.

2. Determine whether there are instances where the timing of keystrokes is required to activate the element

(e.g., the speed at which password keystrokes are typed is part of password authentication).

3. If timing-dependent functionality exists, determine if another keyboard-accessible method on the page does

not require specific timing.

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. A keyboard method is provided for functionality to be activated without requiring users to perform specific

timings for activation.

Act-augmented aspect — Pointer-only (mouse/touch/gesture) handlers on non-native elements with no keyboard equivalent (F54)

A control built from a plain div, span, or image fires only on mouse or touch events with no keyboard handler, so keyboard-only users can never reach or trigger it.

A function is wired up exclusively through pointing-device events (onclick/onmousedown/onmouseup/onmouseover, or touch/pointer/gesture listeners) on an element that has no native keyboard behaviour and no tabindex, role, or key handler — typically a div, span, img, li, or svg. The page looks fully operable, but a keyboard-only user can never reach or invoke the function. The human-judgment core is recognizing that a given visual control (a 'Next' arrow image, a star-rating widget, a custom 'Add to cart' tile, a swipeable carousel) actually IS interactive functionality whose only trigger is a pointer event — i.e. mapping pixels-that-do-something to the absence of any keyboard path — then confirming there is no keyboard route anywhere on the page. This is the canonical F54 failure and the core of Trusted Tester's 'use the mouse to determine available functions, then operate them with the keyboard' procedure.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Neither ACT rule (0ssw9k scroll reachability, akn7bn iframe tab order) inspects element event handlers at all. The corpus contains zero pages where 'this thing does something on click but nothing on keyboard'. The judgment requires using the mouse to discover that a visually-styled element is functional and is semantic, not detectable by a static checker that has no concept of which non-native elements are 'meant' to be operable.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.1 · Trusted Tester 4.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Emulated links/controls that are reachable but not truly activatable by keyboard — wrong element, Enter-only, or no-op handler (F42)

A fake button or link you can Tab to but that ignores Enter or Space (or only one of them), so it looks operable yet does nothing for keyboard users.

The subtle slice between a bare pointer-only fake control and a properly built one. Markup that reads as compliant (tabindex present, an onkeypress/onkeydown attribute present, role=button/link) but where keyboard ACTIVATION silently fails: (a) a <div tabindex=0 onclick> with no key handler at all — focusable, so it appears 'in the tab order', but Enter/Space do nothing because a div has no implicit activation; (b) an onkeypress that listens ONLY for Enter (keyCode 13) while onclick does the work, so Space (and any keydown-only AT) gets nothing; (c) a handler that calls preventDefault/returns early on keyboard, swallowing activation; (d) an <a> WITHOUT href (just onclick) that drops out of the tab order entirely despite looking like a real link in source. F42 only fails 2.1.1 when keyboard activation actually fails — so the human must FOCUS the element and actually PRESS the key, in both Enter and Space, rather than trust the presence of attributes.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT corpus has no scripted-control cases at all; its only 'pass via focusable descendant' uses a genuine native <a href>. There is no case where a fake control is keyboard-reachable-but-not-activatable, no Enter-only/Space-missing handler, and no href-less anchor — so the activation-verification dimension is entirely untested. A static checker sees tabindex+role+a key listener and reads it as compliant; only behavioural key-press verification reveals the gap.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.1 · Trusted Tester 4.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Drag-and-drop / endpoint-style functions without the path exception, lacking a keyboard equivalent (G90 / G202 / Understanding)

A drag-and-drop action like reordering a list or dropping a file has no keyboard alternative, locking out keyboard users from a task mouse users can do.

The SC exempts only functions whose input depends on the PATH of movement, not just the endpoints (free-hand drawing, watercolour). Reordering a list by drag, dragging a file into a dropzone, sorting kanban cards, dragging a map pin, or resizing a panel are endpoint-dependent and therefore do NOT qualify for the exception — they REQUIRE a keyboard equivalent (cut/paste, move up/down buttons, an 'enter position' field, type-to-set coordinates). Two human judgments no checker can make: (1) decide whether a given drag operation is genuinely path-dependent (exempt) or merely endpoint-dependent (must be keyboard-operable) — a semantic call about the underlying function; and (2) determine whether SOME keyboard alternative for the same function exists ANYWHERE on the page, since G202/Understanding allow a separate keyboard mode rather than per-control parity. A drag-to-reorder list with no up/down buttons fails; the same list WITH up/down buttons passes — identical drag markup, opposite verdicts.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: There is no drag-and-drop, sorting, resizing, or dropzone case anywhere in the 2.1.1 corpus. The exception clause (path of movement vs endpoints) is never exercised, and the 'keyboard alternative exists elsewhere on the page' allowance is never modeled. Both ACT rules check single-control reachability, not function-level keyboard parity, and a checker cannot reason about whether a drag is path- or endpoint-dependent.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.1 · Trusted Tester 4.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Hover/pointer-only revealed content carrying essential information or controls, with no keyboard path (Trusted Tester essential-information branch)

Menus, tooltips, or row buttons appear only on mouse hover and never on keyboard focus, hiding essential information or the only way to act from keyboard users.

Content or controls that appear only on mouseover/hover (CSS :hover dropdowns/megamenus, JS mouseover tooltips, hover-revealed action buttons on table rows or cards) with no focus/keyboard trigger and no equivalent elsewhere. Trusted Tester explicitly splits the SC into operable-functionality AND access-to-essential-information, and gives the precise tooltip nuance: place keyboard focus and if the information does not appear within two seconds, keyboard focus will not reveal it — then ask whether that information is available elsewhere on the page. Two human judgments: (1) is the hover-revealed content merely decorative/redundant (no failure) or does it carry ESSENTIAL information or the only access to a function (failure if keyboard can't get it AND it's not elsewhere)?; (2) does focus actually reveal the same content that hover does? Both demand reasoning about meaning and interacting in two modalities. Distinct from 1.4.13's persistence/dismissal requirements — this is purely about keyboard reachability of the function/info.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT corpus has no hover-revealed menus, tooltips, or row-action affordances, and never models the 'essential information available elsewhere' allowance. 0ssw9k/akn7bn never inspect :hover or mouseover content. The essential-vs-decorative distinction and the two-second title-reveal check are wholly absent, and neither is decidable by a static checker (it cannot judge whether hidden text is 'essential' or redundant).

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.1 · Trusted Tester 4.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Scripts that remove or steal focus the moment it is received (F55) — focus cannot rest on a control

A script yanks focus away the instant a control receives it, so even though you can Tab to the control, focus never stays long enough for you to use it.

Content that would normally receive focus has that focus stripped by script (onfocus="this.blur()", a handler that immediately moves focus elsewhere, or a focusin listener that bounces focus back to the top on every Tab). The element appears in the tab order and is technically reachable, but focus cannot remain on it long enough to operate it, so keyboard operation is impossible. This is dynamic behaviour: the static DOM shows a normal, well-formed, focusable control — only by actually tabbing through and watching where focus lands does a human discover focus being yanked away. The judgment is temporal/behavioural: 'I pressed Tab, the indicator flashed on the field, then jumped away.' Real-world variants include an overlay that re-focuses its first element on every focusin, or a sticky-header script that re-focuses the logo whenever a lower control gains focus.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0ssw9k only checks whether a tab stop EXISTS on/within a scroll region; it never checks whether focus can persist there. akn7bn checks iframe tab inclusion. Nothing in the corpus runs a focus-event handler or models focus being removed after receipt, so the 'reachable but focus won't stay' failure has zero coverage. Detecting it requires running the page and observing focus movement — a behavioural trace, not static markup analysis.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.1 · Trusted Tester 4.A · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Keystroke-timing dependence: functions that require specific timing of individual keystrokes (Test 4.B / second SC limb)

A control only works if you hold a key down, press keys within a tight window, or type at a set speed, which many keyboard users cannot reliably do.

The second normative limb of 2.1.1: 'without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes.' A function may be fully keyboard-reachable and activatable yet still FAIL because it demands a timing of keystrokes that keyboard-interface users (especially speech-input, sip-and-puff, switch, and on-screen-keyboard users) cannot reliably produce: keys that must be held down for an extended period before registering, multiple keystrokes that must be entered within a short window, double-press/rapid-repeat shortcuts with a tight interval, or input where the speed/rhythm of typing is itself part of the function (e.g. keystroke-dynamics 'authentication'). Understanding gives the exact examples. The judgment is behavioural and temporal — a human must notice that activation depends on HOW FAST or HOW LONG keys are pressed, not merely on WHICH keys. Per Test 4.B, a pass is still possible if another keyboard-accessible method on the page does not require specific timing.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Both ACT rules (scroll reachability, iframe tab order) test only the operability limb and never the timing limb. There is no corpus case where a control activates only with a held key, a rapid key sequence, or speed-of-typing input. A static checker cannot infer timing requirements from markup; this requires observing time-dependent input behaviour, and judging whether an untimed keyboard alternative exists elsewhere.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.1 · Trusted Tester 4.B · priority medium
