C.9.2.1.2 — SC 2.1.2 No keyboard trap
C.9.2.1.2         No keyboard trap
   Type of assessment                                          Inspection
   Requirement           1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.
   Preconditions
   Procedure             1. Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.2 No
                         Keyboard Trap according to WCAG Conformance Requirements stated in clause 9.6.
   Result                Pass: Check 1 is true
                         Fail: Check 1 is false
                         Not applicable: If any requirement precondition is false or the web page does not
                         contain content relevant to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap. (Do
                         not need to meet or test)

Trusted Tester — SC 2.1.2

SC 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (Level A) — TT Test 4.C

TT section: 4. Keyboard Access and Focus · Baseline: 1. Keyboard Access · also Non-Interference (Con.5)

WCAG SC 2.1.2: If keyboard focus can be moved to a component using a keyboard interface, then focus can be

moved away from that component using only a keyboard interface, and, if it requires more than unmodified arrow

or tab keys or other standard exit methods, the user is advised of the method for moving focus away.

Test 4.C — 2.1.2-no-keyboard-trap

Test Condition: *There is no keyboard trap.*

DNA if the page has no components that can receive keyboard focus.

How to Test

1. Use standard navigation keys (e.g., TAB, SHIFT+TAB, arrow keys, CTRL+TAB, etc.) to navigate through all

keyboard focusable elements on the page.

2. Determine whether there are any instances where keyboard navigation becomes trapped:

  • a. Keyboard users are unable to move away from an element (e.g., using TAB or an arrow key).
  • b. Keyboard access is restricted to a small section of the page with no way to navigate out of the "loop"

to the rest of the page.

  • *Note:* Keyboard focus should remain within a modal dialog box until it is closed (per Test 4.F

Step 3); however, check for keyboard traps within the dialog.

  • *Note:* If a section of a page requires input or interaction before allowing focus to progress to the

rest of the page, this is not a failure.

3. If a keyboard trap is found:

  • a. Inspect any contextual/application help and documentation for notification of **available alternate

keyboard commands** (non-standard controls, access keys, hotkeys) to escape/avoid the trap.

  • b. Determine whether the alternate command(s) work.
Evaluate Results (PASS if ALL true)

1. Keyboard focus can be moved away from an element using either:

  • a. Standard navigation keys, OR
  • b. Custom keystrokes that are documented and available to users in the application.

AND

2. Keyboard focus can be moved away from each section of the page containing elements (not trapped in a "loop"

preventing access to other elements) using either standard navigation keys OR documented custom keystrokes.

Note
  • In case of a keyboard trap, continue to test interactive elements after the trap by using the mouse to bypass

the trap, or by refreshing the page and using the keyboard to navigate backwards through the page.

Act-augmented aspect — F10 cross-format / embedded-application trap (iframe, object, embed, plug-in, shadow-DOM widget) — the SC's central and only mapped failure technique

Keyboard focus moves into an embedded frame, plug-in, or widget and gets stuck there, with no way to Tab back out to the rest of the page.

F10 is the single failure technique mapped to 2.1.2 and it describes the SC's archetypal scenario: keyboard focus enters embedded or cross-format content and cannot be moved back out to the host document. Every ACT case simulates traps with inline JS onblur/onkeydown on bare native <button>s in one document; ZERO cases contain an <iframe>, <object>, <embed>, applet, web-component/Shadow-DOM widget, or any document/format boundary. The human-judgment surface: deciding whether focus that has entered an embedded boundary can return to the parent, whether the embedded content provides an exit, and whether any escape advice is present, keyboard-reachable, and accurate across a boundary the page author may not control. This is exactly the F10 intent the corpus never exercises.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: All ACT cases use plain inline-scripted native buttons in a single document; none contains an iframe, object, embed, applet, web-component/Shadow-DOM widget, or any cross-format boundary, so the corpus never exercises F10 at all despite F10 being the only failure technique listed for the SC. A static checker cannot drive focus across an iframe/shadow boundary and observe whether the next Tab returns to the parent.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.2 · Trusted Tester 4.C · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Modal-dialog / popover focus restriction: legitimate containment vs. an undismissable trap (the Understanding carve-out)

A dialog that keeps focus inside itself is fine only if you can close it by keyboard, such as Escape or a reachable Close button, otherwise it traps you.

The Understanding explicitly states that intentional focus restriction inside a modal dialog or popover does NOT fail the SC, AS LONG AS the user knows how to untrap and leave. Trusted Tester Test 4.C reinforces this: focus SHOULD remain within a modal until it is closed, but you must check for traps WITHIN it. This poses a pure human-judgment question the corpus never asks: is a focus-cycling dialog a CONFORMANT modal (a discoverable, keyboard-operable dismiss — Esc, or a reachable Cancel/Close button) or a TRAP (no keyboard-reachable way to close, a non-functional close, or a focus cycle that EXCLUDES the close control)? Distinguishing the two requires understanding the dialog's intent and confirming the dismiss path actually works — semantic and behavioral judgment a tool cannot make. No corpus case uses role=dialog, aria-modal, <dialog>, popover, or any focus-cycling container.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The corpus contains no dialog/popover construct of any kind; its only focus-cycling cases (Failed 1/2 self-refocus, the 2-button ping-pong) are framed as unconditional traps, never as the legitimate-modal carve-out, so the conformant-containment-vs-trap distinction is never tested. A checker can detect a focus cycle but cannot judge whether the cycle includes a working keyboard-operable dismiss.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.2 · Trusted Tester 4.C · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Esc and other platform 'standard exit methods' as the untrap mechanism — and whether they actually fire

A focus loop that releases when you press a normal exit key like Escape is acceptable and needs no instructions, so flagging it as a trap would be a false alarm.

The Understanding names Esc as a commonly-used standard exit method and notes other platform-specific standard methods may exist; crucially, if focus can be moved away using a STANDARD exit method, NO advice is required — the advice clause only triggers for non-standard methods. Every scripted custom-exit case in the corpus uses Ctrl+M, a non-standard combo that always requires advice. The corpus therefore never tests the judgment call of whether a given key counts as a standard exit method (so no advice is owed), nor whether an Esc-based exit actually works. A human must (a) decide a key qualifies as standard for the platform and (b) verify pressing it genuinely releases focus — behavior a tool cannot evaluate and which the spec deliberately leaves to author/auditor interpretation. This is a false-positive trap: a checker seeing a focus cycle with no advice text would wrongly flag a page that passes because Esc releases focus.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No corpus case uses Esc (or any platform standard exit beyond Tab/Shift-Tab) as the release mechanism; all scripted exits are Ctrl+M, collapsing the standard-vs-non-standard distinction. The spec leaves 'standard exit method' to human interpretation, and verifying that Esc actually releases focus requires driving the keyboard — neither is automatable.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.2 · Trusted Tester 4.C · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Arrow-key / roving-tabindex composite-widget traps (menu, grid, listbox, radiogroup, tablist, slider)

In a menu or grid, arrow keys move you around inside the widget but Tab is also swallowed, so keyboard users cannot move focus out to the rest of the page.

The SC text and Trusted Tester both name unmodified arrow keys as standard navigation, and the Understanding's calendar-widget example is built on arrow navigation. Composite widgets implemented with roving tabindex commonly capture arrow keys inside the widget; the conformance question is whether Tab/Shift-Tab still moves focus OUT of the widget even when arrows are captured. The corpus contains NO arrow-driven widget at all — it only tests Tab/Shift-Tab on flat lists of buttons. The judgment a human must make is semantic: recognize the construct as a composite widget, understand its expected interaction model (arrows move within, Tab moves out), and confirm Tab is not also swallowed. A roving-tabindex widget that also intercepts Tab is a trap; one that lets Tab pass is fine — a distinction tools cannot draw without driving both arrow and Tab keys and understanding widget semantics.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Zero corpus cases use arrow-key handling, roving tabindex, or any composite-widget role (menu/grid/listbox/radiogroup/tablist/slider); the corpus never tests the standard arrow-navigation surface the SC explicitly calls out. Determining whether arrows-captured-but-Tab-exits is a pass requires driving both key classes and understanding the widget's intended model — not automatable.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.2 · Trusted Tester 4.C · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Multi-element region loop: G21 mechanism #1 (Tab must exit the subset after the final location) where no advice is owed

Tabbing through a section wraps back to that section's first control instead of moving on to the rest of the page, trapping the user in an endless loop within one region.

G21's first sufficient mechanism is purely behavioral and needs NO advice: ensure that Tab exits the subset of content after it reaches the final navigation location. The distinguishing failure is a within-region LOOP — focus reaches the last control of a sub-section and Tab wraps back to that section's first control instead of progressing to the rest of the page (Trusted Tester 2.b: access restricted to a small section with no way to navigate out of the loop). The corpus's loops are degenerate — Failed 1/2 self-refocus on ONE element, and the documented-exit ping-pong cases all carry advice or a help link. There is no genuine MULTI-element region loop with NO advice where the only question is the behavioral one: does the final Tab leave the region or wrap? Judging this requires Tabbing to the LAST element of the region and observing whether the next Tab crosses the region boundary — and recognizing that since no escape advice is owed for plain Tab, the page passes iff the loop is broken.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The corpus has no substantive multi-element region whose final Tab wraps internally; its loops are single-element self-refocus or are accompanied by documented Ctrl+M advice/help links, so the pure G21-#1 behavioral question (does the LAST Tab exit?) is never isolated. Detecting it requires Tabbing to a region's last control and observing whether the next Tab crosses the region boundary — driving the keyboard, not static analysis.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.1.2 · Trusted Tester 4.C · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Required-input / sequential-gate exception: a section that demands interaction before focus progresses is NOT a failure

A section that won't let focus move on until you fill a required field looks like a trap but is fine, as long as you can satisfy it by keyboard.

Trusted Tester explicitly carves out a non-failure: if a section of a page requires input or interaction before allowing focus to progress to the rest of the page, this is NOT a keyboard trap failure. The corpus has NO form scenario at all — no <form>, <input>, <select>, or <textarea> anywhere — so this exception is never exercised. The judgment is semantic and easy to get wrong: a required-field gate where focus cannot advance until the user completes the field LOOKS like a trap (Tab does not move focus forward) but is conformant; an actual trap is one where focus cannot advance even AFTER the required interaction is completed, OR where the gate cannot be satisfied by keyboard at all. Distinguishing 'intentional gate the user can satisfy by keyboard' from 'genuine trap' requires understanding the interaction's intent and verifying the gate is keyboard-satisfiable — judgment a tool cannot make.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No required-form-field / sequential-gate scenario exists in the corpus (no form, input, select, or textarea anywhere), so the input-gate exception — a section that legitimately holds focus until the user completes an interaction — is never tested. A checker sees 'Tab does not advance' and cannot tell whether the gate is conformant (satisfiable by keyboard) or a trap.

Act-augmented aspect — Documented custom-exit advice that is unreachable or inaccurate beyond the corpus's Ctrl+M-before-trap pattern

When escaping a focus loop needs a special key combo, the instructions must actually reach the trapped keyboard user and correctly name the key, not be hidden or wrong.

TT Evaluate-Results 1.b requires custom escape keystrokes to be DOCUMENTED AND AVAILABLE, and How-to-Test 3.a/3.b require checking that contextual help discloses the alternate command and that the command actually works. The corpus covers advice-before-trap, advice-within-trap, and a help-link inside the subset (Passed 4/5/6), plus three failure modes (never advised, generic/non-instructive, named-but-broken). But it tests these only on the Ctrl+M-on-flat-buttons template and only with advice that is either plainly present or plainly absent. The uncovered judgment surface is advice REACHABILITY and ACCURACY in harder forms: advice that exists but is itself only reachable by mouse or after the trap; advice located only in collapsed/off-screen help the keyboard user inside the trap cannot get to; advice that names a key combo with a subtle defect (right key, wrong modifier); or advice that is technically present but describes a DIFFERENT trap. Judging whether documented advice is genuinely AVAILABLE to a trapped keyboard user, and whether it accurately matches the working escape, requires reading intent and driving the keyboard.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT tests advice only as plainly-present (before/within trap, help link) or plainly-absent/generic/named-but-broken, all on the Ctrl+M-flat-button template. It never tests advice that is present but unreachable by a trapped keyboard user, hidden in collapsed/off-screen help, located only AFTER the trap, or accurate-looking but subtly mismatched — the reachability/accuracy judgment G21 demands ('accessible manner within the subset'). A checker cannot judge whether advice is genuinely reachable from inside the trap or whether it matches the real escape.

ACT Rule 2779a5 — HTML page has non-empty title

status: approved

implement: auto,manual,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 2.4.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/2779a5/proposed/

Proposed

HTML page has non-empty title

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

2.4.2: Page Titled (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that a non-embedded HTML page has a non-empty title.

Applicability

This rule applies to the root element of the web page , if it is an html element.

Expectation 1

Each target element has at least one descendant that is a title element .

Expectation 2

For each target element, the first HTML title element that is a descendant of the document element has children that are text nodes that are not only whitespace .

Background

This rule is only applicable to non-embedded HTML pages. HTML pages embedded into other documents, such as through iframe or object elements are not applicable because they are not web pages according to the definition in WCAG.

Assumptions

This rule assumes that Success Criterion 2.4.2 Page Titled does not require that a document only has one title element, nor that it is a child of the head element of a document. While this is invalid in HTML, the HTML specification describes what should happen in case of multiple titles, and titles outside the head element. Because of this, neither of these validation issues causes a conformance problem for WCAG. Regardless of whether this is required by 2.4.2 Page Titled, failing this rule means the success criterion is not satisfied.

This rule assumes that the title of the page is not provided by a higher-level protocol. For example, the subject field of an email authored in HTML can provide a title without requiring a title element. In such a case, this rule will fail while Success Criterion 2.4.2 Page Titled may still be satisfied.

Accessibility Support

There are no accessibility support issues known.

ACT Rule c4a8a4 — HTML page title is descriptive

status: approved

implement: auto,manual,semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 2.4.2

Proposed

HTML page title is descriptive

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

2.4.2: Page Titled (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that the first title in an HTML web page describes the topic or purpose of that page.

Applicability

This rule applies to the document title of each html web page , except if one of the following is true:

  • The html web page has no document title ; or
  • The document title contains only whitespace text nodes .

Expectation

The target element describes the topic or purpose of the overall content of the document .

Background

The title elements of embedded documents, such as those in iframe , object , or svg elements, are not applicable because those are not web pages according to the definition in WCAG.

The HTML specification - The title element requires documents to only have one title element; and title elements to be children of the head element of a document. However, current HTML specification also describes what should happen in case of multiple titles, and titles outside the head element. Because of this, neither of these validation issues causes a conformance problem for WCAG.

Assumptions

There are currently no assumptions.

Accessibility Support
  • This rule assumes that browsers only recognize the first title element if multiple title elements are present in the document . Testing shows that this in general is the case. Therefore the scope of this rule is limited to only checking the first title element in a document.

Trusted Tester — SC 2.4.2

SC 2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A) — TT Tests 12.A, 12.B

TT section: 12. Page Titles, Frames, and iFrames → Page Titles · Baseline: 11. Page Titles

WCAG SC 2.4.2: Web pages have titles that describe topic or purpose.

Identify Content

All web pages. Test Conditions 12.A and 12.B always apply — you may NOT evaluate as DNA.

---

Test 12.A — 2.4.2-page-title-defined

Test Condition: *A <title> element is defined for the web page.*

How to Test

1. Launch ANDI: structures. Review the alerts in ANDI's "Accessibility Alerts" section to determine whether

ANDI displays either Invalid HTML Alert:

  • a. "Page has no <title>"
  • b. "Page <title> cannot be empty"
Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. A Page Title is defined for the web page.

---

Test 12.B — 2.4.2-page-title-purpose

Test Condition: *The <title> element identifies the contents or purpose of the web page.*

How to Test

1. Launch ANDI: structures → "more details" → "page title." A modal dialog will appear with the identified

page title listed.

2. Evaluate the purpose and content of the web page.

3. Determine whether the Page Title is a meaningful representation or indication of page content.

  • a. If the web page is part of a set of web pages, determine whether the Page Title is sufficient to

distinguish the web page from other pages.

  • b. For documents or web applications, the name of the document or web application would be sufficient to

describe the purpose of the page.

Evaluate Results (PASS if ALL true)

1. The Page Title accurately identifies the contents or purpose of the web page, AND

2. If the web page is part of a set of web pages, the Page Title accurately distinguishes the web page from other

pages in the web site.

> Note: A web application is an application that runs in a web browser (such as webmail) and may not have a

> URL that changes as content changes.

Act-augmented aspect — Title is a non-empty but non-identifying artifact: authoring-tool default, unfilled placeholder, or filename/code string

The page title is a leftover like 'Untitled Document', a 'TODO' placeholder, or a filename such as 'report.html', which is technically present but tells the user nothing about the page.

F25 names a family of title strings that are non-empty, valid, and pass the presence rule (2779a5), yet fail 2.4.2 because the string itself identifies nothing about the page's content. Three sub-classes, all requiring semantic recognition that the string is residue rather than content: (a) authoring-tool defaults ('Untitled Document', 'Enter the title of your HTML document here', 'No Title', 'New Page 1'); (b) filler/placeholder/unfilled-template text ('Lorem ipsum', 'TODO: title', 'PAGE TITLE HERE', 'xxxxx', 'test'); (c) filenames or machine identifiers that are not descriptive in their own right ('report.html', 'spk12.html', SKUs, build hashes, Drupal-style 'node/3387', raw slugs like 'page_2_final_v3'). The c4a8a4 descriptiveness corpus contains NONE of these named strings — its only non-descriptive case is a wrong-real-subject title (apple vs clementine) and a site-name-only search page. A checker cannot flag any of these because each is non-empty, valid UTF-8, often dictionary words, and structurally indistinguishable from a legitimate terse title; only semantic recognition that 'Untitled Document' announces no-title, or that '.html' / a hash signals machine residue, catches it.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: c4a8a4's failing titles are all natural-language phrases ('Apple harvesting season', 'University of Arkham'); the corpus never presents an authoring default, a placeholder/unfilled-template token, or a filename/code-string title. 2779a5 explicitly passes any non-whitespace title, so 'Untitled Document', 'TODO: title' and 'report.html' sail through both ACT rules. Fully-automated tools cannot distinguish these from a real title: they are non-empty and valid; distinguishing 'report.html' from a genuine 'Report 2024', or 'New Page 1' from a legitimate title, requires understanding that the string is a vestigial tool artifact or unfilled template, not page-identifying content.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.2 · Trusted Tester 12.B · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Title describes a secondary/peripheral block instead of the page's primary topic (rich mixed-content pages)

On a busy page the title names a sidebar, ad, or banner instead of what the page is actually about, so users picking from open tabs or search results are misled.

F25 fails titles that do not identify the contents or purpose of the OVERALL page. On a realistic page with mixed content (a main article plus a sidebar, ad rail, promo banner, related-links, footer tagline), a title can be non-empty and genuinely describe SOMETHING present on the page while completely missing the page's primary subject — e.g. a detailed page about a city budget vote titled after the top promo banner ('Summer Sale - 20% Off'), or a recipe page titled after its sidebar newsletter widget. The c4a8a4 corpus only ever has a single short <p> as the entire body, so the page's topic is unambiguous by construction and 'which of several content blocks is this page about' is never exercised. Identifying a busy page's PRIMARY topic versus peripheral blocks, and checking the title against the dominant content region, is a quintessential human reading-comprehension/visual-prominence judgment that no presence-or-emptiness checker performs.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Every c4a8a4 case has one sentence of body content, so there is exactly one possible topic and no competition between primary and peripheral content; the corpus's own syntheticNarrowness admits 'a single short <p> as the entire page content'. Real pages have headers, sidebars, ads, and related-content rails. Automated tools cannot identify a page's primary topic versus peripheral blocks, have no model of visual or semantic prominence, and do no title-versus-dominant-content comparison; a human must read the page, determine what it is principally about, and judge whether the title names THAT.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.2 · Trusted Tester 12.B · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Stale / copy-paste title: right subject family, wrong specific instance (date, name, version, account)

The title is on-topic but names the wrong specific item, like last month's date or the previous product, usually left over from copying a template or a sibling page.

F25 and Trusted Tester 12.B require the title to accurately identify THIS page. A pervasive real-world failure is a title carried over from a template clone or a prior edit: it is on-topic for the section and looks entirely plausible, but names the wrong specific item — last month's statement title on this month's statement, last year's gala date on this year's event, the donor product's name on a duplicated product page. c4a8a4's 'Apple harvesting season' on a clementine page is the only wrong-subject case, and it is a gross, obvious cross-domain swap (different fruit). The corpus has no subtle in-family mismatch where title and body share the domain and vocabulary but disagree on the specific instance — precisely the case that needs careful human cross-checking of identifiers (date/name/version/number) against the body, and that no presence/emptiness checker, and even a keyword-matcher, can detect (both 'Q3 Report' and a Q4 body contain 'Report').

Why ACT rules can't reach it: c4a8a4's single wrong-subject case is a blatant cross-domain topic swap; there is no near-miss where title and content share the domain but differ in the specific instance, date, name, or version. The corpus never models a body that the title must be cross-checked against beyond one obvious sentence. Automated tools do no title-versus-content comparison for descriptiveness at all; even a keyword-overlap tool would pass a stale title that shares vocabulary with the body. Catching it requires reading the body and noticing that the specific identifiers in the title disagree with the page's actual subject.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.2 · Trusted Tester 12.B · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Title is correct but too generic to distinguish this page from its siblings (site-name-only / template-shared on an inner page)

An inner page's title is only the site name or a shared label every page uses, so users cannot tell this page apart from its siblings in tabs or history.

F25's second example is a distinct failure: 'A site generated using templates includes the same title for each page on the site. So the title cannot be used to distinguish among the pages.' G88 and Trusted Tester 12.B both make distinguish-within-the-set a pass requirement. Here the title may be perfectly accurate about the SITE ('Acme Corporation', 'Online Store', 'Help Center') yet fail 2.4.2 because it carries no page-level information and so cannot distinguish THIS page (Contact) from siblings (Products, About). The single-page-detectable form of this failure — an inner page of an obvious set whose title is only the site name or only the shared template/section label — IS testable on a self-contained HTML page: the body unambiguously reveals the page's specific role, while the title carries only site-level information. Deciding whether 'Acme Corporation' adequately distinguishes the Contact page requires knowing the page's specific role — a human judgment about whether the title carries page-level, not just site-level, information.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT test cases are single self-contained files with no sibling pages, so 'same title across the set' cannot be encoded; the corpus's only inner-page case is one search page, and c4a8a4's 'University of Arkham' touches site-name-only but as an isolated single page, never as the distinguish-among-siblings problem F25 describes. Fully-automated single-page tools have no cross-page corpus to compare titles against, and even on one page cannot decide whether a site-name-only or template-shared title adequately distinguishes this page's specific role — that requires reading the body to learn the page's role and judging whether the title carries any page-level signal.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.2 · Trusted Tester 12.B · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Title is locally descriptive in-page but loses meaning out of context / fails to convey collection position (G88 out-of-context, G127)

A title like 'Step 2' or 'Chapter 3' is clear while on the page but meaningless when seen alone in a tab list or search results, with no surrounding context.

G88 makes 'Make sense when read out of context, for example by a screen reader or in a site map or list of search results' a core requirement, and G127 covers titles that identify a page's RELATIONSHIP to a larger collection (its position in a hierarchy, its parent section). A title can be perfectly clear while reading the page ('Chapter 3', 'Settings', 'Step 2', 'GET /users') yet be uninformative when isolated in a list of open tabs, a search-results list, or a screen-reader page list, because it strips all collection/parent context. The Understanding examples model exactly the good pattern ('Alert Dialog Example | APG | WAI | W3C'; 'Bank XYZ, December 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678'). The ACT corpus has no hierarchical or collection-structured cases — every page is a standalone leaf with no parent context — so the 'descriptive in-page but meaningless out of context' failure is never exercised. Judging whether a title 'makes sense out of context' or conveys collection position requires imagining it isolated and understanding the page's role in a larger information architecture — a human contextual judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT corpus has no multi-level or collection-structured examples; the richest is a flat search-results page, and every case is a standalone leaf with no parent/hierarchy modeled. It never tests a title that is locally descriptive but loses meaning out of context. Automated tools cannot judge whether a title 'makes sense out of context' or conveys collection position — that requires understanding the page's role in a larger information architecture and imagining the title isolated in a list of tabs or search hits; 'Chapter 3' is fine in-page but uninformative as a standalone title, and only a human weighs that.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.2 · Trusted Tester 12.B · priority medium

EN 301 549 — C.9.2.4.3 (SC 2.4.3)

C.9.2.4.3 — SC 2.4.3 Focus order
C.9.2.4.3       Focus Order
   Type of assessment                                         Inspection
   Requirement          1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.
   Preconditions
   Procedure            1. Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.3 Focus
                        Order according to WCAG Conformance Requirements stated in clause 9.6.
   Result               Pass: Check 1 is true
                        Fail: Check 1 is false
                        Not applicable: If any requirement precondition is false or the web page does not
                        contain content relevant to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.3 Focus Order. (Do not
                        need to meet or test)

Heading and Page Structure (cat_3)

Trusted Tester — SC 2.4.3

SC 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A) — TT Test 4.F

TT section: 4. Keyboard Access and Focus · Baseline: 2. Focus

WCAG SC 2.4.3: If a Web page can be navigated sequentially and the navigation sequences affect meaning or

operation, focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability.

Test 4.F — 2.4.3-focus-order-meaning

Test Condition: *The focus order preserves the meaning and operability of the web page.*

DNA if the page has no elements that can receive keyboard focus.

How to Test

1. Use the tab key to move focus through the page.

2. Determine if the focus order impacts the page meaning (e.g., form fields for a mailing address are presented

in the expected sequence).

  • a. Most noticeable when focus order does not follow the logical order of operation (normally top to bottom,

left to right).

  • b. It may be necessary to use the keyboard to activate trigger controls that reveal hidden content with

focusable elements (menus, dialogs, modal dialog boxes, expandable tree list) to check the focus order to,

from, and within the revealed content.

  • c. It may be helpful to launch ANDI: focusable elements and select tab order.
  • d. Backward focus order does not have to mirror the forward focus order. However, it must preserve the

meaning and operability of the page.

3. For modal dialog boxes, keyboard focus navigating both forward and backward should remain within the

modal dialog box until it is closed.

Evaluate Results (PASS if ALL true)

1. The focus order preserves the meaning of the page, AND

2. The focus order preserves the operability of the page.

Notes
  • Focus order does not necessarily need to be top to bottom, left to right.
  • When focus order does not affect meaning or operability, this test Does Not Apply (e.g., a row of icons

linking to social media may not need to be navigated in a particular order).

  • ANDI tab-order markup may differ slightly from actual keyboard tab order in certain browsers — **always use

the results from keyboard tab order**.

Act-augmented aspect — CSS-reordered visual layout makes DOM/tab order contradict the meaningful order (no tabindex, no script)

CSS like flexbox order or absolute positioning rearranges the page so it reads one way visually but Tab moves focus in the unrelated DOM order, confusing keyboard users.

A page uses NO positive tabindex and NO focus-managing script, so every static 'tabindex misuse' heuristic finds nothing. But CSS (flexbox `order`, grid placement, float, absolute positioning) reorders the visual presentation so that the natural DOM tab order no longer follows the meaning conveyed by the rendered layout. G59's core point applies: 'When the source order does not match the visual order, the tab order through the content must reflect the logical relationships in the content that are displayed visually.' Judging a violation requires looking at the RENDERED page, inferring the intended reading/operation sequence from the visual hierarchy, and comparing it to the keyboard sequence. The Understanding makes this an explicit judgment: independent columns out of order do NOT fail, but interdependent content out of order DOES. This is the most semantically demanding limb and the highest-value uncovered space.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT rules/cases for 2.4.3. F44 (the only automatable-adjacent failure) is scoped to the tabindex attribute; a page with zero tabindex and zero script presents nothing for a static rule to inspect. No automated tool can decide whether visually-reordered DOM content is 'independent' (passes) or 'interdependent' (fails) — that is the exact distinction the Understanding flags as requiring human consideration of the rendered presentation.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.3 · Trusted Tester 4.F · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Focus order interleaves between two semantically distinct sections/groups (the canonical Understanding form failure)

Tabbing through a form jumps back and forth between two unrelated sections instead of finishing one before starting the next, breaking the user's sense of what belongs together.

The Understanding's own failing example: a form has a mailing/marketing-data section (name, address, city, state, postal) and a separate newsletter-checkbox section, but the tab order jumps between sections — name, then a checkbox, then street address, then another checkbox. Every field has a correct visible label, correct programmatic name/role, and is fully keyboard-operable; the interleaving can be produced purely by DOM order with no tabindex for a tool to flag. The failure is visible ONLY to an evaluator who understands which fields 'belong together' semantically (mailing-address fields form one group; newsletter choices form another) and that crossing between groups mid-sequence destroys the user's mental model. G59's applicant/spouse example is the passing mirror.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases. The fields are individually valid (labels present, operable), so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing — they have no model of which fields belong together semantically. Deciding that 'street address' belongs with 'city/state/postal' and NOT between two newsletter checkboxes is pure content-meaning grouping, exactly what the SC leaves to human judgment.

Act-augmented aspect — Revealed non-modal dialog/menu is not next in the navigation order (F85, open branch)

Clicking a button opens an in-page dialog or menu, but pressing Tab next lands on unrelated page content instead of inside the thing that just appeared.

F85's core failure: a trigger button reveals an in-page dialog or menu, but the revealed widget is NOT focus-managed AND is not next in the sequential navigation order — typically because the dialog markup sits at the end of the DOM. After activating the trigger, the keyboard user's focus stays on (or just after) the trigger, so to reach the visually-overlaid dialog they must tab through the entire rest of the page. On a self-contained HTML page this is testable with a tiny script that only toggles visibility (no focus move). It requires multi-state interaction judgment: you must activate the control, then evaluate where focus lands relative to where it visually/logically should be. This is the TT 4.F step 2b 'reveal hidden content... check the focus order to, from, and within the revealed content' manual step.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases for 2.4.3, and F85 is explicitly a manual procedure ('Activate the trigger control via the keyboard'). Static analysis cannot know that the visually-overlaid dialog is the user's intended next interaction; it sees a hidden div somewhere in the DOM. No automated tool simulates 'open, then check the next Tab stop is in the dialog.'

Act-augmented aspect — Focus not returned (or returned illogically) after a dialog/menu is dismissed (F85, close branch + modal return)

After closing a dialog, focus is dumped at the top of the page instead of returning to the button that opened it, stranding keyboard users.

F85's second failure branch and the Understanding's modal example: after the user dismisses an in-page menu or dialog, focus is dumped on document.body (or scrolls to top), forcing the user to tab from the very start of the page back to where they were. The pass condition is nuanced: focus should return to the trigger control, OR — if the trigger was removed by the action — to a logical neighboring element (F85's tag-delete note). Evaluating this requires understanding what the 'logical' return point is given what the action did: deleting an item should move focus to the next item, not the top of the page; cancelling should return to the trigger. This is a state-transition reasoning task.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases. The 'where should focus go after close' decision depends on the semantics of the action that closed the widget (cancel vs delete vs save), which no static tool models. F85 marks it manual ('Check whether keyboard focus is put back on the trigger control'). The 'logical neighbor' exception means even a tool that naively checked 'focus == trigger' would mis-fire on the legitimate delete-then-move-to-next case.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.3 · Trusted Tester 4.F · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Modal dialog focus is not contained — forward Tab or backward Shift+Tab escapes behind the inert backdrop

A popup dialog looks like it blocks the page, but pressing Shift+Tab or Tab at its edge lets focus slip out to the hidden content behind it.

The Understanding modal example and TT 4.F step 3 require that for a modal, keyboard focus navigating BOTH forward and backward remains within the dialog until it closes, with outside content inert. The subtle, human-judgment failure: a 'modal' that looks modal (dim backdrop, centered card) and may even trap forward Tab, but Shift+Tab (backward) escapes to the page behind it, or the last element's forward Tab leaks to page content. Because TT says backward order need not mirror forward but must still preserve operability, evaluating containment requires testing BOTH directions and judging whether escaped focus lands the user somewhere that destroys the modal's operability. This is distinct from a 2.1.2 keyboard trap (inability to leave); here the failure is leaving when the user should be contained.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases. Containment is a runtime, bidirectional interaction property: a static rule cannot determine that a div with role=dialog actually keeps focus inside under Shift+Tab, nor that the backdrop content was made inert. The forward-vs-backward asymmetry (forward trapped, backward leaking) is precisely the manual both-directions check TT calls out and no automated checker performs.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.3 · Trusted Tester 4.F · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Multiple valid orders — row-wise vs column-wise grid/table traversal must NOT be flagged

A grid or table of controls can legitimately be tabbed either row-by-row or column-by-column, so flagging the column-wise order as broken would be a false alarm.

The false-positive trap built into the SC: when content has two-dimensional structure (a table of interactive controls, a grid of cards), EITHER row-by-row OR column-by-column focus order can satisfy the SC because both 'reflect the logical relationships in the content.' An evaluator must recognize that a column-wise tab order through a data-entry table is NOT a violation just because it isn't the more common row-wise order — provided meaning/operation are preserved. The hard judgment is distinguishing 'a different-but-valid logical order' from 'an order that destroys meaning.' The SC explicitly says only one valid order need be provided. This aspect exists to measure whether a judge OVER-flags valid alternatives.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases. An automated tool has no concept of 'this alternative order still reflects a logical relationship'; it would either ignore order entirely or naively flag any non-source/non-left-to-right order. The spec demands the evaluator simultaneously hold several acceptable orders — a reasoning task, not a pattern match.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.3 · Trusted Tester 4.F · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Confusing/illogical focus stops from nested focusable wrappers or focusable static content

Making a wrapper div or plain text focusable adds pointless or duplicate Tab stops, so keyboard users land on the same control twice or pause on dead content.

The Understanding note: the SC 'does not prohibit making non-operable content (e.g., static text) focusable,' BUT 'it is a failure of Focus Order if items receive focus in an order that impedes the meaning or operation of content, or creates confusing or illogical focus orders — for example, a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements' (e.g. `<div tabindex=0><button>...</button></div>`). The judgment is whether the extra/duplicate/odd focus stops impede meaning or operability: a control that appears to receive focus twice, a tabindex=0 on a non-interactive wrapper that injects a meaningless stop mid-sequence, or static text that grabs focus between two related controls and breaks the flow. Whether such stops merely add tedium (best-practice, not a failure) or actually 'impede meaning/operation' (a failure) is exactly the human line the note draws.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT cases. A tool can mechanically count tabindex=0 attributes but cannot judge whether a focus stop is 'confusing or illogical' or whether a double-focus (wrapper + child) 'impedes meaning'. The note explicitly permits focusable static content; only the meaning-impeding subset fails, which is a contextual human judgment, not a static pattern.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.3 · Trusted Tester 4.F · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Positive tabindex creates a tab order that does not preserve meaning (F44), with the meaning-judgment a human must make

Hand-numbered tabindex values force Tab to visit controls in an order that contradicts the content's logical sequence, scrambling the experience for keyboard users.

F44: positive tabindex values impose an explicit tab order that does not follow the content's logical relationships and sequences (the <ol> example tabbing Homepage, chapter 3, chapter 2, chapter 1). While a static tool can DETECT the presence of positive tabindex (axe flags it as best-practice), the actual 2.4.3 failure requires judging that the resulting order breaks meaning — a positive-tabindex page whose order happens to match the content sequence is NOT a failure, and a positive tabindex that re-establishes the correct order after a CSS reflow can even be the fix. So the human contribution is deciding whether the imposed numeric order preserves or destroys meaning/operability, and recognizing the common edit-drift case (a new field without tabindex gets pushed to the end).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 0 ACT rules cover F44. Automated tools can surface 'positive tabindex present' as a best-practice warning but cannot decide whether the specific numeric order preserves or breaks meaning — they would either flag every positive tabindex (false positives on correctly-ordered ones, and on the legitimate 'tabindex used to repair CSS reflow' case) or none. The meaning-preservation judgment is human; that is why this is kept but at lower priority than the no-tabindex aspects.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.3 · Trusted Tester 4.F · priority low

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule c487ae — Link has non-empty accessible name

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 1.1.1,2.4.4,4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/c487ae/proposed/

Proposed

Link has non-empty accessible name

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A) ,

2.4.4: Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A) ,

2.4.9: Link Purpose (Link Only) (Level AAA)

Description

This rule checks that each link has a non-empty accessible name.

Applicability

This rule applies to any HTML element that is an inheriting semantic link included in the accessibility tree .

Expectation

Each target element has an accessible name that is not empty ( "" ).

Background

Assumptions

The rule assumes that all links are user interface components as defined by WCAG 2. When the link role is used on elements that do not behave as links, failing this rule might not mean that the success criteria are failed.

Accessibility Support
  • For area elements that have an href attribute, but are not nested inside a map element, there are differences between browsers and assistive technology on if the area is included in the accessibility tree .
  • Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some semantic link elements can fail this rule with some technology but users of other technologies would not experience any accessibility issue.
  • Accessibility support for some elements inheriting the semantic role of link (e.g. elements with doc-* attributes) may vary depending on the assistive technology in use.
Related rules
  • Link in context is descriptive

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 5effbb — Link in context is descriptive proposed

status: proposed

implement: auto,manual,semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 2.4.4

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/5effbb/proposed/

Proposed

Link in context is descriptive

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

2.4.4: Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that the accessible name of a link together with its context describes its purpose.

Applicability

This rule applies to any inheriting semantic link for which all the following is true:

  • the link is included in the accessibility tree ; and
  • the link has a non-empty (“”) accessible name .

Expectation

The accessible name of each target element together with its programmatically determined link context describes the purpose of the link.

Background

Assumptions

This rule assumes that the purpose of the link is not ambiguous to users in general when seen in context on the web page, which is the exception mentioned in success criteria 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) or 2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link only) . If the link is ambiguous to users in general, users of assistive technologies are not at a disadvantage when viewing the link out of context.

This rule assumes that all semantic link elements are used as links. An element marked up as a link, but that does not behave as a link would not fail success criteria 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) or 2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link only) .

Accessibility Support
  • Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some semantic link elements can fail this rule with some technology but users of other technologies would not experience any accessibility issue.
Related rules
  • Link has non-empty accessible name
  • Link is descriptive

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule fd3a94 — Links with identical accessible names and same context serve equivalent purpose proposed

status: proposed

implement: semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 2.4.4

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/fd3a94/proposed/

Proposed

Links with identical accessible names and same context serve equivalent purpose

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

2.4.4: Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that links with identical accessible names in the same context resolve to the same or equivalent resources.

Applicability

This rule applies to any set of two or more HTML or SVG elements for which all the following are true:

  • the elements are inheriting semantic link nodes; and
  • the elements are in the same web page (HTML) ; and
  • the elements are included in the accessibility tree ; and
  • the elements have matching accessible names that are not empty ( "" ); and
  • the elements have the same programmatically determined link context .

Note: The test target for this rule is the full set of link elements that share the same matching accessible name and programmatically determined link context .

Expectation

For each pair of links in each target set, one of the following is true:

  • both links resolve to the same resource ; or
  • both links resolve to equivalent resources ; or
  • there is no visual information within the web page to let users know that both links resolve to non-equivalent resources .

Note : Resolving the links includes potential redirects, if the redirects happen instantly.

Background

There is a difference between two contexts being the same and being identical . This rule specifically targets links within the same context. The same context means exactly the same set of DOM nodes. Identical (but not the same) contexts might have a different set of DOM nodes, but those DOM nodes have equivalent content - such as text content, attribute values, and so on. This difference is similar to the difference in some programming languages between pointer equivalence and deep object equivalence. Links with identical name that are in identical (but not the same) contexts also fail 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) . However, defining “identical context” unambiguously has been deemed infeasible at this time, and so has been left out of this rule.

Links that are ambiguous to users in general are covered by the exception mentioned in Success Criterion 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context). If the links are ambiguous to users in general, users of assistive technologies are not at a disadvantage when viewing the links, which makes it more of a general user experience concern than an accessibility issue.

Pages with links that are not [ambiguous to users in general][], but are ambiguous to some users are likely to fail [success criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships][sc131] if the disambiguation information is conveyed through presentation, but not semantically. Moreover, when this information is non-text content, such a page is likely to fail [success criterion 1.1.1 Non-text Content][sc111].

Assumptions
  • This rule assumes that, within the context of the test subject, the description provided by the accessible name of a link can only accurately describe one resource (notably, homonyms alone are not used as link names). Thus, if two or more links have the same accessible name but resolve to different resources, at least one of them does not accurately describe its purpose.
  • This rule assumes that assistive technologies are exposing all links on the page in the same way no matter which document tree they are in. If an assistive technology requires the user to “enter” an iframe or a shadow tree before exposing its links, then it is possible for two links to have identical name and context but resolve to different resources without failing Success Criterion 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) (if said links are in separate documents or shadow trees ).
  • This rule assumes that reading the URL, such as from the status bar when the link is focused, is not considered part of the context, and therefore, it does not disambiguate links.
Accessibility Support

There are no accessibility support issues known.

<h2 id="glossary"

[Glossary section omitted for brevity — see raw HTML]

EN 301 549 — C.9.2.4.4 (SC 2.4.4)

C.9.2.4.4 — SC 2.4.4 Link purpose (in context)
C.9.2.4.4       Link purpose (in context)
   Type of assessment                                         Inspection
   Requirement          1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.
   Preconditions
   Procedure            1. Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.4 Link
                        Purpose (In Context) according to WCAG Conformance Requirements stated in
                        clause 9.6.
   Result               Pass: Check 1 is true
                        Fail: Check 1 is false
                        Not applicable: If any requirement precondition is false or the web page does not
                        contain content relevant to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In
                        Context). (Do not need to meet or test)

Trusted Tester — SC 2.4.4

SC 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A) — TT Test 6.A

TT section: 6. Links · Baseline: 14. Links · (also covers 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value)

WCAG SC 2.4.4: The purpose of each link can be determined from the link text alone or from the link text

together with its programmatically determined link context, except where the purpose of the link would be

ambiguous to users in general.

Identify Content

Use ANDI: links/buttons to identify all links.

  • DNA if the page does not have links.
  • *Note:* This test does not apply to links that function as an anchor or target and are not perceivable or

selectable by users.

Test 6.A — 2.4.4-link-purpose

Test Condition: *The purpose of each link can be determined from any combination of the link text, accessible

name, accessible description, and/or programmatically determined link context.*

How to Test

1. Evaluate the ANDI Output for link purpose.

2. Determine whether the ANDI Output, in combination with the programmatically determined link context (text

that is in the same sentence, paragraph, list item, or table cell as the link, or in a **table header

cell** associated with the table cell that contains the link), adequately describes the link's purpose or

function.

  • a. In cases where the purpose of the link is intentionally vague or ambiguous (e.g., a "Door 1," "Door

2," "Door 3" surprise), it may be sufficient for the combination of link text, accessible name, accessible

description, and/or link context to refer to the link purpose vaguely or ambiguously.

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. The combination of the programmatically determined link context and the ANDI Output provide adequate

description of the link's purpose.

Note
  • Any changes to links that occur automatically or as a result of interaction with the page should be included.
  • "Programmatically determined link context" is limited to same sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell or

associated table header — not arbitrary nearby text.

Act-augmented aspect — Generic/boilerplate link text with a non-empty name but no purpose, and no context that rescues it (G91/H30 substantive failure)

A link reads only 'click here' or 'read more' (or a raw URL) with no nearby explaining text, so a screen-reader user listing links can't tell where any goes.

A link whose accessible name exists and is non-empty but is generic boilerplate ('click here', 'read more', 'more', 'here', 'details', 'learn more', 'link', 'continue', '>>') or is just the bare URL, AND for which no programmatically determined link context (the same sentence, paragraph, list item, table cell, or associated table-header cell, or aria-label/labelledby/describedby) supplies the missing purpose. The name passes the only APPROVED rule (c487ae) trivially because it is a pure name-presence gate. The judgment is irreducibly semantic: read the link text plus its containing block and decide whether a user can infer the destination's purpose without leaving the link. Includes the bare-URL case, where the Understanding/G91 say the URI is 'generally not sufficiently descriptive'. The borderline case — where context ALMOST but not-quite rescues a generic name — is the hardest and the most valuable.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The only APPROVED rule (c487ae) is a pure name-PRESENCE gate; 'click here' passes it. The substantive limb lives only in PROPOSED, unapproved rule 5effbb, whose failed examples use stilted single-word names ('More', 'Workshop', 'Go') on otherwise-empty pages, never the real-world boilerplate a person actually meets, and never the borderline case where residual context nearly rescues a generic name. A fully-automated checker can flag a hard-coded blocklist of phrases but cannot decide whether the surrounding prose makes the purpose inferable — that is a meaning judgment a human must make.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.4 · Trusted Tester 6.A · priority high

Technique / failure references
  • Understanding 2.4.4 — “Whenever possible, provide link text that identifies the purpose of the link without needing additional context.…”
  • G91 — “The description lets a user distinguish this link from links in the web page that lead to other destinations and helps the user determine whether to follow the link.…”
  • G53 — “Note that simply providing the URI of the destination is generally not sufficiently descriptive.…”

  • case-02 — SaaS pricing page: a paragraph reads '...for full pricing details, click here.' where the generic phrase 'click here' is the link but the pu
  • case-03 — Restaurant site footer 'More' column: three list items, each containing only a link named 'Details', going to three different pages (menu, p
  • case-04 — Investor-relations 'Quarterly Disclosures' page: a link whose entire accessible name is the bare raw URL 'https://example.com/products/2024/
  • case-05 — Electronics shop: the SAME '>>' (raquo) chevron glyph link appears twice. In 'Editor's pick' it sits in the same sentence as a named product

Act-augmented aspect — Purpose visible on the page but located OUTSIDE the programmatic link context (F63 — wrong container, including context that follows the link)

The text explaining a vague link exists on the page but sits in a separate paragraph or cell, so a screen reader never connects it to the link.

The information needed to understand a vague link IS present and visible — a sighted reader can find it — but it sits in content that is NOT programmatically associated with the link: a different paragraph, an adjacent (non-header) table cell, a different list item, a layout-table row above, or text that FOLLOWS the link in the same visual region. The page LOOKS fine, which is exactly the trap. The judgment requires reasoning about DOM container boundaries (sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell/associated <th>) AND about reading-order direction: Understanding and G53 warn that context which follows the link is confusing for screen-reader users reading top to bottom. This is distinct from the generic-text aspect: here the purpose words exist but the question is association and ordering, not absence.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 5effbb has a few canonical F63-flavoured failures (the W3C 'Workshop'-in-a-different-<p>, Gutenberg-list, and table 'Download' examples), but they are the exact W3C fixtures and all use the same 'context-in-the-wrong-block' shape. The corpus does NOT exercise context that FOLLOWS the link in the same region (the explicit ordering hazard), context split across a layout-table row, dt/dd associations, or visually-adjacent siblings a person would assume are associated. Deciding whether nearby text is in the same sentence/paragraph/cell requires parsing prose-sentence boundaries and judging programmatic association — and the residual-context sufficiency is semantic; an automated tool cannot do this reliably.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.4 · Trusted Tester 6.A · priority high

Technique / failure references
  • F63 — “This describes a failure condition when the context needed for understanding the purpose of a link is located in content that is not programmatically determined link context.…”
  • F63 — “Because the link is not in the same paragraph as the lead sentence, the user cannot easily discover what the link will let the user read more about.…”
  • Understanding 2.4.4 — “If the description follows the link, there can be confusion and difficulty for screen reader users who are reading through the page in order (top to bottom).…”
  • Trusted Tester 2.4.4 — “"Programmatically determined link context" is limited to same sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell or associated table header — not arbitrary nearby text.…”

Act-augmented aspect — Image/icon/SVG-only links with a non-empty name that misdescribes or fails to convey the rendered glyph's purpose (F89 semantic-mismatch variant)

An icon-only link has a label, but it misdescribes the icon or is useless (a search icon labeled 'image'), so screen-reader users are misled about it.

A link contains only an image, SVG, or icon-font glyph and DOES have a non-empty accessible name (alt, aria-label, title, or aria-labelledby), so F89's empty-name failure and c487ae both PASS — but the name does not match what the glyph depicts or where the link goes. Examples: a magnifying-glass icon labelled 'image' / 'icon1' / the filename 'search.png'; a social brand glyph labelled the generic 'social'; a printer icon whose alt says 'document'; a hamburger menu whose aria-label says 'logo'; an icon-font link whose accessible name is a literal private-use codepoint that conveys nothing; a back-arrow whose alt says 'forward'. The string exists and looks plausible, so it survives every name-presence check, but a person looking at the rendered icon sees the label is wrong or uselessly generic for the link's purpose. Requires VISUAL judgment of the rendered glyph against the name.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: c487ae's image-link cases only test name presence vs absence on a single stock logo or planets imagemap; a 'wrong but present' alt passes every one. 5effbb's icon examples are always correctly-labelled passes or empty-text fails — never a non-empty-but-wrong label. F89 itself only fires on the empty case. Detecting the mismatch requires looking at the rendered icon and comparing it to the accessible name (and destination) — an automated tool has no notion of what a glyph depicts, so this is irreducibly visual/semantic and human-only.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.4 · Trusted Tester 6.A · priority high

  • F89 — “This failure condition occurs when a link contains only non-text content, such as an image, and that link cannot be identified by an accessible name.…”
  • Understanding 2.4.4 — “The text of, or associated with, the link is intended to describe the purpose of the link.…”
  • H2 — “The img has a text alternative which is the name used for the icon in the site help, which describes clicking the home page icon.…”

Act-augmented aspect — Identical accessible name AND identical context, but the links resolve to genuinely different purposes (fd3a94 equivalence judgment)

Several links share the same text and surroundings yet lead to genuinely different places, so a user picking from them can't tell which one does what they want.

Two or more links on the page share the same accessible name AND the same programmatically determined context, yet lead to different resources serving different purposes — the classic 'three Read more / three Download / two Contact us' problem. The judgment is doubly semantic: (a) are the contexts truly identical, and (b) do the destinations serve EQUIVALENT purposes or genuinely different ones? Equivalent (e.g. the same data offered as PDF/XLSX/CSV) can PASS; genuinely different destinations (chat page vs phone page; sales@ vs support@) FAIL. On a self-contained page this is testable using same-page #fragment anchors and mailto:/tel: targets whose differing purposes are determinable from the page. The disambiguation can also be visual-only (alignment with an image or price block above), which a tool cannot read.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: fd3a94 is PROPOSED/unapproved and explicitly notFullyAutomatable; its examples are fixed W3C 'About us / Contact us' pairs that require fetching external W3C test-asset URLs to resolve, so they are unusable as self-contained single-page fixtures and never cover same-page #fragments or mailto/tel disambiguation. No APPROVED corpus test exercises duplicate-name disambiguation at all. Resolving 'equivalent purpose' is irreducibly a meaning judgment, and visual-only disambiguation cannot be read by an automated tool.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.4 · Trusted Tester 6.A · priority medium

  • Understanding 2.4.4 — “It is also a best practice for links with different purposes and destinations to have different link text.…”

  • fd3a94 — “These two HTML a elements have the same accessible name and context, but go to different resources. Their purpose is disambiguated for sighted users by the alignment of the links w…”

  • case-06 — Volunteer-run tech conference page (negative control): one paragraph contains two inline links both named 'contact us' in the same sentence-

Act-augmented aspect — Sufficiency of preceding-heading / list-grouping context as the purpose carrier (H80 judgment, including when the heading is NOT the link's context)

A vague link like 'Map' or 'Book now' only makes sense from the heading above it, raising whether that heading is really tied to the link well enough.

A vague link ('Map', 'Book now', 'PDF', 'Read more') is rescued — or not — by a preceding heading or by the grouping structure it sits in (a section heading above a nav of links, a hotel-block heading, a document offered in three formats under one heading, a card whose <h2> headline is the appended 'Read more' link's group). The H80 judgment is whether the link text combined with that preceding heading describes the purpose, AND whether the heading is genuinely the link's context versus merely visually-above content. This is distinct from F63 (which is about context in the WRONG container) and from generic-text-alone: here the heading/grouping mechanism is the intended carrier, and the call is whether it sufficiently and correctly associates. Repeated identical link sets under different headings ('Map'/'Photos'/'Book now' for two hotels) are the canonical case where context is the only differentiator.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: H80 is an advisory technique with no ACT rule of its own; the approved c487ae corpus ignores context entirely, and 5effbb's context cases do not exercise preceding-heading or grouped-nav sufficiency, nor the repeated-link-set-under-different-headings pattern where the heading is the sole differentiator. Judging whether 'Map' under a hotel heading conveys 'map of THIS hotel' — and whether the heading is the link's actual context rather than coincidentally-above text — requires reading the heading and the grouping and making a meaning call no automated checker can make.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.4 · Trusted Tester 6.A · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — A specific, well-formed link name that contradicts its actual on-page destination (deceptive but descriptive name)

A link has a clear, specific label that is wrong about its target (a 'Privacy Policy' link jumping to the Terms section), deceiving users about where it goes.

The link has a clear, descriptive, non-empty accessible name that reads as 'good' in isolation, but it is WRONG about where the link goes. On a self-contained page this is testable when the destination is a same-page #fragment anchor (or a labelled on-page section) whose actual content is verifiable: a 'Read our Privacy Policy' link whose href is '#terms' (a Terms section that exists on the page); a 'Skip to main content' link pointing to '#footer' instead of '#main'; a table-of-contents entry 'Chapter 3: Results' whose anchor actually holds Chapter 5; a 'Basic — $0/mo : Get started' link jumping to an '#enterprise-checkout' section. The name passes every presence and descriptiveness heuristic; the failure is that the name does not describe the link's ACTUAL purpose. This is the inverse of generic text — the text is specific but false — and requires a human to cross-check the claimed purpose against the on-page target.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Every ACT fixture (approved and proposed) assumes the name honestly reflects the destination; 5effbb's whole premise is 'does the name describe the purpose' under the implicit assumption the author is not lying. There is NO test where a high-quality descriptive name points to a contradictory target. An automated tool would have to semantically understand the destination and compare it to the link text's claim — a meaning-level cross-check only a human can perform, here scoped to same-page anchors so the destination is verifiable on the single page.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.4 · Trusted Tester 6.A · priority medium

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule b49b2e — Heading is descriptive proposed

status: proposed

implement: auto,manual,semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 2.4.6

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/b49b2e/proposed/

Proposed

Heading is descriptive

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

2.4.6: Headings and Labels (Level AA)

Description

This rule checks that headings describe the topic or purpose of the content.

Applicability

This rule applies to any semantic heading element that is included in the accessibility tree and has a non-empty ( ”” ) accessible name .

Expectation

Each target element describes the topic or purpose of the first perceivable content after the test target that is not decorative . The order of elements is determined by the flat tree .

Note: Headings do not need to be lengthy. A word, or even a single character, may be sufficient.

Background

Headings that are visible but not in the accessibility tree are a failure of Success Criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships . These are not tested by this rule but they can still fail Success Criterion 2.4.6 Headings and Labels .

Assumptions

This rule assumes that the flat tree order is close to the reading order as elements are rendered on the page. Due to positioning, it is possible to render a document in an order that greatly differs from the tree order, in which case the content which is visually associated with a heading might not be the content following it in tree order and this rule might fail while Success Criterion 2.4.6 Headings and Label is still satisfied.

This rule also assumes that the content the heading is intended to describe is visible and not hidden from assistive technologies. Otherwise, cases such as expandable content using a heading might fail this rule while Success Criterion 2.4.6 Headings and Label is still satisfied.

Accessibility Support

Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some semantic heading elements can fail this rule with some technology but users of other technologies would not experience any accessibility issue.

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule cc0f0a — Form field label is descriptive proposed

status: proposed

implement: auto,semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 2.4.6

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/cc0f0a/proposed/

Proposed

Form field label is descriptive

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

2.4.6: Headings and Labels (Level AA)

Description

This rule checks that labels describe the purpose of form field elements.

Applicability

This rule applies to any programmatic label of an element for which one of the following is true:

  • the element has one of the following semantic roles : checkbox , combobox , listbox , menuitemcheckbox , menuitemradio , radio , searchbox , slider , spinbutton , switch , textbox ; or
  • the element is an input with no semantic role and a type attribute value of color , date , datetime-local , file , month , password , time , or week .

In addition, both the element and the programmatic label must be visible .

Expectation

Each test target, together with its visual context , describes the purpose of the associated element.

Background

The list of applicable semantic roles is derived by taking all the ARIA 1.2 roles that:

  • inherit from the input , menuitem or select role; and
  • are form field controls (this notably excludes menu , option or tree ).

This rule also applies to input elements whose type attribute value is color , date , datetime-local , file , month , password , time , or week . These input types have no semantic role but still require a descriptive programmatic label so users can understand their purpose.

Labels in WCAG are not restricted to the label element of HTML and can be any element. This rule is only concerned about actual label elements, and elements that are programmatically marked as labels via the aria-labelledby attribute.

It is possible for an element to have an accessible name but still have a non-descriptive label element (and even a non-descriptive label ). In that case, it would pass Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role and Value but still fail this rule and Success Criterion 2.4.6: Headings and Labels .

Having a label which is not included in the accessible name is a violation of Success Criterion 2.5.3: Label in Name but not of this rule nor of Success Criterion 2.4.6: Headings and Labels .

Assumptions
  • This rule assumes that labels are intended for sighted users, and that hiding a visible label from assistive technologies, is a failure of Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role and Value , but not of Success Criterion 2.4.6: Headings and Labels .
  • This rule assumes that the programmatic labels of an element are also part of its visual context .
Accessibility Support
  • Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some elements can have one of the applicable semantic roles and fail this rule with some technology but users of other technologies would not experience any accessibility issue.
Other Resources

  • ARIA16: Using aria-labelledby to provide a name for user interface controls
