EN 301 549 — C.9.2.4.6 (SC 2.4.6)

C.9.2.4.6 — SC 2.4.6 Headings and labels
C.9.2.4.6       Headings and labels
   Type of assessment                                         Inspection
   Requirement          1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.
   Preconditions
   Procedure            1. Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.6 Headings
                        and Labels according to WCAG Conformance Requirements stated in clause 9.6.
   Result               Pass: Check 1 is true
                        Fail: Check 1 is false
                        Not applicable: If any requirement precondition is false or the web page does not
                        contain content relevant to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.6 Headings and Labels.
                        (Do not need to meet or test)

Trusted Tester — SC 2.4.6

SC 2.4.6 Headings and Labels (Level AA) — TT Tests 5.B, 10.A

TT sections: 5. Forms (label adequacy), 10. Content Structure (heading adequacy) · Baselines: 10/13

WCAG SC 2.4.6: Headings and labels describe topic or purpose.

2.4.6 is split across two TT tests: 5.B judges whether each visual form label is sufficiently

descriptive; 10.A judges whether each visual heading describes the topic/purpose of its content. Both

are pure *adequacy/quality* judgments over visually-present text (presence is 3.3.2 / determinability is 1.3.1).

---

Test 5.B — 2.4.6-label-descriptive (Forms)

Test Condition: *Each visual form label is sufficiently descriptive.*

DNA if the page has no form elements, all form elements are disabled, or no visual labels are provided for

form elements.

How to Test

1. Review the visual labels and/or instructions provided for each form component/control.

2. Determine whether labels and/or instructions for form components sufficiently describe the **purpose and

applicable data requirements** (date formats, required fields, data type, etc.).

Evaluate Results (PASS if BOTH true)

1. Each visual form label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know what input data is expected, AND

2. Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function.

Notes
  • An error message is not sufficient to communicate the expected format to pass this test.
  • The label or instruction can be graphical or textual.
  • Any changes to form labels that occur automatically or as a result of interaction should be included.

---

Test 10.A — 2.4.6-heading-purpose (Content Structure → Headings)

Test Condition: *Each heading describes the topic or purpose of its content.*

DNA if there are no visual headings on the page.

How to Test

1. For each visually identified heading, compare the heading text to the content beneath the heading.

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. The heading describes the topic or purpose of its content.

> Identify Content shared with 10.B/10.C/10.D: identify all visually apparent headings (larger/bolded font,

> extra spacing). 10.A judges adequacy; 10.B/10.C judge programmatic determinability/level (see

> sc-1.3.1-info-and-relationships.md).

Act-augmented aspect — Headings and labels that are present and topically true but too generic/boilerplate to orient (Information, Section 2, Value, Details)

A heading or field label is technically accurate but so generic ('Information', 'Details', 'Value') that users can't predict what the section contains or what to type.

The hardest real-world 2.4.6 calls are headings and labels that are not WRONG but are uselessly generic and therefore non-orienting: section headings like 'Information', 'More', 'Details', 'Section 2', 'Content', 'Misc', or field labels like 'Field', 'Input', 'Value', 'Setting 1'. Each one technically relates to the content beneath/within it, so a naive topic-match passes, yet it defeats the Understanding intent that a user can 'find the information they seek more easily' and 'predict what each section contains'. A heading 'Information' over a refund-policy section is true-but-not-descriptive; a label 'Value' over an email input is true-but-not-descriptive. This is a graded human judgment (two reviewers can disagree on where 'generic' tips into 'inadequate') that no checker has a semantic notion of. It is the borderline tier the entire ACT corpus deliberately omits.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT fails are deliberate absurd mismatches ('Weather' over opening hours, 'Menu' over a name field) — a 100% topic mismatch. The corpus has NO 'technically-relevant-but-vague' case; the SC's own coverage summary admits there are 'no SUBTLE/borderline cases (e.g. a heading that is vague, overly generic like Information, technically-true-but-unhelpful, or only partially relevant) which is where real-world 2.4.6 judgment is hard.' Generic-ness is exactly the graded judgment the binary pass/fail fixtures hide, and a fully-automated checker cannot judge whether a real word is 'too generic to orient'.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.6 · Trusted Tester 5.B, 10.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Repeated or near-identical headings/labels among siblings that fail to differentiate sections (relational/uniqueness facet of G130)

Several headings or labels on the page are identical or near-identical ('Description, Description, Description'), so a screen-reader user skimming them can't tell the sections apart.

G130 states descriptive headings identify sections 'in relation both to the web page as a whole and to other sections of the same web page', so descriptiveness is partly RELATIONAL: a heading or label can describe its own content yet fail to distinguish it from a sibling, defeating heading-to-heading and skim navigation. Real failures: three accordion panels all headed 'Description'; multiple product cards each headed 'Product'; two form fieldsets both holding inputs labeled 'Name' with no Shipping/Billing qualifier on the field; tabs all labeled 'Details'. Each heading/label is individually plausible but collectively non-orienting — a screen-reader user jumping heading-to-heading or scanning a generated heading list hears 'Description, Description, Description'. This is a cross-element, whole-page semantic judgment, not a per-element topic match.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: All b49b2e fixtures are single-heading micro-pages (the coverage summary: 'no multiple headings on a page, so heading-to-section scoping and competing next content situations are never exercised'). The only multi-field ACT fixture (b0b11b83, verified: a Shipping fieldset and a Billing fieldset each with 'Name'/'Street') is a PASS where the section heading disambiguates the repeated labels — there is NO fixture where repeated identical headings/labels are left ambiguous. The relational uniqueness facet of G130 is never failed, and an automated checker cannot judge whether sibling sections are confusable.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.6 · Trusted Tester 5.B, 10.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Graphical/icon-only labels whose glyph is misleading or context-dependent for the control's real function

An icon labeling a control is misleading for its real function, like a floppy-disk icon on a 'Send' button or a magnifying glass on a filter button.

The Understanding text devotes three paragraphs to icon labels: an image can BE a descriptive label, but 'the same image can be interpreted differently in different contexts' — a magnifying-glass icon next to a text field reads as 'Search', the same icon on a picture reads as 'zoom/magnify'. 2.4.6's label limb and TT 5.B ('The label or instruction can be graphical or textual') therefore require a human visual judgment: is THIS glyph, in THIS placement, a commonly-understood cue for the control's actual function? Failures are present-but-misleading icons: a floppy-disk icon labeling a 'Send' button; a magnifying glass on a button that actually filters rather than searches; a funnel glyph on a control accessibly named 'Search'; a gear icon used as the label for a 'Log out' control; or an icon whose accessible name names the GLYPH ('magnifier') rather than the FUNCTION ('Search'). A checker can confirm an accessible name exists; it cannot judge whether the chosen glyph is the commonly-understood cue for the function in that spot.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No cc0f0a fixture uses a graphical label at all — every label is literal text ('First name:', 'Menu', 'Info:'). The icon-as-label scenario, despite being the single most-elaborated example in the Understanding doc (the entire loupe/magnifier discussion), has ZERO fixtures. Context-dependence (same icon, two meanings) and glyph/function disagreement are inherently semantic+visual judgments the rule never instantiates, and an automated tool that only checks for a non-empty accessible name will pass every one of these.

Act-augmented aspect — Labels that name the field's topic but omit required data-format / data-requirement cues (format, required, data type)

A field's label names its topic but hides the format it secretly demands (a 'Date' box requiring MM/DD/YYYY), so users can't tell what input is accepted.

2.4.6's label limb is not satisfied merely by a label that names the field's topic; per TT 5.B and G131 the label must make the field's purpose AND its applicable data requirements clear. A label like 'Date of birth:' on a native date picker is the ACT canonical pass, but real failures are subtler: a free-text field labeled only 'Date' that silently demands MM/DD/YYYY; an 'Amount' field that secretly rejects a currency symbol; a 'Card number' field that only accepts un-spaced digits; a required field whose label gives no required indicator while siblings do. The label is present, grammatically describes the topic, and passes axe — yet a user cannot tell what input is expected, which is exactly the descriptiveness shortfall TT 5.B calls out (and an error-after-submit message is explicitly insufficient).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Every cc0f0a fixture pairs a single bare input with a one-or-two-word label and judges only topic match ('First name:' pass vs 'Menu' fail). No fixture has a field with a non-obvious data format, a required field, or a constrained data type, or a label that is topically right but requirement-blind. The data-requirement dimension that TT 5.B explicitly enumerates is entirely absent, and a checker that only verifies a label is associated and non-empty cannot judge whether the expected format is communicated.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.6 · Trusted Tester 5.B · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Button/control labels (text) that do not make the control's function clear — generic, ambiguous, or mismatched action verbs

A button's text is too vague to reveal what it does, like several 'OK'/'Go' buttons that each behave differently or a 'Continue' button that actually deletes your draft.

TT 5.B has a second explicit prong: 'Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function', and G131's whole objective is that 'the label for any interactive component makes the component's purpose clear.' A textual button label can be present and grammatical yet fail to convey the action: a row of 'Submit'/'OK'/'Go' buttons that each do different things; a 'Continue' button that actually deletes a draft; multiple 'Edit' / 'Remove' buttons in a list where the label alone does not say WHAT is edited/removed; a primary button labeled 'Click here'. This is a function-descriptiveness judgment over interactive controls, distinct from the topic-descriptiveness of input field labels and distinct from icon labels — it is the button-label half of the labels limb, judged on its action verb and specificity.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The cc0f0a corpus tests only single bare INPUT fields with topic-noun labels; it contains no button/control whose label must convey an ACTION, and no case where a generic or mismatched verb leaves the function unclear. TT 5.B's button-function prong is therefore never exercised, and an automated checker that confirms a button has a non-empty accessible name cannot judge whether 'Submit'/'Continue'/'Click here' actually tells the user what the control does in context.

Act-augmented aspect — Heading/label descriptiveness that holds in source order but breaks under visual reading order, or for collapsed/dynamic content

A heading matches the content right after it in the code, but once CSS reorders the layout or a panel collapses, it ends up over unrelated content.

The b49b2e rule's own Assumptions name two hard cases it never instantiates: (a) divergence between flat-tree order and visual reading order via CSS positioning/grid/flex order, and (b) headings for expandable/collapsed (hidden) content. A heading can be descriptive of the content that follows it in the DOM but sit visually above unrelated content (CSS order reorders columns/cards), so a sighted user sees 'Pricing' over the FAQ block; or a heading describes content that is only correct once a panel is expanded, while the collapsed default exposes a different (mismatched) summary. Judging these requires rendering the page and reading it visually AND interacting with disclosure state — neither of which a static automated checker or a flat-tree-only rule performs. TT pointedly judges the VISIBLE heading-to-content relationship, which is exactly what diverges here.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The coverage summary states the rule's own hard cases — 'flat-tree vs visual reading order divergence via CSS positioning/grid/flex order, and headings for expandable/collapsed (hidden) content — are called out in the Assumptions but have NO test fixtures here.' Every b49b2e fixture is heading-then-single-paragraph in trivial DOM order. A static checker reads source order, not rendered visual order or post-interaction state, so it cannot detect a heading that is descriptive in the DOM but mis-orienting on screen or after a disclosure toggles. TT explicitly judges the visible heading-to-content relationship and includes interaction-driven label changes.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.6 · Trusted Tester 10.A · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Visible label/heading and accessible name diverge in descriptiveness — one surface is descriptive, the other is not

The on-screen label and the label a screen reader actually announces disagree (shown as 'First name' but announced as 'field1'), so sighted and screen-reader users get different labels.

2.4.6 is judged differently by the two methodologies: ACT/b49b2e judges the ACCESSIBLE NAME, while TT 5.B/10.A judge the VISIBLE label/heading. The untested gap is when the visible text and the accessible name DIVERGE in descriptiveness. A field visibly labeled 'First name' but given aria-label='field1' (sighted user fine, screen-reader user stranded); or the reverse, a visibly cryptic 'X' button whose aria-label='Close dialog' is the descriptive one; or a heading visibly reading 'Quarterly Earnings' whose aria-labelledby points at a stray 'Q' so AT announces just 'Q'. The Understanding doc warns 2.4.6 is independent of 4.1.2 — a control 'can have an appropriate accessible name and therefore pass 4.1.2, but still fail this success criterion if the label is inaccurate or insufficiently clear.' Deciding which surface to judge, and whether the divergent name is descriptive, is a human call: the name exists (so 4.1.2 / axe pass) but the two surfaces carry different meanings against the field's true purpose.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The coverage summary notes accessible-name computation is exercised 'only trivially (literal text, one img alt, one role=heading); no aria-label/aria-labelledby overrides, no name composed from multiple sources, no name that differs from visible text.' The cc0f0a aria-labelledby fixtures keep visible and programmatic text identical — verified: fixture fa5104f9 sets both the visible <p> and the labelledby source to the same word 'Menu', so there is no descriptiveness DIVERGENCE between eye and AT. A checker confirms a non-empty accessible name (passing 4.1.2) and cannot weigh the visible-vs-announced surfaces against the control's purpose, which is the explicitly-separate 2.4.6 judgment.

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule oj04fd — Element in sequential focus order has visible focus

status: approved

implement: auto,manual,semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 2.4.7

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/oj04fd/proposed/

Proposed

Element in sequential focus order has visible focus

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

2.4.7: Focus Visible (Level AA)

Description

This rule checks that each element in sequential focus order has some visible focus indication.

Applicability

The rule applies to any element which is part of sequential focus navigation in an HTML document .

Expectation

For each target element, there is at least one device pixel inside the scrolling area of the viewport whose HSL color value is different when the element is focused from when it is not.

Background

Default styling in user agents provides a focus indication for focusable elements (even those that are not focusable by default), as shown in Passed Examples 1 and 2. Many examples in this rule need to remove that indicator in order to illustrate various situations. This is bad practice and should normally be avoided.

WCAG 2.0 and 2.1 do not have any requirement of how big or small focus indicator should be, or how far or near from the focusable element it should be. Thus it is possible to pass this rule and Success Criterion 2.4.7 Focus Visible with barely perceptible changes at the other end of the page. That would however still be an accessibility issue. WCAG 2.2 includes Success Criterion 2.4.11 Focus Appearance and Success Criterion 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) specifying how big the focus indicator should be. All Passed Examples in this rule satisfy those success criteria.

WCAG does not require that the focus indicator for each focusable element is unique in appearance. Therefore, this rule can pass even if several focus indicators are identical. Such a situation may nonetheless cause confusion and all examples in this rule avoid it.

Assumptions

There are no assumptions.

Accessibility Support

There are no accessibility support issues known.

Other Resources
  • Success Criterion 2.4.7 Focus Visible
  • Success Criterion 2.4.11 Focus Appearance
  • Success Criterion 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
  • Understanding Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible
  • Understanding Success Criterion 2.4.11: Focus Appearance
  • Understanding Success Criterion 2.4.12: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)

Accessibility Requirements Mapping

2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA)

  • Learn more about 2.4.7 Focus Visible
  • Required for conformance to WCAG 2.0 and later on level AA and higher.
  • Outcome mapping:
  • Any failed outcomes: success criterion is not satisfied
  • All passed outcomes: success criterion needs further testing
  • An inapplicable outcome: success criterion needs further testing

Input Aspects

The following aspects are required in using this rule.

  • CSS styling
  • DOM tree

Examples

These Javascript and CSS files are used in several examples:

File /test-assets/focus-visible-oj04fd/script.js :

function toggleActivation ( id ) {

document . getElementById ( id ). classList . toggle ( ' active ' )

}

File /test-assets/focus-visible-oj04fd/styles.css :

.indicator {

display : inline-block ;

width : 1em ;

height : 1em ;

}

.solid.active {

background-color : navy ;

}

.border.active {

border : medium solid navy ;

}

.no-focus-default :focus {

/* Never do that without defining other focus indication! */

outline : none ;

}

Visual Presentation, Color, and Contrast (cat_6)

Trusted Tester — SC 2.4.7

SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA) — TT Test 4.D

TT section: 4. Keyboard Access and Focus · Baseline: 2. Focus

WCAG SC 2.4.7: Any keyboard operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus

indicator is visible.

Identify Content (applicability)

Use the keyboard to navigate to keyboard-accessible interface components (drop-down menus, form fields,

revealing/hiding content, tooltips, AND all interactive interface components).

DNA if the page has no elements that can receive keyboard focus.

Test 4.D — 2.4.7-focus-visible

Test Condition: *A visible indication of focus is provided when focus is on the interface component.*

How to Test

1. Continue from Test 4.C.

2. Determine whether there is a visible indication of focus on the element that has keyboard focus.

  • a. When keyboard focus is on a frame, some browsers display a visible focus and some may not. Where a

visible focus is not available on a frame, do NOT consider this a failure of the web content.

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. When each interface element receives focus, there is a visible indication of focus.

Note (frame focus disambiguation)
  • To confirm keyboard focus is on a frame when there is no visible focus: use TAB and SHIFT+TAB to deduce that

focus is on the frame. When on the frame, a tab forward moves focus to the first focusable element within the

frame; SHIFT+TAB once moves back to the frame, and another SHIFT+TAB moves to a focusable element before the

frame. Only the frame is permitted to not have a visible focus — confirm it is the frame (not another

element) that lacks the visible focus.

Act-augmented aspect — Focus indicator renders but is perceptually indistinguishable — resting style mimics the ring, or a thick same-color border swallows it (F78 modes 2 & 3)

Every control already has a border that looks just like the focus outline, so when one gets keyboard focus the highlight blends in invisibly.

F78 documents two failures where the focus indicator IS drawn (pixels change on focus) yet a sighted keyboard user still cannot tell which element is focused. Mode 2: the author gives every link/control a permanent static outline that looks identical to the browser focus ring (e.g. a {outline: thin dotted black}); when one element focuses, the UA overlays its own dotted ring, but because all elements already look dotted/outlined, the focused one is not distinguishable from its neighbours. Mode 3: the element has a thick border in the same color as the focus ring (e.g. a {border: medium solid black}); the UA draws its black ring just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker, the ring 'no longer meets the definition of visible' against it. In both, the pixel diff is non-zero so the rule passes, yet the SC purpose — 'help a person know which element has the keyboard focus' — is defeated. Catching this requires a human to compare the focused appearance against the resting appearance of ALL elements (mode 2) or against the adjacent colors (mode 3) and judge whether the difference is genuinely distinguishing, not merely non-zero.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: oj04fd is a pure focused-vs-unfocused pixel diff on a SINGLE element that 'does not care how large it is' or whether it is perceptible, and it never compares the focused element against the resting look of OTHER elements or against its own adjacent colors. The ACT fail fixture is only the blatant outline:none case; there is no fixture pairing a focus-ring-mimicking resting outline or a thick same-color border with the default ring. A fully-automated tool registers the non-zero edge-pixel diff and passes; only human visual judgment about distinguishability/perceptual contrast against context can catch it.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.7 · Trusted Tester 4.D · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Focus indicator present but near the perception threshold — too thin, too low-contrast, or too small to be genuinely seen

The focus highlight technically appears but is so thin, faint, or low-contrast that a keyboard user can't actually see which element has focus.

An indicator can satisfy the pixel-diff rule while remaining effectively invisible to a human. G195 sets concrete guidance for a genuinely visible author indicator: an area at least a 1 CSS px border around the component (or at least 4 CSS px along the shortest side), and a contrast change of 3:1 or more between focused and unfocused states (or, failing 3:1, at least 2px thick). A page can change SOME pixels with a 1px outline whose color barely differs from the background, a faint sub-3:1 box-shadow, or a fractional letter-spacing nudge that only shifts a few antialiased edge pixels — so the diff is non-zero but no human can reliably perceive the focus. The SC's own purpose ('help a person know which element has focus', 'without a focus indicator sighted keyboard users cannot operate the page') implies the change must actually be noticeable; deciding whether a given magnitude/contrast/size crosses the perceptible line is a visual judgment, distinct from camouflage-against-neighbours.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: oj04fd 'does not care WHAT indicator appears... how large it is' and passes on ANY magnitude of HSL change; the corpus uses only high-contrast navy-on-white or strong default outlines and never stresses the HSL-difference test near its detection boundary. There is no near-threshold fixture. A fully-automated 'did a pixel change' checker cannot decide whether a ~1px, ~1.2:1 indicator is noticeable to a human eye in context — that is exactly the human visual judgment the SC purpose requires.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.7 · Trusted Tester 4.D · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Script removes or steals focus the instant an element receives it (F55: onfocus blur / programmatic focus theft)

JavaScript yanks focus away the instant a control receives it, so the focus highlight never appears and keyboard users can't tell where they are on the page.

F55 is a failure where script removes focus the moment an element receives it (onfocus="this.blur()", or a handler that immediately moves focus elsewhere). Because focus never settles, no focus indicator is ever shown for that element, and the control becomes pointer-only. This is a temporal/behavioral failure: a single focused snapshot may even render as unfocused because focus has already been stolen. F55's test requires confirming that 'when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it' — a property over time, not a single render. The brief notes the corpus is static, single-state, with no asynchronous focus changes and no JS that moves focus then immediately blurs.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: oj04fd diffs a single focused snapshot vs an unfocused snapshot of an element it has programmatically focused; if a script blurs immediately, the rule's own focus attempt fails to settle, putting the case outside its clean pass/fail model, and no ACT fixture exercises blur-on-focus. A static pixel-diff cannot model 'focus is removed when received'; F55 explicitly requires a temporal/behavioral check (focus remains until the user moves it) that needs human or dynamic testing.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.7 · Trusted Tester 4.D · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Visual feedback exists only for pointer interaction (:hover/:active) or is suppressed for keyboard (:focus-visible mismatch), leaving keyboard focus bare

Controls only light up on mouse hover and the keyboard outline is stripped, so a keyboard user tabbing through sees no sign of which element is focused.

C15 and C45 stress that the visible feedback must apply to the KEYBOARD focus state, not only pointer interaction. A common real-world failure: authors write ':hover {…}' and ':active {…}' (or rely on JS mouseenter/mouseleave) but never ':focus'/':focus-visible', while also stripping the UA outline. A mouse user sees rich feedback; a keyboard user tabbing through gets nothing. The subtle, judgment-requiring variants are where this matters: :focus-visible heuristics that the UA suppresses for certain elements, :focus reused for both states but styled with mouse-targeted changes, or focus-within applied to a non-focusable wrapper while the real target has outline:none. Distinguishing 'this feedback is pointer-only / modality-mismatched' from 'this is a real keyboard focus indicator' requires understanding the selectors' modality semantics — which input actually triggers the change a keyboard user receives.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT corpus includes only :focus / UA-outline cases and the single outline:none fail; it has no fixture where feedback lives solely on :hover/:active or on a UA-suppressed :focus-visible path. A blatant hover-only-with-outline:none page would fail oj04fd (zero diff under programmatic focus), but the SUBTLE variants — :focus-visible suppressed for a given element type, mouse-driven JS toggles, or focus-within on the wrong node — require a human to reason about which modality actually drives the visible change; a pixel diff cannot attribute a change to input modality.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.7 · Trusted Tester 4.D · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Custom-drawn indicator that vanishes in forced-colors mode or that AT cannot track (G165 / C40 caveats)

A custom focus highlight (a box-shadow or painted square) looks fine normally but vanishes in Windows high-contrast mode or can't be located by screen-reader users.

G165 warns that if you draw your OWN focus indicator (e.g. coloring sections of the page in response to user action) rather than using the native indicator, user/AT system-wide focus customizations 'will not carry over, and AT will not usually be able to find your focus indicator.' C40 adds the forced-colors caveat: relying on box-shadow alone fails because 'user agents commonly suppress the box-shadow property in forced-color modes.' So an indicator can look fine in the single default render oj04fd snapshots, yet disappear (box-shadow / background-image / gradient suppressed) or become orphaned from the real focus position (detached painted square, overlay) for users in Windows High Contrast / forced-colors mode or for AT users relying on the native ring. Judging whether the chosen technique is robust across forced colors and tracks the actual focus is a semantic/contextual judgment about the indicator mechanism, not a default-mode pixel count.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: oj04fd renders one default-mode snapshot and accepts a box-shadow-only, gradient, or JS-painted indicator as a pass because pixels change; it does not simulate forced-colors mode and the corpus has no dark-mode / system-color (Highlight) dependency. The corpus's Passed Examples 3/4 even use the exact 'drawn, detached' indicators G165 warns about, but never test them under forced colors or for focus-tracking robustness. Recognizing that a box-shadow-only / background-image / JS-painted indicator will be suppressed or orphaned for these users requires a human (or a deliberate forced-colors/AT mode toggle) — a default-render checker cannot.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.7 · Trusted Tester 4.D · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Focus indicator drawn but clipped by overflow or pushed outside the visible viewport so the user never sees it

The focus outline is drawn but gets clipped by an overflow container, hidden behind a sticky header, or scrolled off-screen, so the keyboard user never sees it.

The SC requires a perceptible focus indication for the focused element. A real-world failure: the element receives focus and an indicator IS drawn, but it is clipped by an ancestor's overflow:hidden, hidden behind a sticky/fixed header or off-canvas panel, or the focused element sits scrolled out of the visible viewport, so the changed pixels are never actually seen by the user. Because oj04fd counts a pixel change 'inside the scrolling area of the viewport' and never requires the user to be able to see it without manual scrolling — and the corpus places every indicator immediately adjacent in an otherwise empty body — these clipping/scroll cases are untested. Whether the indicator is actually visible to the user (vs technically painted but clipped/offscreen) is a layout/perception judgment; note this partially overlaps WCAG 2.2's 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, but the bare 'I cannot see any focus indicator at all' outcome still implicates 2.4.7.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: oj04fd accepts ANY changed pixel anywhere in the scrolling area and the corpus's single bare element in an empty body never has to deal with clipping containers, sticky overlays, or scroll position; there is no fixture where the indicator is painted but clipped/offscreen. A pixel-diff that scans the whole render surface (or auto-scrolls the element into view) reports a change and passes; judging whether a real user navigating by keyboard would actually SEE the indicator given overflow/sticky/scroll context is a layout-aware human visual judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.7 · Trusted Tester 4.D · priority medium

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 36b590 — Error message describes invalid form field value proposed

status: proposed

implement: semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 3.3.1

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/36b590/proposed/

Proposed

Error message describes invalid form field value

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

3.3.1: Error Identification (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that text error messages provided when the user completes a form field with invalid values or using an invalid format, identify the cause of the error or how to fix the error.

Applicability

This rule applies to each HTML element that has one of the following semantic roles :

  • checkbox ,
  • combobox ,
  • listbox ,
  • menuitemcheckbox ,
  • menuitemradio ,
  • radio ,
  • searchbox ,
  • slider ,
  • spinbutton ,
  • switch or
  • textbox .

Expectation 1

Each test target either has no form field error indicators , or at least one of the form field error indicators allows the identification of the related test target, through text , or through non-text content , or through presentation .

Expectation 2

Each test target either has no form field error indicators , or at least one of the form field error indicators describes:

  • the cause of the error, or
  • how to resolve it,

in text that is visible .

Expectation 3

Each test target either has no form field error indicators , or at least one of the form field error indicators describes:

  • the cause of the error, or
  • how to resolve it,

in text that is included in the accessibility tree or included in the accessible name or accessible description of the test target.

Background

The list of applicable semantic roles is derived by taking all the ARIA 1.2 roles that:

  • inherit from the input , menuitem or select role, and
  • are form field controls (this notably excludes menu , option or tree ).

This rule does not test form field error indicators shown on a different page than that of the test target.

A single form field error indicator can be related to multiple test targets. For example, an error message at the top of a form can list all the form fields that are required and are empty.

A single test target can be related to multiple form field error indicators . For example, a text field can have a red border around it, an error icon adjacent to it, an error message below it, and another error message at the top of the form. All of these are error indicators for the same form field.

Assumptions

There are no assumptions.

Accessibility Support

There are no accessibility support issues known.

Other Resources
  • Understanding Success Criterion 3.3.1: Error Identification
  • G84: Providing a text description when the user provides information that is not in the list of allowed values
  • G85: Providing a text description when user input falls outside the required format or values

Accessibility Requirements Mapping

3.3.1 Error Identification (Level A)

  • Learn more about 3.3.1 Error Identification
  • Required for conformance to WCAG 2.0 and later on level A and higher.
  • Outcome mapping:
  • Any failed outcomes: success criterion is not satisfied
  • All passed outcomes: success criterion needs further testing
  • An inapplicable outcome: success criterion needs further testing

Input Aspects

The following aspects are required in using this rule.

  • DOM Tree
  • CSS Styling
  • Language

<form>

<label for= "age" > Age (years) </label>

<input type= "number" id= "age" aria-describedby= "error" value= "0" />

<span id= "error" > Invalid value for age. Age must be at least 1. </span><br />

<input type= "button" value= "Submit" />

</form>

</strong>

Failed Example 1

Open in a new tab

C.9.3.3.1       Error identification
   Type of assessment                                         Inspection
   Requirement          1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.
   Preconditions
   Procedure            1. Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.1 Error
                        Identification according to WCAG Conformance Requirements stated in clause 9.6.
   Result               Pass: Check 1 is true

Trusted Tester — SC 3.3.1

SC 3.3.1 Error Identification (Level A) — TT Test 5.F

TT section: 5. Forms → Input Error Identification and Suggestions · Baseline: 10. Forms

WCAG SC 3.3.1: If an input error is automatically detected, the item that is in error is identified and the

error is described to the user in text.

Identify Content (Input Error Identification and Suggestions)

1. Use ANDI to identify any form elements on the page.

2. Find all instructions and cues (textual and graphical) related to form components/controls (groupings, order

of completion, special conditions, qualifiers, format instructions).

3. Intentionally enter values and/or make selections that violate format and/or other form instructions to

reveal automatic notifications of input errors.

  • DNA for 5.F and 5.G if there is no automatic input error detection.

Test 5.F — 3.3.1-error-identification

Test Condition: *The item in error is identified in text and sufficiently described to the user in text.*

DNA if the form element does not have automatic error detection.

How to Test

1. Intentionally violate formatting and other form instructions (e.g., leave a required field empty, use a

different date format than required, and/or create a password that does not meet strength requirements).

2. Attempt to submit the form and/or move to the next page.

3. Determine whether the error is identified and described in text.

  • a. The form field with the error is identified in text (e.g., "Error: Password field.").
  • b. Text describes the error (e.g., in a dialog message that states "the Password you entered is incorrect.").
Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. The item that is in error is identified in text and sufficiently described to the user in text.

> Key behavior: This is a trigger-and-observe test — the tester must actively *cause* an error

> (submit invalid input) and then check whether the resulting error is conveyed in text. It is not a static

> inspection.

Act-augmented aspect — Error text is fluent and field-identifying but factually wrong for the value entered / constraint violated (boilerplate mismatch)

A form shows a fluent, field-specific error message, but it describes the wrong problem for the value you actually typed, so you can't tell what's really wrong.

A page shows a non-empty, grammatically descriptive, field-identifying error message that satisfies rule 36b590's 'describes the cause or how to resolve it' check at the string level, but the described cause is factually wrong for the value the user actually entered or the constraint that was actually violated. The text reads as a competent error description in isolation, so it passes every programmatic facet of the rule, but it misidentifies the nature of the error and so defeats the SC's core intent that the user 'can determine what is wrong'. Examples: a phone field that says 'Remove letters and parentheses' against an all-digit value; a date-of-birth field that says 'Please use MM/DD/YYYY format' against a value that already IS in MM/DD/YYYY (the real, undescribed error is a future date); a password field that says 'must be at least 8 characters' against a 12-character value. Detecting this requires reading the field's stated constraints, the entered value, and the error text TOGETHER and judging semantic agreement — a contextual judgment no checker performs.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Rule 36b590 only asks whether at least one indicator describes the cause or fix as a self-contained string; it never compares the message against the actual invalid value or the field's real constraint. Every ACT pass case uses a message that is correct for the contrived value (Age=0 -> 'must be at least 1'), and every ACT fail case fails for a STRUCTURAL reason (generic text, hidden, ambiguous label), never for a message that is fluent-but-wrong. The corpus narrowness 'static hardcoded errors not from real validation' means a plausible message is never pitted against a mismatched value. No automated checker reads the value+constraint+message for semantic agreement.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.1 · Trusted Tester 5.F · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Post-submit page suppresses the error: form silently re-displayed (or shows a neutral/success banner) after a real validation failure — trigger-and-observe failure of NO indicator

After a failed submission the form just reappears with your bad input (or even a success banner) and no error message, so you don't know the submission failed or why.

The SC's most-emphasized procedural limb is trigger-and-observe: submit invalid input, then check whether an error is conveyed in text. The failure the Understanding calls out FIRST is re-displaying the form 'without providing any hint that the submission failed'. On a self-contained page this is staged as the post-submit STATE: the page representing 'the user submitted invalid input and the server bounced it' shows the form again with the bad value retained but NO error message — or worse, shows a neutral/green confirmation that does not mention the failure. A tool inspecting this page finds a form, finds no error indicator, and returns inapplicable/vacuous-pass (like ACT Passed Example 3), while a human who understands the page is the RESULT of a failed submission sees the violation. Distinguishing 'a benign blank form' from 'a post-failure page that suppressed the error' is a contextual judgment driven by page-state cues (retained bad value, submitted indicator, mismatched success banner).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Every ACT page is the already-errored state with a hard-coded span; none represents a submission RESULT, and the 'no indicator -> vacuous pass' branch (Passed Example 3) is treated as legitimately passing. There is no case where the ABSENCE of an indicator is itself the failure because an error genuinely occurred. The corpus is 100% static with type='button', so it never submits, validates, or detects an error dynamically — the entire trigger-and-observe limb is unexercised. An automated checker cannot infer that a no-error page is the aftermath of a failed submission; only a human reading the page-state context can.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.1 · Trusted Tester 5.F · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Inline error message is visually placed next to the WRONG field, with no programmatic association to check

An error message sits visually next to the wrong field with no programmatic link, so you read it against the field it appears to belong to and get misled about what's in error.

A self-contained page renders a descriptive error message physically below / next to a field, but the message's text refers to a DIFFERENT field than the one it visually sits under, and there is no aria-describedby tying it to any control (so no programmatic association exists to evaluate). A sighted user reads the message against the field it appears to annotate and is misled about which item is in error. Because identification by visual proximity ('errors inline ... next to the specific fields') is an explicitly sufficient method under the SC, the message passes every programmatic facet of 36b590 — non-empty, descriptive, visible, in the tree, identification 'through presentation'. The only way to detect the violation is to read the message text, read the label of the field it visually adjoins, and notice they disagree — a visual-spatial + semantic judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT Failed Example 5 fails only because two fields share IDENTICAL labels (a name-collision the rule reasons about via label text); it never tests a message whose text clearly names field A while being positioned next to field B. Rule 36b590 treats 'through presentation' (proximity) as a valid identification path but never builds a case where presentation actively points at the wrong target, and it has no spatial model of which field a message visually adjoins. The corpus narrowness 'contrived id failures no wrong field' explicitly excludes this. Automated checkers cannot judge visual adjacency vs. message semantics.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.1 · Trusted Tester 5.F · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Top-of-form error summary lists fields/causes/counts that do not correspond to the page's actually-flagged fields (summary-vs-state incoherence)

A top-of-form error summary lists fields, counts, or links that don't match the fields actually flagged on the page, so you can't reliably tell what needs fixing.

Following G83/G84/G85's 'text description at the top of the page', a self-contained page shows a top-of-form error summary block — descriptive, visible, in the tree — but the summary's CONTENT is inconsistent with the rest of the page: it lists a field that is not present, omits a field that is visibly flagged, states a count ('2 errors') that disagrees with the number of flagged fields, names a different field than the one displaying an inline error, or contains anchor links that point to the wrong control. Each individual statement may be a fluent error description (passing 36b590 at the message level), but the summary as a whole misidentifies the items in error, so the user cannot reliably 'determine what is wrong'. Judging this requires cross-referencing the summary list against the actual form fields and their flagged states — a holistic reconciliation no rule performs.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT has exactly one top-of-form-list pass (Passed Example 2) where the summary is perfectly coherent, and one shared-message fail (Failed Example 1) that fails only for genericness. The corpus never builds a summary that is internally detailed yet INCONSISTENT with the flagged state — its narrowness 'single form one error pages no multi error summaries' captures that multi-error reconciliation is absent. 36b590 evaluates each indicator's describing text independently and has no notion of summary/field agreement. A checker can verify an anchor target exists but cannot judge whether the summary's claims match which fields are truly in error.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.1 · Trusted Tester 5.F · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Error is signalled ONLY by visual styling (red border / colour / icon glyph) with no error meaning in text anywhere on the page

A field is flagged as wrong using only colour, a red border, or an icon, with no words anywhere saying an error occurred, so a screen-reader user never learns there's a problem.

A field is clearly flagged as in error by purely visual means — a red border, a red/yellow background, a red exclamation-triangle icon, a red CSS glyph, a reddened label with a trailing asterisk — but there is no text anywhere stating that an error occurred or what it is (no message string, no alt/aria-label conveying error, no visually-hidden text). The SC explicitly allows colour/icon IN ADDITION to text but forbids it as the SOLE indicator: 'The error must be indicated in text.' Detecting this requires a human to look at the rendered page, recognise that the ONLY conveyance of the error is visual styling, and confirm the error meaning is absent from text. A CSS-only red border or a decorative icon with empty alt typically does not register to tools as an 'error indicator' at all, so the page passes vacuously while a sighted user is plainly being signalled an error that is never stated in words.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The entire ACT corpus delivers errors as plain text spans; there is NO case with an icon-only or colour-only indicator, and the narrowness 'no color only cue' confirms it. 36b590's Applicability is triggered by 'form field error indicators' and its expectations check the DESCRIBING text — a page whose only error signal is a red border may surface no textual indicator for the rule to evaluate, so it passes vacuously, masking the real violation. Automated colour-only detection (F81) is unreliable and cannot judge whether the field's error meaning is conveyed in text elsewhere; the rendered-vs-text reconciliation needs human visual judgment.

Act-augmented aspect — Error is conveyed via an icon/image that HAS a text alternative, but the alt/name misstates, genericises, or mislocates the error

An error icon has alt text, but the text is wrong, generic, or describes the icon's appearance instead of the actual error, so it doesn't tell a screen-reader user what's wrong.

An error is delivered through an image/icon, which the SC permits provided the meaning is conveyed 'in text or a text alternative'. The page DOES give the icon a non-empty text alternative, so a tool finds the alt/aria-label present and is satisfied — but the alternative is wrong or uselessly generic relative to the actual error: an icon beside a malformed-email field has alt='error' or alt='red triangle' (describes appearance, not the error) or alt='This field is required' (wrong cause — the field was filled but mis-formatted), or two error icons share one generic title 'Invalid input' (cannot identify which field/what error), or the alt is the correct cause for a DIFFERENT field than the one it sits beside. The image exists, the alt exists, the role/name machinery is intact — only a human comparing the alternative's MEANING against the field's actual error state can tell the text alternative fails to identify or describe the error.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT case uses an image as the error indicator at all, so the text-alternative delivery path the SC explicitly blesses is wholly unexercised, and the specific failure of an icon with present-but-misleading alt is impossible in a corpus of plain text spans. 36b590 would see a named non-text indicator and treat Expectation 1 (identification 'through non-text content') as satisfied, never judging whether the alt's semantics match the error. Automated checkers verify alt PRESENCE, not whether the alt correctly describes the field's actual error — that is a semantic comparison only a human (or judging model) can make.

C.9.3.3.2 — SC 3.3.2 Labels or instructions
C.9.3.3.2       Labels or instructions
   Type of assessment                                         Inspection
   Requirement          1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.
   Preconditions
   Procedure            1. Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.2 Labels or
                        Instructions according to WCAG Conformance Requirements stated in clause 9.6.

                        Fail: Check 1 is false

Trusted Tester — SC 3.3.2

SC 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A) — TT Test 5.A

TT section: 5. Forms · Baseline: 10. Forms

WCAG SC 3.3.2: Labels or instructions are provided when content requires user input.

Identify Content (Form Components)

1. Use ANDI: focusable elements to identify any form elements on the page (buttons, text fields, radio

buttons, checkboxes, read-only fields, multi-select lists).

2. Find all instructions and cues (textual and graphical) related to form components/controls (groupings, order

of completion, special conditions, qualifiers, format instructions).

  • EXCLUDE disabled input elements (they do not receive keyboard focus, cannot be selected, cannot be

modified).

  • DNA for 5.A–5.H if there is no such content.

Test 5.A — 3.3.2-label-provided

Test Condition: *Visual labels or instructions are provided for form elements.*

DNA if the page does not have form elements or all form elements are disabled.

How to Test

1. Determine if each form element provides visual labels or instructions.

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. Visual labels or instructions are provided for each form element.

Notes
  • The label or instruction must be visible when the form field has focus.
  • The label or instruction can be graphical or textual.
  • This test only determines whether visual labels/instructions are present, regardless of accuracy. The

form label is tested for sufficient *description* in 5.B (2.4.6-label-descriptive).

  • The programmatic association of the form instruction (text label) to the form field is tested in 5.C

(1.3.1-programmatic-label). See sc-1.3.1-info-and-relationships.md and sc-4.1.2-name-role-value.md.

> Scope note: 3.3.2 in TT is strictly *"is a visible label/instruction present?"*. Adequacy is 2.4.6;

> programmatic name/association is 1.3.1/4.1.2. The three are tested by three separate TT conditions over the

> same fields.

Act-augmented aspect — Instruction promised on focus does not actually become perceivable when the field is focused

A field's only instruction is meant to appear when you focus it, but it never shows, is clipped off-screen, vanishes too fast, or needs a mouse hover instead of keyboard focus.

WCAG explicitly blesses the pattern of withholding a long/verbose instruction until the field receives focus, and Trusted Tester makes 'visible when the form field has focus' a normative requirement. The conformance question is therefore behavioral: when the field is focused, does the promised instruction (password-complexity rule, date-format hint, character rules) actually become visible? The failure is a field whose only instruction is wired to appear on focus but in fact (a) never appears, (b) appears empty/placeholder-only, (c) appears off-screen / clipped / behind another element, (d) auto-dismisses before the user can read or act on it, or (e) requires hover (not keyboard focus) so keyboard users never get it. The static DOM looks fine; only driving the focus state and visually judging the rendered result reveals whether the instruction is honored. This is the entire 'available only when the individual control has focus' limb operationalized as a failure.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: There are zero ACT rules and zero test-case pages for 3.3.2, so nothing exercises any dynamic state. All 8 technique docs show static, always-visible labels; none demonstrates a focus-revealed instruction, let alone one that fails to appear, time out, or trigger on hover instead of focus. The 8-pattern seed file is entirely about placeholder/required/grouping in the static DOM. A linter inspecting static HTML sees the instruction node (or a :focus CSS rule) present and reports a label exists; it cannot drive focus, observe what actually renders, time the appearance/disappearance, distinguish a :hover trigger from a :focus trigger, or judge whether the focused instruction is genuinely perceivable. This requires interacting with the page and visually judging the focused state.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.2 · Trusted Tester 5.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Instruction is present and well-formatted but semantically wrong, stale, or contradicts the field's actual rule

A field shows a clear instruction that's actually wrong for what it accepts (says MM/DD/YYYY but wants DD/MM/YYYY), so following it guarantees an error.

3.3.2 requires instructions that identify the controls so users know what input data is expected and that specify data formats, especially out-of-customary formats or specific input rules. A field can DISPLAY a confident, perfectly-marked-up instruction that is simply incorrect or stale relative to what the field accepts: the visible hint says 'MM/DD/YYYY' but the field enforces DD/MM/YYYY; 'Max 20 characters' while it truncates at 10; 'Enter your 5-digit ZIP' next to a field requiring ZIP+4; or copied boilerplate naming the wrong purpose entirely ('Enter your member ID' on a promo-code field). The user is actively misled — following the instruction guarantees an error — which the Understanding warns is as harmful as too little. The label/instruction is structurally perfect; the defect is purely the correspondence between the words and the field's real behavior.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT rule/test exists; the technique examples only show instructions correct by construction (the date-format example, the username-rules example). There is no failure technique for a wrong/stale instruction and no seed pattern covers content that is present-but-false (the seeds are all about missing/placeholder/color-only labels). Automated tools verify the existence and association of label text; they have no model of what the field actually accepts (the pattern/maxlength/validation logic vs. the prose) to compare against, so they cannot detect a contradiction between a hint and the field's behavior. Catching this requires reading the instruction, inferring the rule, and noticing the conflict.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.2 · Trusted Tester 5.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Image-only / icon-only label that is not 'widely understood by the intended target audience'

A data-entry field's only visible cue is an ambiguous icon or symbol that doesn't make clear what to type, so a sighted user can't tell what input is expected.

The Understanding accepts images as labels but adds the explicit caveat that authors must ensure the images are widely understood by the intended target audience, recommending supplementary tooltips/text for clarity. G167's happy path uses near-universal icons (magnify glass, paper-airplane send). The uncovered failure is a data-entry field whose ONLY visible cue is an ambiguous, decorative, or domain-obscure glyph — a lone '#' next to a field secretly meaning 'enter quantity', a generic gear/sliders icon as the only cue for a 'budget' field, two adjacent fields each cued by indistinguishable icons. A sighted user cannot tell what to type. This is a 3.3.2 visible-cue-adequacy failure even if the icon carries correct alt text giving it an accessible name (which would pass 4.1.2) — the visible cue still fails to communicate purpose to everyone.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT rule/test exists, and G167 only documents well-understood icons; there is no failure technique for an obscure icon and no seed pattern covers image-label adequacy (seeds are all text/placeholder/color cases). Tools can confirm an icon has alt text / an accessible name, but they have no notion of whether the rendered GLYPH is interpretable by a human looking at it. 'Widely understood by the intended target audience' is an irreducibly human, audience-relative semantic judgment that requires actually viewing the icon and reasoning about what a typical user would infer.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.2 · Trusted Tester 5.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Group-level (legend/heading) label is needed where individual labels are insufficient, but is absent or only visual — F82 generalized beyond phone numbers

Several related fields each have labels too vague alone (Street, City, Zip), and the group has no overall heading, so you can't tell what the set is for, like billing versus shipping.

F82 is the one documented failure technique but is narrowly framed around US phone-number fields. The underlying failure generalizes: any set of fields where each field's individual label, read alone, is insufficient and a GROUP-level description is required (H71's core rationale) but the group description is absent or present only as visual proximity/styling, not as a real label. H71 names the test: where a group of controls within a larger form requires an additional heading to provide a description specific to that group. The failure is judging that a particular set DOES need a group label and that the visible page fails to provide one. Examples beyond phone: billing vs shipping address blocks with identical inner labels (Street/City/Zip) and no group heading; a split Given/Family name where neither field alone says 'Name'; date-as-three-selects (Day/Month/Year) with no 'Date of birth' grouping.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT rule/test page exists. F82 is technique prose limited to phone numbers. The seed file's only grouping pattern is custom radios with broken radiogroup semantics — a different, partly programmatic defect that axe-adjacent tooling and the seed already cover, so this aspect must be constructed with otherwise-correctly-labeled native inputs to avoid duplicating it. Recognizing that a set of fields NEEDS a group label, and that visual proximity is doing work the textual labeling does not, is a contextual semantic judgment about whether the per-field labels are sufficient standalone. Tools can detect a missing fieldset/legend, but presence of fieldset/legend is neither necessary (a visible group heading can suffice) nor a reliable signal of the actual failure (two identical address blocks can each have labeled inputs and pass every linter while being genuinely ambiguous). The 'is a group label needed here?' decision is human.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.2 · Trusted Tester 5.A · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Format/required instruction exists but is positioned or styled so it is not perceivable as belonging to the field (visually orphaned instruction)

A field's instruction text exists but sits far away, in a collapsed panel, or is tiny and low-contrast, so a sighted user doesn't connect it to the field or can't read it.

3.3.2 is about whether the instruction is PRESENTED to all users for that control. A subtle failure: the instruction text genuinely exists and is visible somewhere on the page, but is visually disconnected from the field it governs — placed far above the form, after the submit button, in a collapsed/closed-by-default help panel, in a footnote, or styled so small/low-contrast/greyed that a sighted user does not associate it with (or cannot read) the field. The Understanding warns the goal is to provide enough information to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation; an orphaned instruction forces exactly that navigation. The static text node exists, so a 'does instruction text exist?' check passes; whether a real user perceives it as the field's instruction is a layout/visual judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT rule/test exists. Technique examples always place the instruction adjacent to or programmatically tied to the field; there is no failure technique for an orphaned instruction, and the seed patterns center on missing/placeholder/color-only labels, not mispositioned-but-present ones. An automated tool searching the DOM for instruction text would FIND it and not flag a problem; tools cannot reason about spatial proximity, reading-order distance, collapsed-disclosure state, contrast-as-it-relates-to-association, or whether a human would visually bind the instruction to the field. This is a perception/layout judgment requiring a rendered view.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.2 · Trusted Tester 5.A · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — False-positive guard: links and non-data-entry controls correctly out of scope (do not require labels/instructions)

Buttons, links, and toggles aren't data-entry fields, so they correctly need no input instructions and shouldn't be flagged for lacking them.

3.3.2 explicitly does NOT apply to links or other interactive controls that are not associated with data entry (expand/collapse widgets, menu toggles, tabs, pagination links, accordions, dialog-open buttons). The uncovered situation is the INAPPLICABLE / correct-pass case that prevents false positives: a page rich in buttons, links, and disclosure widgets that legitimately have NO field-style instructions because they are not data-entry controls. An evaluator (human or model) must recognize the scope boundary and NOT demand a '3.3.2 instruction' for a non-input control, while still correctly flagging any genuine data-entry field on the same page that lacks instruction. This guards against over-flagging and tests whether the evaluator has internalized the scope clause rather than treating every interactive element as needing input instructions.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT rule/test exists, and there is no inapplicable/pass fixture in the corpus at all (testCaseCount 0). The techniques only demonstrate data-entry controls; nothing operationalizes the scope boundary that links/disclosure widgets are out of scope. The seed file is entirely failing data-entry patterns. Recognizing that a control is NOT a data-entry control — and therefore needs no 3.3.2 instruction — is a semantic/contextual judgment about each control's role and purpose that a naive checker (or an over-eager model) can get wrong by demanding labels everywhere. This is a precision/over-flagging guard that requires reasoning about what each control does.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.2 · Trusted Tester 5.A · priority medium

EN 301 549 — C.9.3.3.3 (SC 3.3.3)

C.9.3.3.3 — SC 3.3.3 Error suggestion
C.9.3.3.3       Error suggestion
   Type of assessment                                         Inspection
   Requirement          1. The ICT is, or includes, a web page.
   Preconditions
   Procedure            1. Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.3 Error
                        Suggestion according to WCAG Conformance Requirements stated in clause 9.6.
   Result               Pass: Check 1 is true
                        Fail: Check 1 is false
                        Not applicable: If any requirement precondition is false or the web page does not
                        contain content relevant to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.3 Error Suggestion. (Do
                        not need to meet or test)

---

Conformance-scope clauses (EN-specific — not per-criterion tests)

Trusted Tester — SC 3.3.3

SC 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (Level AA) — TT Test 5.G

TT section: 5. Forms → Input Error Identification and Suggestions · Baseline: 10. Forms

WCAG SC 3.3.3: If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then

the suggestions are provided to the user, unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.

Test 5.G — 3.3.3-error-suggestion

Test Condition: *Guidance (e.g., suggestion for corrected input) is provided about how to correct errors for

form fields.*

DNA if any of the following apply to the form element:

  • There is no automatic input error detection.
  • Based on the type of input required, suggestions for correction cannot be provided because they are not

knowable.

  • Providing information about how to correct the error would jeopardize the security or purpose of the

content (e.g., details about an incorrect password).

How to Test

1. Continue from Test 5.F.

2. Determine whether guidance provides sufficient details for how to correct the error and/or offers

suggestions of corrected input.

Evaluate Results (PASS if ANY true)

1. Suggestions for corrected input are provided, OR

2. The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error.

> Depends on 5.F: runs only after an error has been triggered (5.F). 3.3.1 asks *"is the error identified

> & described?"*; 3.3.3 asks the harder follow-up *"does it tell you how to fix it?"*.

Act-augmented aspect — Error identified in text but no correction suggestion given, though the fix is clearly knowable

A form says what's wrong ('Invalid date') but never tells you how to fix it, even though the correct format or rule is clearly knowable.

This is the central, distinctive obligation of 3.3.3 versus 3.3.1: the page DOES identify the error in text (so 3.3.1 passes and any 'is there an error message' heuristic is satisfied), but the message stops at naming the problem and never tells the user HOW TO FIX it, even though the correction is plainly knowable from the field's constraints. Examples: 'Invalid date' with no format given, 'Password not strong enough' with no rules listed, 'Invalid entry' for a field that accepts exactly one of a small enumerated set. The required human judgment is twofold: (1) is a correction knowable here, and (2) does the present text actually convey it, or merely restate that something is wrong. A self-contained HTML page can be pre-rendered in its post-submit error state so no interaction is needed.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT corpus for 3.3.3 is entirely empty (0 rules, 0 test cases), so there is no executable case for the pass/fail obligation at all. Automated tools at best detect that error TEXT exists (the 3.3.1 limb); they cannot judge whether that text contains an actionable suggestion versus a bare restatement, because both are valid non-empty strings. Distinguishing 'Invalid date' from 'Invalid date — use MM/DD/YYYY' requires semantic reading of whether a correction is present.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.3 · Trusted Tester 5.G · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Suggestion text is present but wrong, misleading, or contradicts the actual validation rule

A form gives a specific fix-it suggestion, but it's factually wrong for the field, so even following it the input still gets rejected.

The page provides a confident, specific correction suggestion, so every 'a suggestion is present' check passes — but the suggestion is factually incorrect for this field: it names the wrong format, the wrong allowed range, a 'did-you-mean' value that is itself invalid, or a fix the validator will still reject. This is the direct analogue of 'alt exists but misrepresents the image.' Per Trusted Tester the obligation is that the guidance provides SUFFICIENT/ADEQUATE detail to fix the error; a misleading suggestion fails that even though text exists. Only a human who knows the field's true rule can detect the mismatch between the suggestion and reality.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT case exists, and even a hypothetical one would assert on the presence of suggestion text, not its correctness against the field's true constraint. Automated tools have no model of what the field actually accepts, so they cannot tell that 'Use DD/MM/YYYY' is wrong when the parser only accepts MM/DD/YYYY, or that 'Did you mean January?' was offered for an input that was already valid. Correctness is a semantic, ground-truth judgment.

Act-augmented aspect — Suggestion correctly WITHHELD for a security/purpose-sensitive field (exception that must read as PASS)

For a security-sensitive field like a password, giving only a generic error and no specific fix is correct to avoid leaking information, so it shouldn't be flagged as a failure.

The SC explicitly carves out 'unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.' A correct implementation of a security-sensitive field (login password, security-question answer, 2FA code, payment CVV) deliberately gives a generic, non-revealing error and offers no specific correction — and that is the right outcome, a PASS. The hard human judgment is recognizing when withholding a suggestion is correct (and must not be flagged) versus when the same generic message ('Invalid input') on a non-sensitive field is a real failure. This inverts the naive heuristic: here the absence of a suggestion is conformant.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The ACT corpus is empty and, per the survey, no case exercises a security-sensitive field where correctly withholding a suggestion is the right outcome. Automated tools cannot classify a field as security/purpose-sensitive, so they would either never flag missing suggestions at all, or wrongly flag the deliberately-generic login error as a failure. Deciding the field's sensitivity and whether the exception applies is purely contextual.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.3 · Trusted Tester 5.G · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Correction not knowable: no suggestion required and absence must not be penalized (the DNA/precondition gate)

For a free-text field where the system genuinely can't know the right answer, offering only a generic message is fine and shouldn't be penalized for lacking a suggestion.

3.3.3 only obliges a suggestion when 'suggestions for correction are known.' For free-form fields where the correct value is genuinely not inferable by the system (a free-text 'Tell us why', an open-ended display name, a one-time human-verified value), no specific suggestion is possible and the page conformantly provides only a generic 'This field is required' or 'We couldn't verify this.' The judge must decide whether the correction is knowable at all before deciding pass/fail — a precondition gate that distinguishes 'no suggestion because none is possible' (PASS/DNA) from 'no suggestion despite one being obvious' (the first aspect's FAIL). This is a semantic call about the nature of the field, not its markup.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Per the survey the knowability gate is uncovered: no ACT rule/test distinguishes a field whose correction is inferable from one where it is not. Automated tools have no concept of whether a correction is computable for a given field; they cannot tell an enumerable 'month' field (suggestion knowable, absence is a fail) from a free-text 'feedback' field (suggestion not knowable, absence is fine). The distinction is entirely about meaning and field semantics.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.3 · Trusted Tester 5.G · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Suggestion technically present but too vague/generic to actually let the user fix the error

An error message gestures at fixing ('Please check your entry') but is too generic to tell you what to actually change, so you still can't correct the input.

The error message contains language that gestures at a fix but is so generic it does not give the user enough to actually correct the input: 'Please check your entry and try again', 'That doesn't look right — please fix it', 'Enter a valid value', 'Improve your input.' A presence-of-text check passes and even a 'does it mention fixing?' heuristic may pass, yet the user still cannot determine WHAT to change. Trusted Tester requires the description to contain ADEQUATE information for the user to know what is required to fix the error; vague filler fails that bar. The judgment is whether the words, in this field's context, are actionable — distinct from the 'wrong/misleading' aspect (which is confidently specific but false) and from the 'no suggestion' aspect (which has no fix language at all).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT case exists. Even a presence heuristic that scans for fix-oriented phrasing ('please correct', 'try again') is satisfied by vague filler. Judging whether the suggestion actually conveys what to change — given the specific field's constraints — is a semantic adequacy call no automated tool can make; 'Enter a valid value' is a syntactically valid suggestion but conveys nothing.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.3 · Trusted Tester 5.G · priority medium

  • Trusted Tester 5.G (How to Test) — “Determine whether guidance provides **sufficient details** for how to correct the error and/or offers suggestions of corrected input.…”
  • WCAG Understanding (In brief) — “Where errors are detected, suggest known ways to correct them.…”

Act-augmented aspect — Suggestion present but stranded far from its field with no proximity, association, or jump mechanism (locatability of the fix)

A correct fix-it suggestion exists but is placed far from its field with no link or proximity, so you can't find it or connect it to the field that needs fixing.

The page contains a correct, adequate suggestion for the erroring field, but it is placed where the user cannot reasonably connect it to or reach the field: a correct 'Use MM/DD/YYYY' tip buried in a footer while the date field is at the top; a top-of-page error summary that names the fix but offers no working link to jump to the field and no near-field repetition; or a suggestion placed inside the wrong section so it reads as belonging to a different field. G177 and G139 make proximity/locatability part of HOW the suggestion must be provided. Whether the suggestion is close enough, associated with the right field, or reachable is a visual/spatial and contextual judgment about the rendered page, not a property of any single element.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT case exists, and the survey notes proximity/locatability is covered only as authoring techniques with manual procedures. Automated tools can confirm the suggestion string exists somewhere in the DOM but cannot judge whether it is positioned close enough, visually/semantically associated with the right field, or reachable via a working jump link — these are layout/relevance judgments. A scanner sees the text and passes; a human sees a suggestion stranded far from its field or pointing at the wrong one.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.3 · Trusted Tester 5.G · priority medium

  • Technique G139 — “a link to that error is provided so that the user does not have to search for it.…”
  • Technique G84 — “describes the nature of the problem, and provides ways to locate the field(s) with a problem easily.…”

Act-augmented aspect — Color/asterisk/icon-only error indication with no text suggestion — the 'in text' limb

A field's error and how to fix it are conveyed only by colour, a red asterisk, or an icon, with no text describing the correction, so a screen-reader user gets no guidance.

The page communicates that a field is in error and what to do purely through non-text means: turning the label red, adding a red asterisk, swapping in a warning icon, or showing a red border — with NO text description of the problem or the correction. G84 explicitly states this is insufficient: an asterisk or red label does not satisfy the SC; a text description is required. The judgment is visual and semantic: confirm that the red/icon is the ONLY carrier of the error+fix information and that no equivalent text suggestion accompanies it. The 3.3.3-specific limb is the missing CORRECTION TEXT, distinct from the 1.4.1 'use of color' / 3.3.1 'error identification' framings.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT case exists for 3.3.3, and while a generic 1.4.1 'use of color' scanner might flag the red, it cannot determine that the missing element is specifically a TEXT SUGGESTION for correction (the 3.3.3 obligation) rather than just identification. Confirming there is no accompanying correction text anywhere, and that the visual carries the whole job, requires reading the rendered page and judging meaning.

Associates with: guideline SC 3.3.3 · Trusted Tester 5.G · priority medium

  • Technique G85 — “information about the nature and location of the input error is provided in text to enable the users to identify the problem.…”
