Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 59796f — Image button has non-empty accessible name

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 1.1.1,4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/59796f/proposed/

Proposed

Image button has non-empty accessible name

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

1.1.1: Non-text Content (Level A) ,

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that each image button element has a non-empty accessible name.

Applicability

This rule applies to any input element with a type attribute value of image , and that is included in the accessibility tree .

Expectation

Each target element has an accessible name that is neither empty ( "" ), nor the default name for this element (localized version of “Submit Query”).

Background

Unlike for img elements, an empty alt attribute ( alt="" ) does not make an image button decorative; image buttons have a button role and are therefore exposed as interactive elements. An empty alt attribute therefore does not provide a “usable string” for image buttons and the computation defaults to other means of providing a name, as defined in input type=”image” Accessible Name Computation algorithm .

Assumptions
  • This rule assumes that all image buttons are user interface components as defined by WCAG 2 .
  • This rule assumes that the default name for image buttons (“Submit Query”), as defined by the HTML Accessibility API Mapping , is never descriptive.
Accessibility Support

The input type=”image” Accessible Name Computation algorithm uses the first defined attribute, even if the attribute has an empty value. In contrast, some user agents and assistive technologies ignore empty attributes.

Related rules
  • Button has non-empty accessible name

Inapplicable
Inapplicable Example 1

Inapplicable Example 2

Inapplicable Example 3

Inapplicable Example 4

Inapplicable Example 5

Open in a new tab

The image button is ignored by assistive technologies because it is not included in the accessibility tree . These are not required to have an accessible name. If at some future state of the page the element gets included in the accessibility tree , an accessible name will be necessary.

<input type= "image" src= "/test-assets/shared/search-icon.svg" style= "display: none;" />

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule c487ae — Link has non-empty accessible name

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 1.1.1,2.4.4,4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/c487ae/proposed/

Proposed

Link has non-empty accessible name

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A) ,

2.4.4: Link Purpose (In Context) (Level A) ,

2.4.9: Link Purpose (Link Only) (Level AAA)

Description

This rule checks that each link has a non-empty accessible name.

Applicability

This rule applies to any HTML element that is an inheriting semantic link included in the accessibility tree .

Expectation

Each target element has an accessible name that is not empty ( "" ).

Background

Assumptions

The rule assumes that all links are user interface components as defined by WCAG 2. When the link role is used on elements that do not behave as links, failing this rule might not mean that the success criteria are failed.

Accessibility Support
  • For area elements that have an href attribute, but are not nested inside a map element, there are differences between browsers and assistive technology on if the area is included in the accessibility tree .
  • Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some semantic link elements can fail this rule with some technology but users of other technologies would not experience any accessibility issue.
  • Accessibility support for some elements inheriting the semantic role of link (e.g. elements with doc-* attributes) may vary depending on the assistive technology in use.

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 4e8ab6 — Element with role attribute has required states and properties

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 1.3.1,4.1.2,ARIA:

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/4e8ab6/proposed/

Proposed

Element with role attribute has required states and properties

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

Description

This rule checks that elements that have an explicit role also specify all required states and properties.

Applicability

This rule applies to any HTML or SVG element that is included in the accessibility tree and has an explicit semantic role , except if the element has an implicit semantic role that is identical to the explicit semantic role .

Expectation

For each test target, the WAI-ARIA required states and properties for the role are set and not empty ( "" ), unless the state or property has a default value listed under WAI-ARIA implicit value for role .

Background

Omitting WAI-ARIA required states and properties is often the result of a developer error. When required properties are missing and a default value is not specified by WAI-ARIA Specifications , the behavior is not defined. For WAI-ARIA 1.2 , the only explicit semantic roles with a required property with a default value are the option and tabs roles for the aria-selected property.

This rule is testing author built components that specify explicit semantic roles and not components that keep their implicit semantic role . For components that keep their implicit semantic role , all native HTML and SVG elements have native attributes that are mapped to all of the WAI-ARIA required states and properties . Most of these mappings are defined in the HTML Accessibility API Mappings, Attribute State and Property Mappings .

Assumptions
  • The ARIA role is being used to conform to WCAG.
Accessibility Support

This rule relies on browsers and assistive technologies to support leaving out WAI-ARIA required states and properties when a WAI-ARIA implicit value for role is specified in WAI-ARIA Specifications .

Note: The required states and properties with implicit values can be found in the Core Accessibility API Mappings 1.1 Overview of default values for missing required attributes .

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 5c01ea — ARIA state or property is permitted proposed

status: proposed

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 1.3.1,4.1.2,ARIA:

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/5c01ea/proposed/

Proposed

ARIA state or property is permitted

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

Description

This rule checks that WAI-ARIA states or properties are allowed for the element they are specified on.

Applicability

This rule applies to any WAI-ARIA state or property that is specified on an HTML or SVG element that is included in the accessibility tree .

Expectation

For each test target, one of the following is true:

  • global : the test target is a global state or property ; or
  • semantic role : the test target is an inherited , supported , or required state or property of the semantic role of the element on which the test target is specified; or
  • language feature : the test target is specified on an HTML element and is allowed on that element. Which ARIA states or properties may be used on which element is described in ARIA in HTML .

Background

The use of ARIA attributes that are not supported by a role is often the result of a developer using either an incorrect role, or misunderstanding the attribute. These attributes are ignored by browsers and other assistive technologies. This often means that information that should exist is missing to assistive technology users.

In HTML, there are language features that do not have corresponding implicit WAI-ARIA semantics. As per ARIA in HTML , those elements can have global states or properties . Some of those elements can also have inherited , supported , or required states or properties that correspond to a WAI-ARIA role . For example, the audio element has no corresponding ARIA semantics but it can have inherited , supported , or required states or properties of the application role .

Note that required WAI-ARIA states or properties for a role may change with the advance of the WAI-ARIA specifications. For example, both aria-expanded and aria-controls were required in ARIA 1.2 for combobox role, but the aria-controls was removed from required states or properties in ARIA 1.3 . The examples in this rule follow ARIA 1.3 .

Assessing the value of the attribute is out of scope for this rule.

Assumptions

There are no assumptions.

Accessibility Support

Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some elements can have a semantic role of none and their attributes fail this rule with some technologies but users of other technology would not experience any accessibility issue.

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 674b10 — Role attribute has valid value

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 1.3.1,4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/674b10/proposed/

Proposed

Role attribute has valid value

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

Description

This rule checks that each role attribute has a valid value.

Applicability

This rule applies to any role attribute for which all the following are true:

  • the attribute has a value that is neither empty (“”) nor only ASCII whitespace ; and
  • the attribute is specified on an HTML or SVG element which is not programmatically hidden .

Expectation

Each test target has at least one token which is a valid value corresponding to a non-abstract role from WAI-ARIA Specifications .

Background

Using an invalid role is often the result of a typo or other developer error. Unknown roles are ignored by browsers and assistive technologies, and the element’s implicit role is used. This often means that a role that should exist is missing.

The role attribute is a set of space separated tokens . Having a whitespace separated list of more than one token in the value of the role attribute is used for what is known as fallback roles . If the first token is not accessibility supported (or valid), the next one will be used for determining the semantic role of the element, and so forth. The rule applies to attributes containing at least one non- ASCII whitespace character so that there is at least one token in the set.

Not every role can be used on every element. Which ARIA roles may be used on which HTML elements is defined in ARIA in HTML . Testing this is not part of this rule.

Assumptions

There are no assumptions.

Accessibility Support

There are no accessibility support issues known.

ACT 6a7281 — ARIA state or property has valid value

⚗ Act-augmented WIP tests address this rule's blind spots:
  • 4.1.2 Exposed ARIA state/value is present and valid but contradicts the rendered contr — 6 pages
  • 4.1.2 User-settable state/value cannot be programmatically set via AT or its change is — 6 pages

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 6a7281 — ARIA state or property has valid value

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 1.3.1,4.1.2,ARIA:

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/6a7281/proposed/

Proposed

ARIA state or property has valid value

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

Description

This rule checks that each ARIA state or property has a valid value type.

Applicability

This rule applies to any WAI-ARIA state or property that has a non-empty (“”) attribute value , and that is specified on an HTML or SVG element .

Expectation

Each test target has an attribute value that is valid according to its WAI-ARIA value type .

Exception : For value types ID Reference and ID Reference List no ID referenced elements are required.

Background

Using invalid ARIA attribute values is often the result of a typo or other developer error. These attributes are then either ignored, or a default value is assumed by browsers and assistive technologies. This often means that a state or property which should exist is missing or has an unexpected value. If the default value for invalid attribute values happens to match the author’s intention for the value, there will not be an accessibility issue.

This rule does not require the target of an ID Reference to exist. This is because referencing an element that does not exist, and not having the reference at all has the same end result. A common use case for using ID Reference for a non-existing ID is to use a static aria-errormessage on an input element, and to only insert the element with the error message if there is an actual error. There are some cases in which ID references are required. These are tested in a separate rule.

Assumptions

There are no assumptions.

Accessibility Support

Some user agents treat the value of aria-* attribute as case-sensitive (even when these are not ID) while some treat them as case-insensitive.

Related rules
  • ARIA state or property is permitted
  • ARIA required ID references exist

  • DOM Tree
  • CSS Styling

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule e086e5 — Form field has non-empty accessible name

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 1.3.1,4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/e086e5/proposed/

Proposed

Form field has non-empty accessible name

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that each form field element has a non-empty accessible name.

Applicability

This rule applies to any element that is included in the accessibility tree and for which one of the following is true:

  • the element has one of the following semantic roles : checkbox , combobox ( select elements), listbox , menuitemcheckbox , menuitemradio , radio , searchbox , slider , spinbutton , switch , textbox ; or
  • the element is an input with no semantic role and a type attribute value of color , date , datetime-local , file , month , password , time , or week .

Expectation

Each target element has an accessible name that is not empty ( "" ).

Background

The list of roles in the applicability is derived by taking all the roles from WAI-ARIA Specifications that:

  • have semantic roles that inherit from the input , menuitem or select role; and
  • are form field controls (this notably excludes menu , option or tree ).

This rule does not test other control-like roles such as button and menuitem , because these do not inherit from input or select ; these should be tested separately. This rule tests explicitly input types such as date and color because they have no semantic role, but still require an accessible name.

This rule does not map to 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions as there are sufficient techniques within 3.3.2 that don’t need the elements to have an accessible name . For example “ G131: Providing descriptive labels ” AND “ G162: Positioning labels to maximize predictability of relationships ” would be sufficient.

Assumptions

There are no assumptions.

Accessibility Support
  • Several assistive technologies have a functionality to list all form fields on a page, including the disabled ones. Therefore this rule is still applicable to disabled form fields. If an assistive technology consistently ignores disabled form fields in all its interactions, then it is possible to have a disabled form field with no accessible name without creating accessibility issues for the user.
  • Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some elements can have one of the applicable semantic roles and fail this rule with some technology but users of other technologies would not experience any accessibility issue.
Other Resources
  • Understanding Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value
  • H91: Using HTML form controls and links
  • H44: Using label elements to associate text labels with form controls
  • H65: Using the title attribute to identify form controls when the label element cannot be used

Accessibility Requirements Mapping

4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)

  • Learn more about 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
  • Required for conformance to WCAG 2.0 and later on level A and higher.
  • Outcome mapping:
  • Any failed outcomes: success criterion is not satisfied
  • All passed outcomes: success criterion needs further testing
  • An inapplicable outcome: success criterion needs further testing
Secondary Requirements

This rule is related to the following accessibility requirements, but was

not designed to test this requirements directly. These

secondary requirements

can either be stricter than the rule requires, or may be satisfied in ways

not tested by the rule:

  • 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A) : This success criterion is more strict than this rule. This is because 1.3.1 Info and Relationship requires that information, structure, and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined or are available in text, while 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value only requires an accessible name.
  • 2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A) : This success criterion is more strict than this rule. This is because 2.5.3 Label in Name requires that if a label is visible, the accessible name contains the label that is presented visually, while 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value only requires an accessible name.

Input Aspects

The following aspects are required in using this rule.

  • Accessibility Tree
  • CSS styling
  • DOM Tree

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 2t702h — Summary element has non-empty accessible name

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/2t702h/proposed/

Proposed

Summary element has non-empty accessible name

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that each summary element has a non-empty accessible name.

Applicability

This rule applies to HTML summary elements for which all the following are true:

  • the element is included in the accessibility tree ; and
  • the element works as the summary button for its parent details element ; and
  • the element has no explicit role , or the explicit role is ignored due to a presentational role conflict .

Expectation

Each target element has an accessible name that is not empty ( "" ), nor just the name of the ::marker pseudo element.

Background

This rule is only applicable to summary elements that the browser will use as controls for a details element. Even though the HTML specification - The summary element requires the summary element to be the first child of details , this is not required for WCAG. And while this rule is not applicable to summary elements with an explicit role , most of the time these likely do still require an accessible name . This is covered by other rules, such as the Button has non-empty accessible name .

If the summary element is not included in the accessibility tree, but is still included in sequential focus navigation, this can result in accessibility issues not tested by this rule. This is covered under Element with aria-hidden has no content in sequential focus navigation .

Note that some user agents expose the summary element with a button role. This deviates from the implicit ARIA semantics described in ARIA in HTML . Because some browsers do not give summary elements a button role, these elements need to be tested separately from the Button has non-empty accessible name ACT rule.

Assumptions

The rule assumes that all summary elements are user interface components as defined by WCAG 2 .

Accessibility Support

There is a difference in how user agents expose the triangle indicating the control’s expand state. As a result, some user agents include the triangle in the accessible name of the summary element.

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 307n5z — Element with presentational children has no focusable content

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/307n5z/proposed/

Proposed

Element with presentational children has no focusable content

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that elements with a role that makes its children presentational do not contain focusable elements.

Applicability

This rule applies to any HTML or SVG element with a semantic role that defines its children to be presentational children .

Expectation

None of the target elements have descendants in the flat tree that are part of sequential focus navigation .

Background

This rule applies to elements with a semantic role that defines its children to be presentational children , which are all of the following: button , checkbox , img , meter , menuitemcheckbox , menuitemradio , option , progressbar , radio , scrollbar , separator , slider , switch , and tab .

Elements with a semantic role that has presentational children will not have any descendants in the accessibility tree. If any of those descendants are included in sequential focus navigation , this causes the focus to land on an element that has no corresponding node in the accessibility tree . The result is that there is no programmatic name or role available for assistive technologies. There are other problems that can come from presentational children too. These must be tested separately.

Assumptions

This rule assumes that elements that are part of sequential focus navigation do not immediately blur, or move focus to another element. Such elements will fail this rule, but may still satisfy success criterion 4.1.2.

Accessibility Support

Several major browsers ignore the WAI-ARIA requirements on presentational children for most or sometimes all roles, or in presence of focusable content. Since some browsers implement presentational children while others do not, pages failing this rule may only be problematic with some browsers.

This rule is often misunderstood as applying to elements with an explicit role of presentation . In fact, this rule only applies to elements which have been given an implicit role of presentation through the presentational children mechanism. Similarly, this rule does not apply to elements with aria-hidden="true" .

Related rules

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 4b1c6c — Iframe elements with identical accessible names have equivalent purpose proposed

status: proposed

implement: semi-auto

requirements(in-scope): 4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/4b1c6c/proposed/

Proposed

Iframe elements with identical accessible names have equivalent purpose

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that iframe elements with identical accessible names embed the same resource or equivalent resources.

Applicability

This rule applies to any set of any two or more iframe elements which:

  • are in the same web page (HTML) ; and
  • are included in an accessibility tree ; and
  • that have matching accessible names that are not empty ( "" ).

Expectation

The iframe elements in each set of target elements embed the same resource or equivalent resources .

Background

When determining if target elements embed the same resource, resolving the embedded resource includes any redirects that are instant.

Assumptions

This rule assumes that, within the context of the test subject, the description provided by the accessible name of an iframe can only accurately describe one resource (notably, homonyms alone are not used as iframe names). Thus, if two or more iframe elements have the same accessible name but embed different resources, at least one of them does not describe its purpose.

Accessibility Support

This rule assumes that assistive technologies are exposing all iframe elements on the page in the same way no matter which document tree they are in. If an assistive technology requires the user to “enter” an iframe or a shadow tree before exposing its content (notably nested iframe ), then it is possible for two iframe to have identical name but embed different resources without failing Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (if said iframe are in separate documents or shadow trees )

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 6cfa84 — Element with aria-hidden has no content in sequential focus navigation

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 4.1.2,ARIA:

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/6cfa84/proposed/

Proposed

Element with aria-hidden has no content in sequential focus navigation

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that elements with an aria-hidden attribute do not contain elements that are part of the sequential focus navigation and focusable.

Applicability

This rule applies to any element with an aria-hidden attribute value of true .

Expectation

None of the target elements has an inclusive descendant in the flat tree that are focusable and part of the sequential focus navigation .

Background

Using aria-hidden="false" on a descendant of an element with aria-hidden="true" does not expose that element . aria-hidden="true" hides itself and all its content from assistive technologies.

By adding aria-hidden="true" to an element, content authors ensure that assistive technologies will ignore the element. This can be used to hide parts of a web page that are pure decoration , such as icon fonts - that are not meant to be read by assistive technologies.

An element with an aria-hidden attribute set to true that is also part of the sequential focus navigation may cause confusion for users of assistive technologies because the element can be reached via sequential focus navigation , but it should be hidden and not included in the accessibility tree .

The 1 second time span introduced in the exception of the definition of focusable is an arbitrary limit which is not included in WCAG. Given that scripts can manage the focus state of elements, testing the focused state of an element consistently would be impractical without a time limit.

Assumptions

Interacting with the page does not result in changing the aria-hidden attribute value of target elements. An example of such a situation would be when closing a modal dialog makes previously hidden elements that were not focusable or part of the sequential focus navigation become focusable and part of the sequential focus navigation .

Accessibility Support

Some user agents treat the value of aria-hidden attribute as case-sensitive.

This a element is not focusable because it moves focus to the input element whenever it receives focus. These elements

a screen reader. But, they do want the element to be part of the sequential focus navigation . This allows the page author

to detect that focus has left the dialog in order to wrap it to the top/bottom as appropriate.

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule 97a4e1 — Button has non-empty accessible name

status: approved

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/97a4e1/proposed/

Proposed

Button has non-empty accessible name

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that each button element has a non-empty accessible name.

Applicability

This rule applies to elements that are included in the accessibility tree and have a semantic role of button , except for input elements with a type attribute value of image .

Expectation

Each target element has an accessible name that is not empty ( "" ).

Background

This rule considers an exception for “image buttons” (i.e., input elements with a type attribute value of image ). Image buttons failing this rule would fail Success Criterion 4.1.2 and Success Criterion 1.1.1 which is not part of the accessibility requirements for this rule.

Assumptions

The rule assumes that all buttons are user interface components as defined by WCAG 2 .

Some elements have a role of button and a default accessible name defined by the HTML Accessibility API Mapping , for example input elements whose type attribute value is either submit or reset . This rule considers that these default names can be descriptive and therefore does not fail them.

Accessibility Support
  • Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some elements can have a semantic role of button and fail this rule with some technology but users of other technologies would not experience any accessibility issue.

Rule (verbatim)

ACT Rule cae760 — Iframe element has non-empty accessible name proposed

status: proposed

implement: auto,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/cae760/proposed/

Proposed

Iframe element has non-empty accessible name

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that each iframe element has a non-empty accessible name.

Applicability

This rule applies to iframe elements that are included in the accessibility tree except if at least one of the following is true:

  • the iframe has a negative tabindex attribute value ; or
  • the iframe is marked as decorative .

Expectation

Each target element has an accessible name that is not empty ( "" ).

Background

The frame element is deprecated, this rule does not consider frame or frameset elements.

Due to inconsistencies in handling focus on iframe , this rule ignores iframe elements for which there is an attempt to hide them from assistive technologies. Whether iframe elements that are inapplicable to this rule still require an accessible name varies between browsers.

Assumptions

If an iframe is not perceived by the user as a single control, it does not qualify as a user interface component under WCAG 2. In such a scenario, failing this rule would not fail success criterion 4.1.2 . Unless the iframe is both removed from the accessibility tree and removed from sequential focus navigation , they usually are considered to be user interface components .

Accessibility Support
  • Browser and assistive technology support for iframe elements is currently inconsistent . Some examples of inconsistencies include (but are not limited to):
  • There is a known combination of a popular browser and assistive technology that ignores aria-label and only announces title attribute as an accessible name
  • Some assistive technologies ignore empty iframe elements, regardless of if they are focusable or if they have an accessible name.
  • Some browsers instantly redirect focus from iframe elements to the first focusable element inside that iframe. This redirect makes it appear as though the iframe never receives focus. This occurs even if the iframe has a non-negative tabindex attribute value .
  • Not all browsers redirect focus on iframe elements. This ensures that the contents of iframe elements can be scrolled and accessed by using the keyboard. This must not be circumvented by using a negative tabindex, as this will make the iframe completely inaccessible for keyboard navigation.
Other Resources
  • H64: Using the title attribute of the frame and iframe elements
  • Understanding Success Criterion 4.1.2
  • User interface component

ACT Rule m6b1q3 — Menuitem has non-empty accessible name

status: approved

implement: auto,manual,semi-auto,lint

requirements(in-scope): 4.1.2

url: https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/m6b1q3/proposed/

Proposed

Menuitem has non-empty accessible name

Rule Mapping

This is an Atomic rule

to test

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value (Level A)

Description

This rule checks that each element with a menuitem role has a non-empty accessible name.

Applicability

This rule applies to HTML elements that is a semantic menuitem included in the accessibility tree .

Expectation

Each target element has an accessible name that is not empty ( "" ).

Background

Assumptions

This rule assumes that all menuitems are user interface components as defined by WCAG 2 . If an element has a role of menuitem that would not be perceived as a single control by users, 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value would not apply and so failing this rule would not result in a conformance issue.

Accessibility Support

Implementation of Presentational Roles Conflict Resolution varies from one browser or assistive technology to another. Depending on this, some semantic menuitem elements can fail this rule with some technology but users of other technologies would not experience any accessibility issue.

Semantic Structure and Reading Order (cat_2)

Trusted Tester — SC 4.1.2

SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A) — TT Tests 12.C, 12.D, 2.D (+ covered within 5.C, 6.A, 7.A–7.D)

TT sections: 12. Page Titles, Frames, and iFrames; 2. Auto-Updating Content · Baselines: 19/21/10/14/6

WCAG SC 4.1.2: For all user interface components (including but not limited to: form elements, links, and

components generated by scripts), the name and role can be programmatically determined; states, properties, and

values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items

is available to user agents, including assistive technologies.

4.1.2 is not a single standalone TT test; it is woven through several:

  • Form elements: name/role/value tested within 5.C (1.3.1-programmatic-label) — see

sc-1.3.1-info-and-relationships.md.

  • Links: name/role tested within 6.A (2.4.4-link-purpose) — see sc-2.4.4-link-purpose.md.
  • Images: name/role tested within 7.A–7.D — see sc-1.1.1-non-text-content.md.
  • Frames / iFrames: dedicated tests 12.C / 12.D (below).
  • Notification of automatic changes: dedicated test 2.D (below).

> Removed/obsolete in v5.1.3: 5.E 4.1.2-change-notify-form and 6.B 4.1.2-change-notify-links were

> removed (no longer required as of the Section 508 ICT Testing Baseline for Web v3.1, April 2024). Changes

> resulting from user interaction with forms are folded into 5.D (3.2.2 on-input, out of our scope); changes

> from automatic updates remain in 2.D.

---

Test 12.C — 4.1.2-frame-title (Frames)

Test Condition: *Each <frame> has a title attribute that describes its content.*

DNA if no Frames are identified.

How to Test

1. Launch ANDI. If a Frame is used, ANDI provides a notification that Frames have been detected. Select "Cancel"

to test an individual Frame.

2. ANDI lists each Frame and, if available, the associated title attribute. If there is no title attribute,

ANDI reveals an "alert."

3. Select each link to access each frame. Review the Frame to understand its content. Navigate back to the page

being tested and launch ANDI again.

4. In ANDI, review each frame's corresponding title attribute for a meaningful description of content.

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. All frames have a title attribute that describes its content.

Notes
  • <frame> is obsolete in HTML5, but testers may still encounter it; it can and should still be accessible.
  • Frame content must be tested for conformance with all other applicable tests (12.A/12.B do not apply to frame

content).

---

Test 12.D — 4.1.2-iframe-name (iFrames)

Test Condition: *The combination of accessible name and description for each <iframe> describes its content.*

DNA if no iframes are identified or the iframes are explicitly excluded from the tab order (negative

tabindex).

Identify Content

Use ANDI: iframes to identify all iframes in the tab order.

1. Launch ANDI: iframes to navigate to and highlight iframes on the page. (No iframes module → no iframes.)

2. Use "Next Element" to find iframes that have a non-negative tabindex (0, 1) or no tabindex shown.

Test only these <iframes>. *(Negative tabindex like -1 = explicitly excluded; do not test.)*

How to Test

1. Launch ANDI: iframes.

2. Review the ANDI Output for each iframe with a non-negative tabindex (or where tabindex is not defined) to

determine whether the accessible name and description accurately describe the content of each <iframe>.

Evaluate Results (PASS if)

1. The ANDI Output for each <iframe> in the tab order sufficiently describes its content.

Note
  • All iframe content must be tested for conformance with all other applicable tests (12.A/12.B do not apply).

---

Test 2.D — 4.1.2-change-notify-auto (Auto-Updating Content)

Test Condition: *The page provides notification of each automatic update/change in content.*

DNA if the page content does not update or change automatically.

Identify Content

Identify content that changes automatically on the page as part of auto-update.

How to Test

1. Identify how the user is notified of the change in content:

  • a. Identify any dialogs that alert the user to changes; determine whether they provide sufficient

programmatic notification of content changes.

  • b. Identify content changes that result in focus moving to the changed content; determine whether

moving focus is sufficient to notify the user (e.g., by describing the change directly in the content the

focus moved to).

  • c. Identify content changes occurring in an ARIA Live Region:
  • i. Launch ANDI: structures.
  • ii. Click "live regions," then hover over any identified live region (or use ANDI's previous/next element

buttons to navigate to identified Live Regions).

  • iii. Determine whether the changing content is contained within the Live Region.
Evaluate Results (PASS if ANY true)

1. The page notifies the user about a change via a keyboard-accessible dialog, OR

2. The page moves focus to the changed content, AND the changed content provides sufficient description about the

change, OR

3. The content that has changed is contained in an ARIA Live Region.

Note
  • This is a test for notification of automatic changes. Testing the content before/after the change is done

in other tests. Changes due to user interaction are tested elsewhere (e.g., form elements that change in

response to user selections → Test 5.D, 3.2.2 on-input).

> Note on overlap with our 4.1.3 lane: 2.D's live-region path is essentially the WCAG 2.0-era home for what

> WCAG 2.1 split out as 4.1.3 Status Messages. TT (WCAG 2.0) has no 4.1.3; the closest manual anchor for our

> status-message instrument is this 2.D live-region procedure (dialog / focus-move / live-region trichotomy).

Act-augmented aspect — Accessible name does not contain the visible label text (F111 / label-in-name overlap, 4.1.2 limb)

A control's spoken name leaves out the words printed on it, so a voice-control user who says the visible label can't activate the control.

A control has BOTH a visible text label AND a non-empty accessible name, but the accessible name omits, contradicts, or wholly replaces the words a sighted user reads on the control. Every ACT 4.1.2 name rule (97a4e1 Button, e086e5 Form field, c487ae Link, 59796f Image button, m6b1q3 Menuitem, 2t702h Summary) terminates the instant accName !== ""; none compare the computed name STRING against the rendered visible label STRING. F111 maps explicitly to 4.1.2 (its title is 'Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.5.3, and 4.1.2 due to a control with visible label text but no accessible name') and demands the third check the rules never perform: the accessible name must CONTAIN the visible label, or speech-input users cannot speak what they see to activate the control. Detection requires rendering the page, reading the visible label off the pixels, computing the accessible name, and judging textual overlap — pure visual+semantic comparison, not present in the corpus where any non-empty name is a uniform PASS.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The six non-empty-name ACT rules stop at accName !== ""; none of 4.1.2's mapped rules compare the accessible-name string against the rendered visible label string. The corpus contains no fixture where a present visible label and a present-but-divergent accessible name coexist, so a non-empty-but-mismatched name is always a PASS. The string-comparison only lives in 2.5.3 (not in this SC's rule set), and no fully-automated checker reliably extracts the 'visible label' from pixels to compare it, so this needs human visual judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.2 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Accessible name is present but uninformative / does not communicate the control's purpose (ARIA14 name-quality)

A button has a screen-reader name like 'button' or an icon filename, so the user hears something but still has no idea what the control does.

A user-interface control has a non-empty, machine-valid accessible name, but the name does not identify what the control DOES — it is placeholder text, an asset filename, a developer string, or a generic token duplicated across distinct controls. Every ACT 4.1.2 name rule is scoped to non-emptiness only and explicitly does not assess descriptiveness, so a name like 'button', 'icon_search_24px.svg', 'TODO label', or five identical 'star' labels passes uniformly. ARIA14 sets the actual bar: 'users with assistive technologies rely on accessible names that clearly communicate the purpose of components,' and the Understanding doc requires controls to 'provide important and appropriate information to assistive technologies.' Judging adequacy requires inferring the control's function from its icon, position, and behavior, then deciding whether the name conveys that function — semantic judgment no non-emptiness scan performs. (This is distinct from F111: here there may be no visible text label at all; the name is simply meaningless, not mismatched against a visible label.)

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT 4.1.2 name rules check non-emptiness only and per the inventory do NOT assess name quality, descriptiveness, or uniqueness; the synthetic fixtures use either one clean correct name or a degenerate empty/default name, never a non-empty-but-useless name (which by rule definition PASSES). Whether a present name actually communicates purpose depends on the control's visual/behavioral identity, which a fully-automated checker cannot reliably infer — it requires human semantic judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.2 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Role is syntactically valid but is the wrong role for the control's appearance/behavior (F15/F59 semantic variant)

A toggle switch is coded as a checkbox (or a heading, link, etc.), so the screen reader announces the wrong kind of control and the user misjudges how to use it.

An interactive element carries a role that is a real ARIA token (so 674b10 'Role attribute has valid value' passes) and whose required states are present (so 4e8ab6 passes), but the role is WRONG for what the element actually is and does. A sliding toggle switch coded role="checkbox", a control that depresses and fires an in-page action coded role="link", an operable disclosure header marked role="heading", a clickable star coded role="img". F59's literal failure is a div/span with NO role (axe-core flags clickable-with-no-role); the genuinely uncovered, automation-resistant case is a VALID but inappropriate role. Deciding the role is wrong requires seeing the rendered widget, reasoning about its affordance and behavior, and comparing that to the announced role — visual+behavioral judgment, not a token-validity check. The Understanding doc anchors this: when elements 'are programmed... to have a different role and/or function than usual, then additional measures need to be taken.'

Why ACT rules can't reach it: 674b10 only checks the role VALUE is a real ARIA token and 4e8ab6 only checks the declared role has its required states present; neither checks the declared role MATCHES the element's visual/behavioral identity. The corpus's role fixtures cover invalid tokens and missing required states, never a valid-but-inappropriate role. A fully-automated checker cannot determine the 'correct' role from rendered appearance and behavior — that is human judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.2 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Exposed ARIA state/value is present and valid but contradicts the rendered control state (value correctness, not presence)

A toggle looks ON but is still coded as 'off' (aria-checked false), so the screen reader tells the user the opposite of what's actually showing on screen.

A custom control exposes a state/value (aria-checked, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-pressed, aria-valuenow) that is a permitted, syntactically-valid value (so 4e8ab6, 5c01ea, 6a7281 all pass) but that does not match the control's CURRENT visible state: a toggle rendered ON with aria-checked="false", an accordion visibly expanded with aria-expanded="false", a highlighted active tab while aria-selected stays on the first tab, a slider thumb at max with aria-valuenow="0". SC 4.1.2 requires that states/values 'can be programmatically set' AND that 'notification of changes... is available'; a stale value silently lies to AT. Catching it requires rendering the widget, reading its true visual state, and comparing against the exposed attribute — a visual comparison the static-string ACT rules structurally cannot perform.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT state rules (4e8ab6, 5c01ea, 6a7281, 5f99a7) check presence, permittedness, and value-validity — all static-string checks. None compare the state value against the actual rendered/interactive state of the widget. The corpus has no fixture where a syntactically perfect aria-checked/aria-expanded/aria-valuenow disagrees with the visual state, because asserting that disagreement requires rendering and visual judgment a fully-automated checker cannot supply.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.2 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Accessible name/text alternative on a dynamic named component goes stale after the content changes (F20, temporal correctness)

A button's content changes by script, but its screen-reader name stays frozen on the old content, so the user is told about something that's no longer there.

A named or interactive component whose visual content is swapped by script (a status-icon button, a favorite/star toggle, a refreshable image control, a rotating banner acting as a named region) keeps its accessible name/alt frozen on the OLD content. F20 is explicit: 'the non-text content is updated, but the text alternative is not updated at the same time.' The name was once correct and is non-empty, so every presence rule passes when sampled once; after the state change it describes a different thing than what is rendered. Catching it requires triggering the change on the page, then comparing the NEW visual to the UNCHANGED name — a temporal + visual judgment no one-shot static scan performs. Scope this to named/interactive components (the 4.1.2 limb) rather than purely decorative images (that angle is 1.1.1).

Why ACT rules can't reach it: All ACT 4.1.2 fixtures are static single-state snapshots; none mutate component content via script and re-check the name afterward. The non-emptiness rules sample the name once and pass. There is no temporal/diff dimension in the corpus, and F20's failure is fundamentally name-correct-then-stale, which a one-shot automated scan cannot represent — it needs interaction plus before/after visual judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.2 · Trusted Tester 2.D · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — User-settable state/value cannot be programmatically set via AT or its change is not notified (F15, the 'can be set / notification of changes' limb)

A custom slider or switch only updates its value for mouse users, so a keyboard or screen-reader user can't change it or never hears that it changed.

SC 4.1.2 requires that states/values 'that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available' to AT. A custom control can expose a valid role and a valid initial value (so 674b10/4e8ab6/6a7281 pass) yet be uncontrollable or non-reactive for AT: a slider widget that updates aria-valuenow only on mouse drag and never on keyboard/AT activation, a custom switch whose aria-checked never flips when toggled via the accessibility tree, an expander whose aria-expanded never updates when programmatically activated. F15 covers custom controls that 'do so incompletely' — exposing some semantics statically but failing the set/notify contract. Detecting this requires operating the control through the keyboard/AT path and observing whether the exposed value actually changes — interactive behavioral judgment, not a static attribute scan. (Distinct from the stale-value aspect: there the initial value is simply wrong; here the value is initially correct but cannot be changed or its change is never propagated.)

Why ACT rules can't reach it: All ACT 4.1.2 state/value rules inspect static attribute presence/validity at a single snapshot; none operate the control through the keyboard or accessibility API to verify the value can actually be changed and that the change is reflected/notified. The corpus has no interactive set-and-observe fixture, and a fully-automated checker cannot determine settability/notification without driving the control's interaction and observing AT-visible updates.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.2 · Trusted Tester 2.D · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Iframe has a non-empty accessible name that does not describe its actual content (TT 12.D)

An embedded frame has a vague title like 'iframe' or 'content', so a screen-reader user jumping between frames can't tell what each one actually contains.

An <iframe> has a non-empty title / aria-label (so cae760 'Iframe element has non-empty accessible name' passes), but that name does not describe what the frame actually contains — a payment widget iframe titled 'iframe', an embedded map titled 'content', a video-player frame titled 'frame1', or two distinct frames sharing a generic name. Trusted Tester 12.D's pass condition is that 'the combination of accessible name and description for each <iframe> describes its content' — the tester must look INSIDE the frame and judge whether the name matches. The only iframe rule that goes beyond non-emptiness, 4b1c6c (same-name-must-have-equivalent-purpose), is flagged notFullyAutomatable and covers only the narrow duplicate-name case; nothing covers a single non-empty-but-undescriptive frame name. Judging adequacy requires rendering the frame's content and comparing it to the name — human content judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: cae760 checks iframe-name non-emptiness only; 4b1c6c is notFullyAutomatable and only checks that iframes sharing an identical name have equivalent purpose — neither evaluates whether a single frame's name describes its content. TT 12.D requires looking inside the frame to judge descriptiveness, which a fully-automated checker cannot do; the corpus has no fixture pairing a generic iframe name against meaningfully different embedded content.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.2 · Trusted Tester 12.D · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Each part of a multi-part field has a present but ambiguous/undifferentiated sub-name (F86 semantic variant)

A phone or date split into several inputs labels every box the same ('Phone', 'Phone', 'Phone'), so a screen-reader user can't tell which box is which part.

A compound field (US phone as 3 inputs, date as day/month/year, credit card in 4 groups, time as hour/minute/AM-PM) gives EACH sub-input a non-empty accessible name (so e086e5 passes on every part) — but the per-part names fail to convey each part's role within the whole: all three phone parts named 'Phone', a date's three fields all named 'Date', or area-code and prefix both named 'Number'. F86's intent is that without correctly differentiated per-part names users experience 'undefined text fields'; the automation-resistant case is when names exist but are interchangeable/unhelpful. Deciding the sub-names are inadequate requires understanding the compound semantics and the visual grouping (the punctuation/layout that signals 'this is area code, this is prefix') — semantic judgment the per-field non-emptiness rule cannot express.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: e086e5 fires only when a sub-field's accName is empty; it cannot judge whether three present names ('Phone','Phone','Phone') collectively fail to identify area/prefix/suffix. F86's requirement is a multi-part SEMANTIC one (each part named for ITS role in the whole) that a per-field non-emptiness check structurally cannot express, and the corpus has no grouped multi-part fixture with present-but-undifferentiated sub-names. A fully-automated checker cannot infer the intended per-part roles from layout.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.2 · priority medium

Reflow and Content on Hover/Focus (cat_8)

Act-augmented aspect — Live-region politeness is semantically wrong for the message's urgency and update frequency

A live region announces with the wrong urgency, so either a trivial ticking counter rudely interrupts the screen reader constantly, or a critical warning gets queued and arrives too late.

The status message IS in a working, present live region and IS announced, so every automated tool and every seed (which all model the crude 'no live region at all' failure) passes it. The defect is that the chosen politeness is semantically wrong for what the message MEANS and how often it fires. Two opposite failure shapes: (a) a low-value, high-frequency message (a ticking stock/crypto price, a per-keystroke 'N results' count, a 'last saved 3s ago' autosave heartbeat, a 'people viewing this item: 14' badge) is wired role=alert / aria-live=assertive, so it rudely interrupts and clobbers whatever the screen reader was reading every few seconds, making the app intolerably 'chatty'; (b) conversely a genuinely time-critical / blocking message (session-expiry countdown, 'payment declined — do not navigate away', a security warning) is wired only aria-live=polite, so it is queued behind ongoing speech and the user acts before hearing it. Both politeness values are syntactically valid, so there is no markup error; judging the right priority requires understanding what the message means to the user and its cadence — a contextual call no checker can make from static markup.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT corpus is completely empty (actRuleCount:0, testCaseCount:0). All 25 seeds model only the binary 'message not in a live region -> silent' failure; none models a message that IS announced but at the WRONG priority. Automated tools (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse) cannot flag it because polite and assertive are both valid attribute values — correctness depends on the human meaning and update frequency of the message, which a static or single-snapshot scan has no way to weigh.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.3 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Partial update without aria-atomic announces only the changed fragment, losing meaning

Only the changed value is announced without its surrounding label, so the screen reader says a bare 'three' instead of 'three items in cart' and the meaning is lost.

A persistent status region is correctly marked (role=status / aria-live=polite) and DOES announce on change — passing every tool and every seed. But only an inner sub-node holding the volatile value is updated, and the region is not atomic, so the screen reader speaks just the bare changed token in isolation: 'three' instead of 'three items in cart', 'red' instead of 'filtered to red, 24 products', '2' instead of '2 errors on this page', '85' instead of '85 percent complete'. The visible string is perfectly meaningful because the sighted user sees the surrounding static label; the announced fragment is meaningless because the static context was not re-read. Catching this requires judging whether the spoken fragment alone conveys the same information as the visible whole — a semantic equivalence judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT case exists, and the seeds only cover regions that announce nothing at all — none covers a region that announces the wrong (truncated) thing. Automated tools cannot detect it: aria-atomic defaults differ by role and by AT, the page has valid markup with a present live region, and whether the announced fragment is intelligible on its own depends entirely on the human meaning of the surrounding (un-announced) label. There is no rule for 'announced text is grammatically/semantically incomplete'.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.3 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Role/aria-live added together with (or after) the content, instead of pre-existing empty

The live region is created at the same instant its message is, but screen readers only announce changes to regions that already existed, so the message is never spoken.

The FINAL DOM looks perfect: there is a <div role="status" aria-live="polite"> containing the message, with valid markup. A static scan and the seeds (which key on absence of role/aria-live) both pass it. But the region — or its role/aria-live attribute — was created/attached at the same moment the message text was injected, rather than existing as an empty container at page load. Most screen readers only announce mutations to live regions that were already present and registered, so a region born with its content never fires. F103 calls out this timing limb explicitly; ARIA19 requires the empty container at page load; ARIA22's test step 1 requires the role to be present BEFORE the message occurs. Confirming it requires reasoning about the ORDER of DOM operations (and ideally observing AT behavior), not the resting markup.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Empty ACT corpus; the seeds detect the static absence of a live region, so a page whose final DOM HAS a correct live region sails through — yet it can still fail because the region was injected with its content. Automated single-snapshot tools see only the end state (a valid live region with text) and have no signal that the container was not present-and-empty at load; the failure is purely temporal/behavioral.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.3 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Announced text lacks the visual context that makes it meaningful (no offscreen text for AT)

The visible text only makes sense from its on-screen position (a lone '3' beside a cart icon), and no hidden context is added, so a screen-reader user just hears an orphaned '3'.

The status is announced cleanly and the whole atomic string is read — so tools and seeds pass. The failure is that the VISIBLE text relies on spatial/visual proximity for meaning, and no offscreen/extra text was added to the live region to supply that context to a non-sighted user. The Understanding's canonical example: a bare '3' appears next to a shopping-cart icon — sighted users understand 'cart: 3', AT users hear an orphaned '3'. Likewise a green checkmark + 'Done' next to a specific row, or 'Saved' with no album name where the visible popup sits over the 'Wedding' album. The remediation (add offscreen 'in shopping cart' / the album name, or place the icon's alt text inside the atomic region) is exactly the human judgment the SC's 'Non-displayed text specific to AT users' section calls for, and it cannot be derived from markup.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Empty ACT corpus; the seeds only test missing/silent live regions, never a present-and-announcing region whose announced content is contextually impoverished. Automated tools cannot judge that '3' is insufficient without 'items in cart' — the text is non-empty, the region is valid, and inferring that the VISUAL layout supplied context the AT string lacks requires reasoning about meaning and spatial relationship, not parsing the DOM.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.3 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Removal/absence of status text conveys meaning, but nothing is announced when it disappears

A 'Loading…' message is announced when it appears, but its disappearance (which signals 'done' to sighted users) is silent, so a screen-reader user never learns it finished.

A 'Loading…' / 'Busy' / 'Processing payment…' message is correctly placed in a live region and IS announced when it appears — so it passes the appearance-only test. The failure is on the OTHER edge: for sighted users the DISAPPEARANCE of that message signals 'now done / available', but for AT users the silent removal conveys nothing, and no replacement 'system available' / 'results ready' message is announced. The SC explicitly flags that absence can itself be status. Detecting this requires reasoning that the END of the waiting state is itself information the user needs — a temporal/semantic inference, not a markup check; tools never even observe the removal, let alone judge that it carried meaning.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: No ACT case; the seeds model only the additive direction ('message appears but isn't announced'). The removal-conveys-status case is entirely absent. Automated tools cannot catch it: removing a node from a polite region produces no announcement by design, the DOM after removal is clean, and inferring that 'busy text vanished, therefore the author owed a non-visible system-available message' demands understanding the workflow's meaning over time.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.3 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Non-textual status (icon/sound) given a status role but no usable text alternative

A status shown only by an icon or chime is placed in a live region but has no text alternative, so the region fires yet the screen reader announces nothing meaningful.

A status is conveyed purely by a non-text change — a spinner->checkmark icon swap, a red 'x' badge, a color/shape change, or an audio chime — and the author DID wrap it in a live region (role=status/alert), so the absence-of-role checkers and the seeds pass. The failure is that the icon carries empty/decorative/absent alt (alt='', aria-hidden, a CSS background image with no text, an SVG with no accessible name) or the sound has no visual+text equivalent, so the live region fires but announces nothing, or announces a filename, or announces a meaningless symbol. The SC routes this through 1.1.1: the role surfaces the change, but only a correct text alternative makes the change intelligible. Deciding that the icon IS a status indicator (not decoration) and that its alt misrepresents/omits the state is a semantic + visual judgment a checker cannot make — the markup is valid and a missing-alt linter cannot tell that this particular swap conveys status.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Empty ACT corpus; the seeds model only missing/silent live regions on textual messages, never a present live region whose status is carried by a non-text change with a missing/empty/wrong text alternative. Automated alt-text checkers cannot tell that a specific icon swap conveys status (vs. decoration), and a present role=status region with an alt='' icon is structurally valid; recognizing the state change is meaningful and the alternative fails to convey it requires visual + semantic reasoning.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.3 · priority medium

Act-augmented aspect — Mis-scoping the status-message boundary: change-of-context exceptions vs. genuine in-scope status

Either real status text ('No results found') is left unannounced, or trivial changes are wrongly forced into urgent announcements, because someone misjudged what truly counts as a status update.

This aspect tests the threshold judgment that precedes every other limb: does the dynamic change even MEET the definition of a status message (success/result, waiting, progress, or error AND not delivered via a change of context)? Two failure directions, both requiring semantic judgment: (a) FALSE POSITIVE pressure — content that the Understanding explicitly EXCEPTS is treated as needing a live region or, worse, is force-fed into role=alert and over-announces: an error shown in a focus-taking dialog (already a change of context, governed elsewhere), expand/collapse of a menu/accordion/tab (governed by 4.1.2), or new survey questions added after a response (not a status by definition); and (b) FALSE NEGATIVE pressure — a genuine status (e.g. 'No results returned', 'Your form was successfully submitted') is left out of any live region because the author wrongly decided it was 'just content' like the search results list. The distinction between 'no status message present (N/A)' and 'status message present but not programmatically determinable (fail)' is itself uncovered. Tools cannot make this call: it is about whether the message MEANS success/waiting/progress/error and whether focus moved — pure human interpretation.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Empty ACT corpus has nothing distinguishing 'no status message present (N/A)' from 'status message present but not programmatically determinable (fail)', and nothing modeling the three excepted change-of-context cases. The seeds only assume a status message exists and check for a live region. Automated tools cannot determine whether a content change meets the status-message definition (success/waiting/progress/error AND no change of context) or falls under an exception — that classification is the human judgment the whole SC pivots on.

Associates with: guideline SC 4.1.3 · priority medium

EN 301 549 — C.9.2.4.10 (SC 2.4.10)

EN clause C.9.2.4.10 is a pass-through to WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.10 (Conformance Requirements clause 9.6). Conformance-scope is checked separately — see the EN-scope section.

Act-augmented aspect — A genuine content section in a multi-section page has no heading while sibling sections are headed

A page split into topical sections gives most of them real headings, but one substantial section is left un-headed, so a screen-reader user can't find or label it.

The heart of 2.4.10 is providing a heading for EACH section when a page is organized into sections, not merely 'the document has a heading somewhere.' The realistic violation is a page divided into several topical content sections where most carry headings but one substantive, topically-distinct section is left un-headed (e.g. a headed 'Abstract', 'Introduction', 'Results', 'Discussion' with a 500-word 'Methods' block of new subject matter wedged between two headed sections carrying only a bold first sentence and no heading). Recognizing that the un-headed prose is a distinct section that 'introduces' new subject matter — and therefore needs its own heading — requires reading the body and topically segmenting it, which is semantic human judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Every ACT failure (7505d/81d501/929079/4e34ca) removes or hides the ONE heading of the ONE non-repeated #main block, so the corpus encodes only the binary 'document has a heading at all.' There is NO case with 3+ sibling content sections where one mid-document section is missing its heading while others are headed, so the actual 'heading for EACH section' obligation is untested. Automated checkers (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse) cannot detect this: the page contains valid headings and valid HTML; deciding that a particular un-headed prose block is a separate section needing its own heading requires reading and topically segmenting the content.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.10 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Visually-demarcated sections (cards, columns, bands, rules, big gaps) with no programmatic heading for each

Sections are shown only through visual styling like cards, columns, colour bands or whitespace, with no heading markup, so a screen-reader user perceives one undifferentiated blob.

The Understanding explicitly warns that 'visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections,' yet a very common pattern lays a page out as visually obvious sections — boxed cards, color-banded rows, multi-column blocks, large whitespace gaps, horizontal rules, or tab panels — where each visual block is plainly a distinct section to a sighted user but NONE carries a programmatic heading. The page may have a single page-level h1 (so 047fe0's non-repeated-block check passes) while the several visually-demarcated content sections beneath it use only styled bold leading text, a CSS border, or color to signal a new section. A human must perceive that the layout communicates multiple sections to sighted users and confirm those sections lack the headings that would convey the same structure to AT users.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: ACT exercises the 'visual not sufficient' limb only inside the single-heading template: 7505d (one big bold strong = visual-only, FAIL) and 33fcbd (one <hr> alongside one real heading, PASS). It never builds a multi-section page where visual layout alone (cards/columns/bands/gaps/tabs) implies several sections without a programmatic heading for each. Automated tools cannot infer from CSS layout, whitespace, borders, or background color that a sighted user perceives several headed-looking sections — perceiving a visual section boundary and judging that it lacks a programmatic heading is inherently a visual + semantic human judgment.

Associates with: guideline SC 2.4.10 · priority high

Act-augmented aspect — Heading element present but its text does not name/introduce its section (wrong, copy-pasted, placeholder, or generic)

A section's heading text is wrong, copy-pasted, or a vague placeholder like 'More', so it doesn't actually name the section and gives a screen-reader user no orientation.

The SC requires headings that 'introduce' their sections and 'clearly indicate the organization of the content' and let users 'know the purpose of each section' — a heading must actually NAME the section it sits above. A page can satisfy the binary presence test while a heading's text is functionally wrong: it describes a DIFFERENT section, was copy-pasted from a template and never updated ('Section Heading', 'Lorem Ipsum'), names the wrong topic (an h2 'Shipping Information' actually heading the returns policy), or is a content-free generic placeholder ('More', 'Stuff', 'Other', 'Untitled') that gives a screen-reader user no orientation. Judging whether a heading's text fits the section body it introduces requires reading both — pure semantic human judgment.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Every heading in the ACT corpus carries text that genuinely matches its block ('Three Heroes Swear Brotherhood...', 'Content' for nav). No case has a heading whose text is mismatched to, copied across, or generic for its section. Automated tools only verify a heading element exists and is non-empty and exposed; they have no model of a section's meaning and cannot tell that 'Shipping Information' is the wrong name for a returns-policy block, or that 'Section Heading' is a leftover placeholder. Heading-to-content fit is inherently semantic and beyond axe/WAVE/Lighthouse.

Act-augmented aspect — Multiple distinct navigation/landmark regions, none demarcated by a heading (H69 nav demarcation sub-limb)

A page has several distinct navigation areas (top nav, sidebar, footer links) but none has a heading, so a screen-reader user can't tell them apart when jumping by heading.

H69 calls for heading markup 'to demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation.' Real pages frequently carry several distinct navigation regions — a primary top nav, a secondary/left sidebar nav, in-page section nav, and a footer link nav — yet provide a heading for none of them, so a screen-reader user navigating by heading cannot distinguish 'main navigation' from 'footer navigation' from 'related links.' A human must recognize that the page contains several functionally distinct navigation/grouping regions and judge that each needs a section heading to be told apart by AT.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The corpus contains only a single <nav> block (its heading text is 'Content'); there is no footer nav, no secondary/left nav, and no page with multiple navigation regions each requiring its own heading. Automated tools detect landmark roles but cannot judge that two functionally distinct navigation regions are genuinely separate sections that each warrant a distinguishing section heading — that is a semantic/structural judgment about the page's organization. (Visually-identical link lists may be different navigation purposes; only meaning distinguishes them.)

Act-augmented aspect — Heading levels contradict the true content hierarchy (a subsection marked as a sibling, or peers given different levels)

Heading levels don't match the real content hierarchy, so a sub-topic reads as a sibling or two equal sections read as parent-and-child, confusing how a screen-reader user understands structure.

H69 and G141 require headings 'properly nested' so the level structure conveys the logical hierarchy: a subsection should be one level below its parent, and the level numbers should match the topical containment relationships. A page can pass presence and even level-consistency checks while its heading LEVELS misdescribe the actual nesting — e.g. a sub-topic that is logically inside a chapter is marked h2 (sibling of the chapter) instead of h3, or two co-equal major sections are marked h2 and h3 so the second falsely reads as a subsection of the first. Whether a given block is conceptually a subsection of the one above it (and so demands a deeper level) is a content-meaning judgment, NOT the syntactic numeric-skip check that tools perform.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The corpus has exactly one nested case (9b25d8: h1 page title + h2 section) and that nesting is correct; there is NO case where the level assignment contradicts the content's true hierarchy. Crucially, axe-core/Lighthouse flag only empty headings or a RAW NUMERIC skip (e.g. h1 then h4) — they cannot tell whether a block is SEMANTICALLY a subsection of the preceding one, so an h2 that should be h3 (or peers arbitrarily given h2/h3) over level-consistent-looking markup passes automation. Deciding the correct level requires understanding the topical containment between sections. NOTE: scope test pages to the semantic-mismatch case (avoid bare numeric h1->h4 skips, which automation already catches).

Act-augmented aspect — Heading element present and exposed but conveying no section name (whitespace-only, decorative-image-only, CSS-image, or dingbat-only)

A heading element exists but holds only whitespace, a decorative image, or ornamental glyphs, so a screen-reader user hears 'heading' with no name and gains no orientation.

A heading can satisfy the structural presence requirement — an h2 or role=heading element exists, is visible, and is exposed to AT — yet carry no meaningful accessible name for its section: it holds only whitespace / a non-breaking space, only a decorative <img alt=''>, only a CSS background-image of the title text with empty real text, or only ornamental glyphs/dingbats. The screen-reader user hears 'heading, level 2' with no label and gains no orientation; the 'mental handle' the SC promises is absent. Whether the rendered heading actually names the section (versus being functionally empty) is something a human reading the page must judge.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: Every ACT heading carries meaningful text. The corpus tests a fully ABSENT heading (4e34ca) and HIDDEN headings (81d501 off-screen, 929079 aria-hidden), but never a heading element that is PRESENT-and-exposed-but-nameless — a distinct failure mode. While a strictly empty <h2></h2> is flagged by axe-core, the human-judgment variants are NOT: an h2 holding only a non-breaking space, only a decorative <img alt=''>, only a CSS background-image with empty real text (image-of-text-as-heading without a text alternative — F2/H69 sub-limb), or only dingbat glyphs all look like 'a heading exists' to a tool but provide no section name. Scope test pages to these non-empty-but-meaningless variants, not bare <h2></h2>.

Act-augmented aspect — Genuinely unsectioned prose (letter / pre-existing document / continuous narrative) correctly NOT requiring headings

A page is genuinely one continuous document like a letter or narrative with no real sections, so it correctly needs no section headings and should not be flagged as a failure.

2.4.10 is Level AAA precisely because 'it cannot be applied to all types of content and it may not always be possible to insert headings' — posting a pre-existing document whose author included no headings, or a long letter covering several topics where 'putting headings into a letter would be very strange.' Correctly judging that such a page is NOT in scope (the content is genuinely a single flowing document, not 'organized into sections') versus a page that IS sectioned and merely lacks headings requires reading the prose and deciding whether it has the topical structure the SC targets. This is a content-genre judgment and a false-positive guard: the verdict should be PASS / not-applicable, not a violation.

Why ACT rules can't reach it: The corpus models inapplicability with one degenerate artefact (ecc29b: a bare SVG with only a <title>, no HTML document) and one single-paragraph stub (4f112d). Neither models the realistic AAA inapplicability scenario: a multi-paragraph, multi-topic but legitimately heading-less prose document (letter / pre-existing reproduction / continuous narrative) that a human must recognize as out of scope. Automation cannot make this call — it cannot distinguish 'a long letter that legitimately has no headings' from 'a sectioned page missing its headings'; both are just paragraphs with no heading elements. The distinction is entirely about content genre and authorial intent, so this also guards against false-positive flagging.

EN 301 549 — conformance-scope gaps

C.9.6.2 — Full pages
Requires: conformance cannot be achieved if part of a web page is excluded
⚠ The collector caps at ~80 elements; elements past the cap are invisible. Disclosed, but not full-page.
C.9.6.5 — Non-interference
Requires: 1.4.2 (audio control) and 2.3.1 (three flashes) must hold for the whole page
⚠ No lane verifies 1.4.2 or 2.3.1; 2.2.2 is rubric-only. 2.1.2 is covered.
C.9.7 — User preferences
Requires: must not block user-agent presentation modes, nor override platform accessibility settings
⚠ No lane checks prefers-reduced-motion override, forced-colors, or zoom blocking.
C.9.6.3 — Complete processes
Requires: all web pages in a process must conform
⚠ Single-page evaluation; multi-step process conformance is out of scope.
